While girls had severely limited access to schooling in 2001, nearly 1 million were enrolled in secondary education by 2021, according to UNESCO.

Five years later, an estimated 2.4 million girls are excluded from secondary education.

"Five years is not a temporary interruption in a child's education," Hoda Jaberian, UNESCO's program coordinator for education in emergencies, said during a video news conference Tuesday, according to The AP. "It is clearly almost an entire secondary school cycle."

UNESCO warned that denying education to girls while restricting women's ability to work could deepen Afghanistan's already severe economic problems.

Nearly half of Afghanistan's population lives below the poverty line, according to UNESCO, which said preventing women from studying and working further limits their ability to support their families and contribute to the country's economy.

The agency also warned that excluding girls from school can damage their mental and physical well-being and increase the risk of early marriage.

The effects could also reach Afghan boys.

UNESCO said the Taliban's ban on female teachers teaching boys is worsening teacher shortages and undermining the quality of education across Afghanistan.

TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN

Women wear burqas in Kabul, Afghanistan on May 7, 2022. (Sayed Khodaiberdi Sadat/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)

With formal secondary and higher education closed to women and girls, UNESCO says it has turned to community-based education, literacy and skills development programs and psychosocial support to keep them learning.

Nearly 70,000 people have participated in UNESCO's programs, with women accounting for 73% of the learners, according to the agency.

Some literacy and skills classes take place in community spaces and in the homes of facilitators with the knowledge of authorities, according to The AP. More than 1,000 literacy facilitators are involved, most of whom have been trained by UNESCO and its partners.

UNESCO said a recent study found evidence that its literacy and skills programs have helped increase household incomes and improve livelihoods.

The agency acknowledged, however, that such efforts cannot replace formal schooling.

"Afghanistan's girls and women have the right to learn, to work, to move freely, and to shape their own futures," UNESCO said, adding that "the world must not look away until their human rights are restored."

UNESCO said it would continue working with local communities and partners to maintain alternative opportunities for Afghan women and girls while pressing for the education ban to be lifted.

"UNESCO continues to call for the immediate and unconditional restoration of girls and women's right to secondary and higher education," Jaberian said Tuesday. "It is not negotiable. It's a basic human right and we reiterate that there is no substitute for this."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Male redback spiders invite cannibalism through a ‘self-sacrificial somersault’ during sex – but why?
articles.excerpt:
New research sheds light on the genetic basis of the venomous insect’s ‘weird mating behaviour’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily ...
articles.body_text:
New research sheds light on the genetic basis of the venomous insect’s ‘weird mating behaviour’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

If you think you’ve had a bad one-night stand, spare a thought for the male redback spider, whose sole reproductive partner eats him after sex.

Male redbacks appear to invite this cannibalism through a “self-sacrificial somersault”, with new research shedding light on the genetic basis of the behaviour.

The redback, also known as the Australian black widow, is one of two monogynous widow spider species – meaning that males typically only mate with a single female.

During copulation, a male redback uses his pedipalps – two arm-like appendages – to transfer sperm to the larger female’s two sperm storage organs. He also somersaults into the jaws of the female.

“He’s pumping sperm, he flips his abdomen right over into her mouthparts and then he constricts his abdomen … to make it hard for the female to get a purchase on his abdomen. That lets him survive the first mating,” said Cor Vink, an associate professor and spider expert at Lincoln University in New Zealand.

The self-sacrificial flip is thought to help maximise reproductive success, but the males risk being eaten before they are able to transfer sperm to the female’s second storage organ.

To avoid becoming a post-coital meal, previous research has found that some males have developed the survival tactic of mating with immature females not yet experienced in eating their partners.

The venomous redback spider is widespread throughout Australia and has been unintentionally introduced to other countries including New Zealand, Japan and the United Arab Emirates.

Redbacks are closely related to the New Zealand katipō, which do not engage in sexual cannibalism. “In the katipō, the male inseminates the female and runs off the web – that’s the same for most widow spiders,” Vink said. “The term widow is actually a misnomer.”

Of the 31 species of widow spider, male sacrificial behaviour is only usually observed in redbacks and brown widows.

In a study published in Biology Letters on Wednesday, German researchers investigated the genetic basis for why redback males perform a “self-sacrificial somersault” during mating, but katipō males do not.

To do so, they bred female katipō with male redbacks to determine how many offspring inherited the somersaulting behaviour. Close to half of their third-generation offspring also somersaulted, leading the scientists to conclude that the behaviour was linked to a specific location on the spider’s X chromosome.

“It is quite remarkable that a highly complex phenotype such as somersaulting, which may lead to partial reproductive isolation, can have such a simple genetic basis,” the researchers noted.

In New Zealand, Vink has found evidence that interbreeding between native katipō and invasive redbacks occurs in the wild. “This is a concern because we could lose our endemic protected species just through hybridisation,” he said.

Vink, who sourced the katipō spiders for the study but was not otherwise involved in the research, described the work as an “elegant paper” that shed light on the redback’s “weird mating behaviour”.

Katipō are thought to have diverged genetically from redbacks about 100,000 years ago. “It’s really neat that they’ve lost this behaviour in 100,000 to 200,000 years,” Vink said.

“The more we know about the interbreeding, the more we know about what we can do to combat redbacks and katipō interbreeding in New Zealand,” he added.

articles.title: Tyler Feehan's mother and fiancée recall his excitement before fatal Middle East deployment
articles.excerpt:
Mother of US soldier Tyler Feehan, who was killed in an Iranian attack, Shari Feehan, and Feehan's fiancée, Claire Fletcher, discuss Tyler's impact and legacy on 'The Story.'

The grieving family of s...
articles.body_text:
Mother of US soldier Tyler Feehan, who was killed in an Iranian attack, Shari Feehan, and Feehan's fiancée, Claire Fletcher, discuss Tyler's impact and legacy on 'The Story.'

The grieving family of slain Army 1st Lt. Tyler Feehan remembered him as brave and passionate about life during an exclusive interview with "The Story" on Tuesday.

Feehan, a 25-year-old Army soldier from Georgia, was one of three U.S. service members killed in an Iranian drone attack at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on July 18.

"We are so proud of him, and it's just so touching that the country is also sharing in that pride with us," his mother Shari Feehan said.

In the emotional tribute, Feehan’s mother and fiancée shared details about his final resting place in Georgia and recalled how elated he was to be deployed to the Middle East.

TRUMP GIVES EMOTIONAL TRIBUTE TO FALLEN ARMY LT TYLER FEEHAN AFTER FLYING GRIEVING FAMILY ON AIR FORCE ONE

Shari Feehan reflected on the family’s flight home to Georgia aboard Air Force One following an invitation from President Donald Trump after the death of her son in Jordan.  (Getty Images)

"He was so excited to go," Feehan’s fiancée Claire Fletcher told Fox News. "He was just so excited to finally do his job that he's been training for and working towards, and he was so excited to get out there and make a difference and change lives."

While she was upset about her fiancé leaving on deployment, Fletcher said she was also excited for him to do what he loved and ultimately "come home."

US SERVICE MEMBER KILLED IN IRAQ AS TROOPS RECOVER UNIDENTIFIED REMAINS IN JORDAN: CENTCOM

"I was obviously very sad when I got the news that he was going to go, but I was very proud of him. I was like, ‘You know what, I just — I just want you to go out there. I want you to get the experience that you are wanting to get out of this, and to come home,'" Fletcher said.

U.S. President Donald Trump salutes as a U.S. Army carry team carries the flag-draped transfer case containing the remains of 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, during a dignified transfer solemn event for U.S. service members killed during operations in the Middle East, at Dover Air Force Base in Dover, Delaware, on July 22, 2026. Feehan was killed in action on July 18 during an enemy attack at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan. (Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP via Getty Images) ( )

"He was positive the entire time, and he was always like, ‘Oh yeah, I did so great today. We shot down 10 missiles,'" she added.

Feehan was assigned to the 2nd Battalion, 55th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 32nd Army Air and Missile Defense Command at Fort Bragg, North Carolina.

The Gold Star family told Fox News that military service is important to the Feehan family.

TRAVELERS UNITE IN POWERFUL MOMENT OF SILENCE AS FALLEN US SERVICE MEMBER RETURNS HOME

"He [Tyler] loved serving his country. His father did 26 years in the Army, and so the military and the country have always been very important to our family, and he carried that legacy on," Shari Feehan said.

Soldier places flag on the grave of Medal of Honor recipient Michael Crescenz at Arlington National Cemetery. (Patrick Hughes)

The 25-year-old was laid to rest in Georgia on Friday, directly beside his grandfather, a Vietnam War veteran, who died a few days after the soldier’s tragic death in Jordan.

"Georgia National Cemetery, where Tyler is laid to rest with his grandfather, is just such a beautiful, peaceful place for our son," his mother told Fox News.

"They were together and very close in life, and now they can rest next to each other," she added.

Feehan’s mother also reflected on the family’s flight home to Georgia aboard Air Force One following an invitation from President Donald Trump.

Shari and Stephen Feehan, the parents of 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan, react as President Donald Trump talks about their son at Wheeler High School on Wednesday, July 22, 2026, in Marietta, Ga. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

"It was such a nice experience to be able to meet and talk with the president," she said. "I feel like he was very genuine in speaking with us, and we got to let him know a little bit more about Tyler and the wonderful young man that he was."

Tyler Feehan will posthumously receive the Bronze Star, Purple Heart and Combat Action Badge.

Nora Moriarty is a Writer at Fox News Digital.

Back in July, the New York Islanders announced plans to toss fans the keys and let them take a crack at designing the team's next third jersey.

I figured at the time that it would mean fans couldn't complain about this third jersey — as they did about so many jerseys the Isles have worn — if they were the ones responsible for the masterpiece or abomination.

Well, how wrong I was, because the team has unveiled the eight finalists, one of which will be selected by way of a bracket, and social media hates all the options.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

None of those are offensively awful... but none seem that exciting.

If I had to pick one because my life depended on it — and man, what a terrible stroke of luck that would be, huh? — I would probably go with the one all the way on the bottom right. Navy with the "ISLANDERS" wordmark and chest stripe.

I'm a sucker for a good ol' fashioned chest stripe.

The Isles' third jersey history is not stellar. These were used from 2011 to 2014, but if you mentally blocked these out, you're forgiven. At least they tried something different. (Photo by Bruce Bennett/Getty Images)

It's kind of a shame that the Elite 8 is a little lackluster, because the design tool the team rolled out was great.

JOSH ALLEN DELIVERS FULL-THROATED UNSOLICITED DEFENSE OF BUFFALO BILLS' HIDEOUS NEW UNIFORMS

In fact, yours truly submitted at least one design that I thought was pretty great...

But these all seem pretty tame, and one even looks almost exactly like the Edmonton Oilers' old orange jerseys that they used to wear.

NHL fans, many of whom likely had their designs shot down as I did, took to social media to voice their displeasure with the team's selected crop of potential sweaters.

Well, while the reception has not been warm, it looks like one of those eight sweaters will be hitting the ice.

With how good their home and away jerseys look, do the Islanders even need a third jersey? (Photo by Dennis DaSilva/NHLI via Getty Images)

According to the team's original release about the contest, the winner will debut next season, with the winning designer earning themselves a "VIP gameday experience."

articles.title: Carville warns Democrats may need to block far-left candidates from joining caucus, moderate group disagrees
articles.excerpt: Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville warned that as far-left candidates win primaries, Democratic Party leaders may have to contain them to stop them from co-opting the party or ruining its br...
articles.body_text:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville warned that as far-left candidates win primaries, Democratic Party leaders may have to contain them to stop them from co-opting the party or ruining its brand.

Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville warned last week that the Democratic Party may need to consider shutting out far-left candidates in order to keep them from co-opting the party.

In recent months, several high-profile elections have seen far-left candidates, including candidates aligned with or backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, defeat their establishment opponents. Carville has warned in response that there may need to be a formal "schism" within the Democratic Party to stop it from being taken over.

Last week, "The Sharpe Exchange" podcast host Wyatt Sharpe asked Carville about whether he sees this phenomenon of anti-establishment Democrats as a growing phenomenon.

"Well, it's certainly getting more common. I mean, you can't deny that," Carville replied. "They’re very aggressive. The country overwhelmingly rejects their agenda."

JAMES CARVILLE PREDICTS 2028 DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY WILL TEST TRUE STRENGTH OF PARTY'S SOCIALIST WING

Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville suggested that the Democratic Party's leadership may need to take institutional measures to ensure the party is not co-opted by the new, far-left faction. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

He lamented that even though many of the far-left candidates identify themselves as democratic socialists, they run in primaries as Democrats.

"Why do you want the name Democratic? Call yourself something else. You're not you're not a Democrat! These people are not Democrats," he said. "Why not get your own name? Why do you have to appropriate our name?"

He then suggested that the Democratic Party’s leadership will need to take concrete institutional steps to protect its brand and its control of the party.

"I think that Hakeem [Jeffries] and other people are going to have to consider some of these people who run against Democrats, should they be allowed in the Democratic caucus? Should they be assigned committees, assuming that we win the House?" Carville asked.

He also wondered if there are certain politicians whom Democrats will have to tell, "‘Well, no, you can't. You're not a member of our party.’"

"At some point, it's, you know, political parties, and you can say, ‘Hey, I feel like I'm a Republican. I feel like a Democrat. I feel like I'm an independent.’ But there are people that are actually appropriating the name of the Democratic Party while they're running against the Democratic Party," Carville said. "Well, the party should be able to take some measures to protect its brand."

JEFFRIES' SOCIALISM DILEMMA: NEW YORK VICTORIES EXPOSE DEMOCRATIC PARTY DIVIDE

Democratic strategist James Carville has warned multiple times about a potential schism within the Democratic Party as far-left candidates have risen in popularity and won elections. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

He listed several centrist Democrats running for office, arguing that the party of those candidates "is being hijacked" by the new faction.

The center-left think tank Third Way spoke to Fox News Digital about Carville's comments.

"If someone gets elected as a Democratic Socialist and wants to caucus as a Democrat in the House and the Senate, they should be able to do so. Let’s not forget, Bernie Sanders has never been a registered Democrat in his life, and he’s caucused as a Democrat in both the House and the Senate for more than three decades," Jim Kessler, Third Way's executive vice president for policy said.

"Is there a line that could get you tossed out of the tent? Yes, but it has to be truly abhorrent personal behavior or taking a political position that is deeply offensive to a segment of the population," he added.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Democratic strategist James Carville suggested that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., will need to take serious measures to keep the far-left from co-opting the Democratic Party. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Kessler shared one key warning, however, about the worst-case scenario.

"My issue with the DSA members potentially coming to the caucus is whether they are trying to hold a place in the tent or trying to burn the tent to the ground," he said. "Listening to some DSA members, they seem to be armed with a torch. Nonetheless, if they get elected fair and square, they should have their place. But only their place."

Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

When the deputy asked him the reason he was driving so fast, Ames didn’t dispute that he was speeding or even trying to play word games in order to search for an excuse.

A Florida man claims he was driving nearly double the speed limit on Aug. 1 to catch his girlfriend cheating.  (DeSoto County Sheriff's Office)

FLORIDA MAN IN BUNNY HELMET ALLEGEDLY LED POLICE ON 120 MPH CHASE BEFORE SURRENDERING TO TROOPERS

He didn’t need to. He had a perfectly good excuse. Not one that was going to get him out of trouble, but one that anyone who has been cheated on can relate to.

He replied to the deputy, "I'm actually on my way to my cheating girlfriend's house." That answer was met with the customary step out of the vehicle and put your hands behind your back.

Florida man was pulled over for allegedly driving 110 mph in a 60 mph zone. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

The deputy then explained that anything over 50 mph over the speed limit was good for a free trip to jail. He placed Ames in cuffs and then in his vehicle for his free trip.

Trying to process the fact that he had ended up in the back of a police vehicle while he was on his way to catch his girlfriend cheating on him brought Ames an interesting realization.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

He was going to be calling this cheating girlfriend of his to bail him out.

A man pulled over for speeding in Florida tells officers he was on his way to catch his cheating girlfriend. (Getty Images)

articles.title: Georgia teacher, father hailed as hero after dying to save girl from Myrtle Beach rip current
articles.excerpt: Brevard County officials are urgently recruiting to fill at least 45 lifeguard vacancies following a tragic double drowning in South Cocoa Beach where two adults died attempting to rescue a child from...
articles.body_text:
Brevard County officials are urgently recruiting to fill at least 45 lifeguard vacancies following a tragic double drowning in South Cocoa Beach where two adults died attempting to rescue a child from a rip current.

A beloved Georgia elementary school teacher and father died after jumping into the ocean to save a young girl caught in a rip current off Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, according to authorities and his family.

Derrick Moore, 47, entered the water near 10th Avenue South after a young girl became caught in a rip current at approximately 7:53 p.m. Friday, according to the Myrtle Beach Police Department.

Moore was able to get the girl to safety but was then pulled underwater by the rip current and disappeared, police said. The incident occurred after lifeguards had gone off duty.

MAN, WOMAN KILLED IN RIP CURRENT AS LIFEGUARD SHORTAGE LEAVES DANGER ZONES IN BEACH DESTINATION

Derrick Moore, a Georgia teacher and father, is being remembered as a hero after saving a young girl from a rip current in Myrtle Beach. (DeKalb County School District)

Myrtle Beach police and firefighters continued searching for Moore into Saturday morning. Police announced Saturday afternoon that his body had washed ashore and was recovered.

Moore's daughter told WRAL that her father did not know the girl he risked his life to save.

"We loved him and are truly heartbroken that he's gone," his daughter said in a statement to the outlet. "He was a great father and we are all going to miss him."

Moore leaves behind four children, according to a GoFundMe page.

As news of his death spread, tributes poured in from Moore's friends, former teammates and family members, who remembered him as a devoted father, gifted athlete and selfless man whose final act reflected the way he lived his life.

HEROIC 16-YEAR-OLD LIFEGUARD RESCUES CHILD FROM MONSTER SURF IN HEART-STOPPING VIDEO

Derrick Moore, the Georgia teacher who died after rescuing a young girl from a Myrtle Beach rip current, pictured in an undated family photo. (GoFundMe)

The DeKalb County School District confirmed Moore was a current teacher at Rockbridge Elementary School in Georgia, where his students affectionately referred to him as "Coach." He previously taught at Jolly Elementary School.

"The DeKalb County School District is deeply saddened by the passing of Mr. Derrick Moore, a beloved educator and valued member of the DeKalb County School District (DCSD) family," the district said in a statement.

The district said Moore "made a meaningful impact on the students, families, colleagues, and communities he served," adding that his "presence, care, and dedication to education will be deeply missed."

Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp also paid tribute to Moore.

"Marty and I were heartbroken to learn of the tragic loss of Derrick Moore, a father, teacher, and coach," Kemp said. "Please join us in praying for this hero’s family and the DeKalb County community as they mourn his loss."

LIFEGUARDS SAVE YOUNG BOY, 5 YEARS OLD, AS HE'S PULLED UNCONSCIOUS FROM OCEAN

Derrick Moore pictured with family members before his death in a Myrtle Beach rip current rescue. (GoFundMe)

Moore was also remembered as a standout athlete whose ties to sports stretched back to his college years.

Samford University said Moore graduated in 2001 and competed in both football and track and field.

"The Samford community mourns the loss of alumnus Derrick Moore, who tragically passed after rescuing a girl struggling in a rip current in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina," the university said in a statement.

The university remembered Moore as a "beloved teacher" and "true hero" and asked the Samford community to keep his family in their prayers.

Friends and former teammates also remembered Moore as someone who showed up for others, with one writing that the fact he gave his life trying to save someone else "tells you everything you need to know about the kind of man he was."

Family members echoed that sentiment, sharing memories of Moore as a devoted father, son and brother who made a point of being present for the people he loved.

One family member described Moore's decision to enter the water to save a child he did not know as a fitting final example of his selflessness.

"You died a HERO. You died saving the life of a child, a stranger. What a Legacy," the family member wrote.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Riley Green shares how Luke Grimes unexpectedly launched his acting career, reveals job he left behind
articles.excerpt:
Riley Green told Fox News Digital that he doesn't get nervous going on stage anymore, but his nerves were wrecked when he walked on the "Marshals" set.

Riley Green may be one of country music’s risin...
articles.body_text:
Riley Green told Fox News Digital that he doesn't get nervous going on stage anymore, but his nerves were wrecked when he walked on the "Marshals" set.

Riley Green may be one of country music’s rising stars, but his latest on-screen career move came with a little help from a famous friend.

During an appearance on "CBS Mornings" on Monday, the 37-year-old Alabama native revealed that "Yellowstone" star Luke Grimes helped open the door to his first acting role, encouraging Green to step outside his comfort zone and eventually helping land him a part on the CBS drama "Marshals."

"It happened so organically because he was starting his music career and coming to Nashville a little bit. We wrote together," said Green, who made his acting debut as Garrett — a former Navy SEAL struggling with PTSD — alongside Grimes in the "Yellowstone" spinoff.

TAYLOR SHERIDAN SHOCKS 'YELLOWSTONE' FANS WITH NEW SPINOFF SERIES, PROVIDES VIEWERS WITH DARK RIDE

Riley Green opened up about how his friendship with Luke Grimes led to an unexpected career move. (Getty Images)

"He mentioned something about maybe I should act. I said, 'Well I'm interested.' He said, 'I've got this show.' A couple months later, I went out and read for a part. They said I got it. I flew back out to Utah and we filmed the show."

Earlier this year, Green admitted it's not every day an opportunity like that presents itself.

"I guess that doesn't happen all the time, where the star of the show sits in with somebody trying out for a part," Green told USA Today. "But man, I've got to be such good friends with Luke, and it makes it so much easier to step into a world that I wasn't necessarily comfortable in."

It was a dramatic change for a performer accustomed to playing sold-out concerts.

TAYLOR SHERIDAN’S 'YELLOWSTONE’ FORMULA TURNS COUNTRY STARS INTO SCENE-STEALERS AS MORGAN WADE MAKES HER DEBUT

Green previously admitted acting was considerably more intimidating than taking the stage.

Riley Green as Garrett and Luke Grimes as Kayce Dutton appear in a scene from the CBS original series "Marshals." (Cam McLeod/CBS)

"I don’t get nervous going on stage anymore," Green previously told Fox News Digital at the "Marshals" premiere. "I’ve played enough shows now it kind of comes naturally, but this was a completely different world, and it’s not my set, it’s not my stage."

His Hollywood debut was the latest unexpected chapter in a career Green never necessarily envisioned for himself.

Long before he found fame, Green was earning his living as a construction worker, framing homes until he signed a record deal in 2018.

LAINEY WILSON SAYS CITY PEOPLE HAVE WRONG VIEW OF COUNTRY TOWNS AS SHE DEFENDS HER 'BLUE COLLAR' ROOTS

And according to Green, he wouldn't have been able to handle the spotlight at the time.

"I've been so fortunate that my success was gradual," he told the CBS hosts. "Early 20s, I don't know if I could have handled what I've got going on right now, but it's been really motivating. I've done it for well over 10 years now."

Green prefers life on his farm over Hollywood fame.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"I was building houses for a living. And I signed a record deal in 2018 and put my tool belt up and really went on the road heavy and it's just, as a songwriter, it's so great when people are like relating to the music, and you hear them singing those songs back to you."

"When you see it growing, it just makes you want to go play more shows and keep grinding," he continued. "So it's a really great time to be in country music because I think the genre as a whole is becoming more popular everywhere."

COUNTRY STAR RILEY GREEN REVEALS WHY FAN EMOTION AT HIS SHOWS BEATS INDUSTRY AWARDS EVERY TIME

Green signed with Big Machine Label Group in 2018 and broke through with "There Was This Girl," followed by hits including "I Wish Grandpas Never Died," "Half of Me," "Different 'Round Here," "You Look Like You Love Me" with Ella Langley and "Worst Way."

Yet despite his success — and his unexpected entry into Hollywood — Green has remained closely tied to the life he had before fame.

Prior to finding mega success as a country music star, Green made a living as a construction worker framing homes.  (Christopher Polk/Dick Clark Productions via Getty Images)

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

He continues to live on his farm in Alabama rather than relocating full-time to Nashville.

"I feel like I’ve got every reason in the world to move to Nashville, and it’s just never crossed my mind," Green previously told Fox News Digital.

"Me in real life, I'd rather be on my bulldozer on a farm, or hunting somewhere."

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

articles.title: Man, 20, dies in 'horrific accident' after slipping from towering Oregon waterfall
articles.excerpt:

A 20-year-old male ...
articles.body_text:
Alaska hikers Dr. Michelle Lynn Thaller, Tony Cutraro and Tanya Thompson join ‘Fox & Friends Weekend’ to recall their frightening encounter with a grizzly bear on an Alaska trail.

A 20-year-old male hiker reportedly died Monday in what park officials described as a "horrific accident" following a devastating fall from a 177-foot waterfall at an Oregon state park.

Authorities said the man was from out of state and was visiting Silver Falls State Park, more than an hour south of Portland, according to Central Oregon Daily.

The visitor reportedly went off-trail while trying to reach an area where he could pose for a photo, crossing a barrier and making his way over a creek directly above the falls.

The incident happened at the upper viewpoint of South Falls, the park’s tallest waterfall, which cascades into a large pool below, Oregon State Police said, according to the outlet.

NPS INVESTIGATES AFTER 23-YEAR-OLD REPORTEDLY SWEPT OVER NOTORIOUS YOSEMITE WATERFALL

Autumn colours add beauty to the South Falls in Silver Falls State Park. Oregon, United States of America. (Craig Tuttle/Design Pics Editorial/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

He then fell into the pool below at around 6:30 p.m.

Bystanders at the park reportedly tried to help, performing CPR as emergency responders rushed to the scene.

The victim died at the scene, according to KPTV. Authorities did not release his identity.

RESCUERS FREE CLIMBER TRAPPED BENEATH 16,000-POUND BOULDER ON OREGON'S MOUNT HOOD IN COMPLEX OPERATION

Hikers walk on a paved trail behind South Falls at the Silver Falls State Park in central Oregon. (Education Images/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

"It was a pretty horrific accident," Silver Falls State Park regional manager Chris Gilliand said, according to Central Oregon Daily. "A very tough situation."

The Marion County Medical Examiner reportedly released the man's body to Marion County Search and Rescue.

Search and rescue personnel then completed the recovery from the base of the falls.

Unger Funeral Chapel later took custody, according to reports.

A hiker walks on a bridge at an Oregon state park near Portland on Aug. 17, 2025. (Wolfgang Kaehler/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Silver Falls State Park is known for its Trail of Ten Falls, a popular hiking route featuring 10 waterfalls and attracting visitors from across Oregon and beyond.

South Falls is considered one of the park's main attractions and features a trail that allows visitors to walk behind the waterfall. The waterfall has been described as the "crown jewel" of Oregon's state parks.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Oregon State Police and Silver Falls State Park for more information.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

A federal judge on Tuesday blocked ⁠the US Postal ⁠Service ​(USPS) from implementing part of Donald Trump’s executive order that aims ⁠to tighten rules for mail-in voting ahead of November midterm elections that ⁠will decide control of Congress.

The ruling by ​US district ‌judge Indira ‌Talwani in Boston in effect expanded on an ‌earlier order she had issued in June that had prevented Trump’s administration from implementing it in 23 mostly Democratic-led states.

Several voting rights groups had ‌urged her to go further and prevent USPS from implementing anywhere ​in the nation a proposed rule requiring states to provide lists of voters and adopt new balloting procedures before ⁠the mail agency would make deliveries.

articles.excerpt:

EXCLUSI...
articles.body_text:
New York Jets Director of Player Performance Erik Korem spoke about the team's new training facility renovations and the new technological approach toward getting players ready for the field.

EXCLUSIVE: The most important feature of the New York Jets’ next-generation Player Performance Center may be that no single feature defines it.

Jets owner Woody Johnson has invested in growing the facilities by more than double for this upcoming season, as the team looks to turn the page on the 2025 season and make strides in 2026.

"We are investing in an exceptionally dynamic, innovative training staff with experience designing and utilizing advanced performance systems to support our players. Our new facilities will be 250% larger, allowing us to increase training capacity and centralize strength and conditioning, recovery, and nutrition," Johnson said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"We have already implemented state-of-the-art equipment in our temporary facility, granting our team access to some of the most advanced training resources in the league."

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Jaden Keller No. 48 of the New York Jets warms up during training camp at Atlantic Health Jets Training Center in Florham Park, N.J., on July 29, 2026. (Getty Images)

There will be new technology: vibroacoustic recovery pods, multimodal wellness chambers, pneumatic resistance equipment, computer-vision tracking and a custom-built, AI-powered player performance app.

But when Jets director of player performance Erik Korem describes the project, he repeatedly returns to a broader idea.

"We’re building a holistic health and human performance ecosystem," Korem said. "We’re taking some big steps in our strength and conditioning, nutrition, sports science and recovery departments. The use of data and AI will be part of this, but I think it extends beyond that."

That distinction is the center of the Jets’ Phase 2 renovation at the Atlantic Health Jets Training Center. The team is not just replacing an aging weight room with a larger one. It is redesigning the way players move through the daily cycle of assessment, training, practice, fueling and recovery, all while giving the practitioners responsible for those areas a shared environment in which to work.

The planned two-story performance center will expand the former space by 250%, according to the Jets’ official construction announcement. Its four stated priorities are player performance, recovery, efficient daily flow and the integration of new technology. Dedicated zones will support strength, power, speed and mobility work, while expanded nutrition and recovery areas are intended to make individualized programs easier to deliver.

The investment is already affecting the current roster. During construction, players are working in a temporary training structure with a footprint more than 70% larger than the former weight room. The Jets moved equipment into the interim facility after mandatory minicamp, and demolition of the old space was completed in July. New equipment and technology have been installed in the temporary building rather than held back for the finished center.

That approach reflects an instruction Korem said has come consistently from chairman Woody Johnson, general manager Darren Mougey and head coach Aaron Glenn: The long-term project cannot compromise the team’s short-term preparation.

Korem credited Johnson for his investment in the facility, as they look to translate that investment into on-field results for the 2026 season.

"It just is a reflection of Mr. Johnson's investment," Korem said. "It's only going to help them as individuals and as a team."

The promise of the new center is personalization.

Football teams have never trained every player identically; a 300-pound lineman and a 180-pound defensive back have different jobs, bodies and physical demands. Korem’s goal is to make those distinctions more precise. More frequent assessments, he said, can help the staff identify whether a player needs additional mobility, strength, power, speed work or a change in training volume. The team’s custom app is designed to help organize those inputs and deliver more individualized recommendations.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

The New York Jets renovated training facility. (Dylan Goodman, courtesy of the New York Jets)

"The more tools you have and the more appropriate data you have from a serial perspective, you can then develop more specific training programs and interventions for each individual athlete," Korem said. "To me, that’s really where data collection and AI is going to help the field of human performance in general."

The key word is "serial." A force-plate test or motion-capture assessment offers a snapshot; repeated measurements can reveal how an athlete is changing across a week, a training block or a rehabilitation program. Korem said the Jets will expand their use of 3D motion capture, force plates and other telemetry tools to better understand movement and physical readiness.

That approach reflects a wider development in elite sport. A 2025 scoping review indexed by the National Library of Medicine described force plates as one of the most commonly used technologies for monitoring acute changes in athletes’ neuromuscular function. The practical value, however, depends on reliable testing and sound interpretation. Data is useful only when it changes a decision.

The same principle applies inside the rack. Computer vision can track a bar’s path and speed, while connected resistance systems can record ranges and angles and adjust loading as fatigue develops. This is part of a training method often called velocity-based training: Instead of prescribing work only from a previously measured one-repetition maximum, coaches can use the speed of the current lift to judge the quality of the rep and the athlete’s readiness that day. A systematic review of elite-athlete research found that velocity-based resistance training can support strength and power development, while also noting that protocols and results vary.

Geno Smith No. 7 of the New York Jets stretches during a joint practice between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and New York Jets at Atlantic Health Jets Training Center in Florham Park, N.J., on Aug. 11, 2026. (Getty Images)

For the Jets, the technology is meant to sharpen the judgment of coaches, not replace it. The facility can capture more information, and AI can help sort and present it, but the performance staff still has to decide what matters for a particular player on a particular day.

The project also fits a broader organizational move toward analytics. Mougey said in July that the Jets are using AI to automate time-consuming work and help staff digest large amounts of information in scouting and personnel. In that context, the performance app is another expression of the same idea: use automation to make information easier to act on, then leave consequential decisions with football and performance professionals.

Korem describes training and recovery as an arc. Players must first rise into the highly activated state required for lifting, practice and games. Then they must come down from it.

"The recover part is how quickly can they go from being in this highly active state, or what we call a sympathetic state, to getting in this rest-and-digest state," he said.

One of the center’s most distinctive tools, the TERSA SAVA Sound Pod, is designed for that transition. The memory-foam pod surrounds the user with music and low-frequency vibration. TERSA describes the system as combining spatial audio with vibroacoustic frequencies to encourage deep calm. Korem said players have been able to enter a relaxed state quickly in the pod, making it a useful option after demanding work.

The Ammortal Chamber takes a different approach, stacking several modalities into one session. The manufacturer lists red and near-infrared light, pulsed electromagnetic fields and vibroacoustic sound among the chamber’s components. Korem’s interest is partly logistical: If a player can use multiple recovery modalities at once, the intervention may fit more easily into a tightly scheduled NFL day.

These systems are the most futuristic pieces of the renovation, but Korem presents them as additions to a much larger recovery program—not substitutes for foundational work. Training load, sleep, hydration, nutrition and the ability to downshift after practice still form the base. The devices expand the menu available to players and staff.

The same individualized philosophy carries into the kitchen.

Under director of performance nutrition Carmen Spencer, the Jets’ nutrition staff works with team chefs to provide protein, carbohydrates, healthy fats, fruits and vegetables in forms players will actually want to eat. Korem described menus that might include salmon, several chicken preparations and action stations serving items such as poke bowls.

The objective changes with the player and the moment: A whole-grain option may make sense in one meal, while a fast-digesting carbohydrate may be more useful immediately before practice.

"What undergirds all this is: What fuels performance?" Korem said. "What are the things that we need to deliver to the players to help their bodies recover, to help fuel in-game performance and practice performance, and hydration?"

It is an area in which the organization has something to prove. In the NFL Players Association’s 2025 team report card—based on responses from players on 2024 rosters—the Jets ranked 29th overall. Players gave the club a C-minus for food and dining, a D-plus for the locker room and a C-plus for the weight room. They were more positive about the nutritionist/dietitian category, which received a B-plus, and 87 percent said they received an individualized nutrition plan.

The Jets have not publicly characterized the renovation as a response to that survey. Still, the sequence is significant. Phase 1, unveiled in 2025, replaced the locker room with 92 custom lockers and added a redesigned wet area, a larger sauna and a barbershop.

Phase 2 directly addresses the scale and function of the old weight room while expanding nutrition, recovery and performance services. Whatever the motivation, the work creates a visible standard against which players can judge the club’s promise of improvement.

For all the technology going into the building, Korem is direct about the most difficult and important workout of training camp: practice.

The purpose of camp is to prepare players for game demands. Depending on position and role, that can mean building toward 65 to 75 snaps while reaching the necessary speed and volume benchmarks. The weight room supports strength, power, speed, endurance and mobility, but it cannot become the main event once football work intensifies.

"Think about the weight room on the field," Korem said of practice. "There’s qualities that you’re developing on the field. What’s happening in the weight room is you’re supporting" those qualities.

A view of a Jets training scene. (Dylan Goodman, courtesy of the New York Jets)

That is also the most realistic way to understand what the Player Performance Center can—and cannot—do. No recovery pod, data platform or force plate can guarantee wins or prevent every injury. What an integrated center can do is give coaches and practitioners more chances to identify needs, individualize work, recover efficiently and keep players available to develop their football skills.

Korem ultimately measures the investment less by the sophistication of the equipment than by the quality of the system around it. Johnson, he said, has supported not only new tools but the hiring of practitioners who know how to use them.

"You can have tools, but do you have the people behind those tools?" Korem said. "It’s the whole ecosystem of the people and the resources that make any type of building come to life."

That may be the defining ambition of the renovation. The Jets are building a much larger performance center, but the competitive bet is on something harder to photograph: better information, shared more quickly, turned into better daily decisions for every player.

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

articles.title: 'Blue Bloods' star Jennifer Esposito says she was locked in psych ward as health battle spiraled
articles.excerpt:
Donnie Wahlberg told Fox News Digital that he did everything he could to keep "Blue Bloods" on-air before pivoting to the spin-off series.

This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is ...
articles.body_text:
Donnie Wahlberg told Fox News Digital that he did everything he could to keep "Blue Bloods" on-air before pivoting to the spin-off series.

This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Jennifer Esposito is opening up about the yearslong health battle that she says derailed her career, left her severely depressed and eventually landed her in a psychiatric ward before doctors diagnosed her with celiac disease.

During an appearance on Maria Menounos' "Heal Squad" podcast, Esposito, 53, recalled being a young actress in New York City when unexplained physical and mental health problems became so debilitating that she was forced to put her life on hold.

"I had a whole life beginning in the city, and I was a young actor and I had to stop everything," Esposito said.

MAYIM BIALIK DETAILS 'NIGHTMARE' AFTER ONE INJECTION OF GLP-1 DRUG LED TO WEEKS OF DEBILITATING SIDE EFFECTS

Jennifer Esposito detailed years of misdiagnoses before she was ultimately diagnosed with celiac disease. (WireImage)

The actress said she became "deeply depressed" and began having "thoughts of suicide" as doctors struggled to determine what was wrong.

"They brought me to a psychologist, like they had me on every medication," she recalled. "They wanted to give me shock treatment at one point because I wasn't responding. I'm very sensitive to medication. It was a really bad time. And my mother had people pray over me."

Esposito said she eventually began to suspect that her physical and mental health symptoms could be connected to nutrition.

"I realized that there was a major connection with what I was eating and my vitamins and then my body," she said.

DAMON WAYANS REVEALS THE SCARY SYMPTOM THAT LED TO HIS TYPE 2 DIABETES DIAGNOSIS

Her health began to "collapse" while she was working on the ABC comedy "Samantha Who?," which aired from 2007 to 2009, according to the actress.

Esposito recalled experiencing alarming physical symptoms, including losing her hair and fingernails.

The 53-year-old actress said the symptoms took a toll on her physically and mentally. (JC Olivera/Getty Images)

"I had hair falling out, nails falling off," she said.

Then, she said, a tooth fell out while she was filming a scene.

CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS

"A tooth fell out of my mouth, like literally in the middle of a scene," Esposito recalled. "I was mortified but also had been so ill that I just — I went hysterical. Like, somebody has to help me."

Esposito said she was misdiagnosed several times, with doctors considering conditions including multiple sclerosis and irritable bowel syndrome. She said a therapist suggested stress was behind her symptoms.

"We don't ever treat the actual underlying issue. We treat symptoms in this country, in America," Esposito continued. "I went for years on that, and I tried everything myself. I went to holistic healers. I went to get my aura cleansed. I was vegan."

Desperate for answers, Esposito said she began attending a non-denominational church in an effort to "feel recharged."

On one drive there, she recalled reaching a breaking point.

Esposito said she was losing her hair and nails were falling off due to her nutrition issues. (Getty Images)

"I remember saying to myself, because I was so depressed of being so sick all the time and fighting panic disorders … ‘If you don't get a diagnosis, you have to accept the fact that you're crazy, and you've created this, and you're going to let it go because I can't keep doing this.’"

Moments later, she said, a large piece of wood flew from a truck in front of her and smashed through her windshield.

RANDY TRAVIS' HEALTH CRISIS BEGAN WITH 'CONGESTION' AND ENDED IN A FIVE-MONTH HOSPITAL STAY

"I'm sitting with glass all over me," Esposito said. After managing to pull to the side of the road, she took the frightening accident as a sign to continue looking for answers.

Two days later, Esposito said, a doctor called with her diagnosis: celiac disease.

"I’m not sure how you’re alive," Esposito recalled the doctor telling her.

According to Esposito, her case was so severe that her liver was failing.

The "Blue Bloods" star recalls being taken to a psych ward amid her misdiagnoses period. (Getty Images)

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition in which consuming gluten — a protein found in wheat, barley and rye — triggers an immune response that damages the small intestine. That damage can interfere with the body's ability to absorb nutrients and can cause symptoms extending well beyond the digestive system, including fatigue, anemia, neurological problems and elevated liver enzymes. A strict, lifelong gluten-free diet is the primary treatment and can allow the intestine to heal, according to the Mayo Clinic.

After receiving her diagnosis, Esposito immediately eliminated gluten from her diet, but said her body was in such poor condition that her recovery was grueling.

She recalled being severely deficient in vitamin D and developing welts when exposed to sunlight. Her nervous system was also so overwhelmed, she said, that ordinary stimulation became difficult to tolerate.

"They had me on four Klonopin a day, and I was still a trembling mess," Esposito said. "I was literally sleeping in my kitchen because it was the only place that didn't have a window, because the light — the stimulus from the light — would make me tremble and shake."

'GAME OF THRONES' ACTRESS SAYS SHE JOINED A WELLNESS CULT THAT LED TO A PSYCHOTIC BREAK

About two months after her diagnosis, Esposito began seeing a medical expert who she said wanted to study her because of the severity of her case.

Esposito said she eventually took matters into her own hands. (Getty Images)

She underwent regular blood and urine testing, but during one appointment, Esposito said she was in such distress that she pleaded with the doctor to keep her in the hospital.

"Doctor, you got to keep me here because I'm jumping out of my skin. I'm going to jump out the window," she recalled saying.

Esposito said the remark was interpreted as a threat of self-harm.

Within half an hour, she said, she was taken to a psychiatric ward under the alias "Betty Franklin."

"I will say it was seven of the most excruciating hours of my entire life because I was yet again pleading for my sanity," she said.

Esposito said her father was with her and recalled fearing that she would not get out if he left.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"If you leave me here, I'm dying because I'm going to fight these people," she recalled thinking.

The actress said the experience became even more frightening when a doctor asked her father for permission to restrain her if she got "out of hand."

Esposito hopes her story can help others.  (FilmMagic)

Esposito forced herself to remain calm. "I thought, if I ever get out of here, I have to do something," she said.

After returning home, Esposito said she took an increasingly active role in understanding her condition and recovery.

"If you heal your gut, I promise you, not everything can go away," she said, adding that recovery "takes time."

Esposito, who said she now lives outside the United States, told Menounos that she no longer experiences panic attacks and has adopted a dramatically different pace of life.

"This is my life. I get to enjoy time," she said. "I sit down and eat lunch. I sit down and talk to people. There's no phones on the tables."

"There’s a grace given for enjoyment in life," Esposito continued. "I just think we've lost the plot with that. And no wonder why we're all sick."

Looking back on the ordeal, Esposito said she ultimately views her diagnosis as something that changed the trajectory of her life.

"Celiac disease saved my life. One hundred percent," she said.

Esposito said she believes the years of stress and living in "fight or flight" would eventually have taken an even greater toll had her illness not forced her to change course.

"I 100% would have been somewhere not good," she said.

Now, she said, she is "very, very, very clear and grateful" — including for the opportunity her experience has given her to help others.

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

articles.title: Trump warns of ‘jihadists’ ruling in Washington as Democrats show momentum
articles.excerpt: United States President Donald Trump has described Democratic candidates in the midterm US elections as “jihadists” in an apparent reference to Muslim Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed securing his ...
articles.body_text:
United States President Donald Trump has described Democratic candidates in the midterm US elections as “jihadists” in an apparent reference to Muslim Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed securing his party’s nomination for the Michigan primary elections last week.

The pronouncements fuel a proliferating wave of Islamophobic discourse among Republican lawmakers and elected officials in the sprint to lock down ballots ahead of November’s midterm elections.

“We have jihadists being elected all over the place, whether it’s communism [or] jihadism,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday. “A friend of mine called up, he said, ‘You know […] you should use the word jihadist’, that’s what’s happening. If you take a look at what’s happening in other countries, I’m not really sure that’s the way we want to live.”

Trump also hurled another tirade against people of Somali descent, of which there are upwards of 260,000 across the US. He called them “not smart”, and said they have “no aptitude” and “nothing going” for them to “tell us how to run our country”.

Edward Ahmed Mitchell, the national deputy director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), a Muslim civil rights and advocacy organisation in the US, said that Trump’s hateful anti-Muslim rhetoric “is putting a target on the back of Muslim elected officials across our nation” and that “this type of dangerous rhetoric is fueling the surge in complaints of anti-Muslim bigotry that our civil rights organization has documented over the past three years”.

Although the president refrained from explicitly naming any individual candidate, hours later, he focused his attention on El-Sayed, who is a son of Egyptian immigrants. The president shared a photo on Truth Social showing the Democratic contender positioned before a gathering that featured two women in headscarves, accompanied by the caption: “They are coming for your home and your belongings.”

Trump also targeted El-Sayed’s victory directly last week, calling him a “hater of Jews” and “hater of Israel” who will bring “filth, crime, death, destruction, embarrassment”.

Several other Republicans also beefed up their anti-Muslim rhetoric, following El-Sayed’s win, parroting remarks that Muslims do not belong in American society. Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina claimed on social media that “every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic”.

Meanwhile, Alabama Senator Tommy Tuberville labelled El-Sayed a “TERRORIST” and wrote on social media that “Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed is a RADICAL ISLAMIST.”

This outburst occurred just two days after Trump shared a social media post comparing a photo of himself and First Lady Melania Trump with one of El-Sayed and his wife Dr Sarah Jukaku, who is a psychiatrist. The image was captioned: “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s.”

Speaking on CNN’s State of the Union with host Jake Tapper on Sunday night, the Democratic Senate candidate hit back, saying, “Sarah and I actually like each other”, adding “I don’t know about the first lady and the president, but from what I’ve heard, it’s a bit of a rocky road”.

With less than 90 days to go until the highly anticipated midterm elections come to a head, and with all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 34 Senate seats up for grabs, Democrats are confronting an ideological schism between moderate leaders and triumphing democratic progressives, some of whom are increasingly being characterised as an endangerment to Washington’s national security establishment altogether.

“People don’t want to have radical lunatics involved in running our country,” said Trump on Monday, “and that’s what we have.”
