articles.title: Zac Taylor admits breaking NFL challenge flag rule for 8 years as league makes change
articles.excerpt:
A slight change to an NFL rule has been set before the start of the 2026 season, but it’s nothing new for Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor.

He admitted he’s technically been breaking an NFL r...
articles.body_text:
A slight change to an NFL rule has been set before the start of the 2026 season, but it’s nothing new for Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor.

He admitted he’s technically been breaking an NFL rule for the past eight years.

The change is that each team’s head coach will be able to delegate the ability to use the red challenge flag to someone else on the staff if they so wish.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Zac Taylor, head coach of the Cincinnati Bengals, talks to the media during training camp at Kettering Health Practice Fields in Cincinnati, Ohio, on July 29, 2026. (Getty Images)

It was the responsibility of the head coach to challenge a play, throwing the red flag on the field for review.

Now, the head coach has the ability to name a pregame challenge designee that will be responsible for those moments during the game.

VIKINGS QUARTERBACK BATTLE MEETS EXPECTED END AS KYLER MURRAY BEATS OUT JJ MCCARTHY FOR STARTING JOB

But in 2019, when Taylor was named the Bengals’ head coach, he wasn’t the one holding the flag. It was Doug Rosfeld, his chief of coaching staff, throwing the flag instead.

That’s the way Taylor has been running that aspect of his many duties as head coach, which he revealed on Tuesday during his press conference.

"We’ve been breaking that rule for eight years because I’ve never thrown a challenge flag," he said.

Taylor even added that he’d let referees know he wasn’t the one throwing it before the game, and they never took an issue with Rosfeld having that duty.

"They ask you that in pregame, who’s got the flag," Taylor mentioned. "It’s never been an issue. I didn’t even know it was frowned upon. I know there’s other coaches in the league, I’m not the only one who’s done that. I saw they implemented a new rule, so maybe we’ll get a retroactive fine or something."

Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor calls out during the first half of an NFL football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Pittsburgh, Saturday, Jan. 4, 2025. (AP Photo/Matt Freed)

Many coaches are creatures of habit so, despite the rule change, those that have the red challenge flag on their person during games will likely keep it that way. Some leave it in their pant pockets, while some even have it tucked into their socks (Bill Belichick’s favorite spot).

For Taylor, he said "it’s easier for me" not to have the flag on him during the game. One of the reasons is due to the ending of an offensive series, which he does the play-calling for, where he’ll immediately go talk to his players.

In that time, if there is a challengeable play, Rosfeld will be the one watching and determining whether it’s worth throwing the flag.

Every team, every coach works different from each other. But this slight rule change is something Taylor isn’t even batting an eye at.

Zac Taylor stands on the sideline at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, Ohio, on Jan. 4, 2026. (Getty Images)

He’s been handling it that way the entire time.

"They always made it clear to me that I have to be next to Doug," Taylor added. "I guess if we ever need to sneak one by them when I was back there [talking to Joe Burrow] and they couldn't get me in the headset, Doug could have done it, but that's never come up. It's just part of our routine now. I feel better with Doug having it."

Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Australia politics live: Coalition to heavily cut net migration and shred 96% of house construction code; CBA posts bumper $11bn profit
articles.excerpt:
Policy comes as debate continues over causes of and solutions to housing issues. Follow today’s news live

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Coalition has promised to dr...
articles.body_text:
Policy comes as debate continues over causes of and solutions to housing issues. Follow today’s news live

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Coalition has promised to drop net overseas migration to under 180,000 a year over the forward estimates, including by cutting family and international student visas, as part of a push to open up more housing supply.

The shadow housing minister Andrew Bragg will be up at the national press club and says the opposition will strip the 2000 page national construction code, which he says makes it “illegal to build a cheap safe house”, down to an 80-page “basic Australian standard”.

The current permanent migration level is set to 185,000 while the net overseas migration figure has been trending downwards from post-covid peaks and is anticipated to be 245,000 for 2026–27.

Net overseas migration is the total number of people coming into the country against those going out – which means it can be tricky to have total control over.

Bragg will tell the press club that the government has sat over a shortfall of 130,000 dwellings which can be closed if the NOM drops under 180,000 over four years.

double quotation markA NOM reduction on this scale is manageable and in line with reductions we have managed in recent history – for example in 2009-2010 when the NOM declined from 300,000 to 175,000 in around 18 months.

This will be achieved through a higher share of skilled migrant workers linked to jobs that meet Australian industry needs. This includes more reductions in other streams like family, international students and other temporary migrants.

Australian homes are so energy inefficient they’re often too hot and too cold

Tim Wilson says through on a jumper if you’re feeling a bit cold in winter instead of spending thousands on fixing the energy efficiency rating of a home – but Australian homes are pretty notorious for being really energy inefficient.

They’re either too hot in summer or too cold in winter – and often times it’s both.

In fact, the average Australian home built before 2003 averaged just 1.8 stars on a scale from zero to 10 stars under the Nationwide House Energy Rating Scheme.

Any many Australian homes are closer to tents than insulated eco-buildings.

With the cold also sometimes comes mould, with some Australian rental homes are colder and more damp than is considered safe by the World Health Organization.

Should energy efficiency standards in housing be optional? The opposition is considering it.

Andrew Bragg says under his 80-page national construction code essential structural, fire safety and health requirements will be compulsory but additional features will be “optional”.

The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, is in the RN Breakfast hot seat after Jim Chalmers and is asked whether that sounds about right to him.

Wilson says there are “risks on all side” in whether you make energy efficiency standards compulsory or not, and that different parts of the country have different climates so there shouldn’t be a “one size fits all approach”.

double quotation markWe have a risk that Australians can’t afford to rent or to buy their own home by the government’s own budget design.

There are some places in the country where you will get cold spells or hot spells for a very small amount of the year, whereas for the rest of the year, it’s not necessary … Some people call it putting a jumper on in winter rather than spending huge amounts of money, tens of thousands of dollars.

Commonwealth Bank has recorded a bumper $10.9bn full year cash profit, up 7%, after recording strong growth in home and business lending, despite recent weakness in the housing market.

The robust result, for the 12 months to 30 June, was largely locked in before mortgage volumes started to fall in response to a series of interest rate hikes and Labor’s investor tax changes, announced in May.

CBA told shareholders this morning that while the economy had remained resilient, growth was slowing with “higher interest rates and inflation placing uneven pressure on households incomes and economic activity”.

There are signs of distress among some of the bank customers, with arrears among personal loan customers surging. Arrears for home loans and credit cards have also ticked higher in recent months, although they remain at modest levels.

The bank declared a final dividend of $2.70, representing a 10c increase on the last half year dividend.

Bragg ‘bit late to the party’ on reforming construction code: Chalmers

Jim Chalmers says the government is already acting on simplifying the 2000-page construction code to make it easier to build houses in Australia.

Today the shadow housing minister, Andrew Bragg will announce that the Coalition wants to slash that code down to 80-pages, but Chalmers says he’s “late to the party”.

The government has frozen the code for four years, and Chalmers says a revamped code is coming soon:

double quotation markWe’re going to present a final plan to building ministers later this year and that will streamline the code, reduce variations, improve where the provisions are too complicated, make the code relevant in an age of AI.

Don’t judge the housing market over a few months of data, says Chalmers

The government is facing heat over a cooling housing market across Australia, which the treasurer says is due to a range of factors, not just the changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax announced in the May budget.

Jim Chalmers is on ABC RN Breakfast this morning welcoming the Reserve Bank’s decision to hold rates yesterday, and says that there have been several housing downturns in recent decades.

double quotation markYou shouldn’t judge the housing market by volatility over a period of a few months.

If you think about house prices in this country in the 2000s, even with that quite remarkable house price growth over that period. If you take the last 10 years or so, we’ve actually seen prices go down at least seven times by our count … The Reserve Bank Governor said yesterday, I’ve said on a number of occasions, the private sector market economists have said as well, what we’re seeing in the housing market is a consequence of a whole range of factors, economic conditions, interest rates, policy changes, not any one factor on their own.

Asked about data from Westpac showing a dropping number of home loan applications, Chalmers takes the same argument, that “you shouldn’t jump to conclusions based on a few months of data”.

‘The Liberals have absolutely lost the plot’ says O’Neil on melon-gate

The regular Wednesday TV sparring match between the housing minister, Clare O’Neil, and shadow attorney general, Michaelia Cash, has spent half the morning debating … you guessed it … melon-gate.

O’Neil says the opposition has frankly “lost the plot” by referring the leak of a diplomatic note sent by Japan to the Australian federal police.

double quotation markThe Liberals have absolutely lost the plot here. They are referring this podcast matter to the Australian federal police. My personal view is that the Australian federal police should be allowed to focus on their job, which is keeping Australians safe and fighting crime for Australians.

Cash says it’s totally justified for the police to dedicate their time to investigating that leak to the media, and takes aim at O’Neil for defending the PM:

double quotation markThis has now gone from embarrassing to extraordinary. A sensitive diplomatic cable from one of our closest allies has ended up in the media, and the AFP should investigate that. But I actually think the hypocrisy from the Labor women like Clare – that is an utter disgrace. You have just defended the grubby, dirty comments of our prime minister.

Let this be over soon one way or another.

Are the Coalition 100% set on cutting net overseas migration to 180,000?

Despite Andrew Bragg’s speech being sent to the media overnight, this morning the shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, doesn’t seem to want to lock in the 180,000 net overseas migration target.

Speaking to News24, Wilson was asked a couple of times about the details of Bragg’s announcement but wouldn’t commit to the figure.

He said, “I’ll leave Senator Bragg’s speech in his National Press Club address to Senator Bragg” and stuck to more general statements about migration intake in Australia.

Asked directly whether the Coalition is looking at the 180,000 target, Wilson replies:

double quotation markI don’t think you should bank that at all. Let’s just wait and see, firstly, what Senate Bragg’s saying in his speech – and we haven’t made an announcement about where we’re going to be going into the next election – but our focus is actually about what we need to do to invest in the long-term growth and success of our country.

The Coalition has promised to drop net overseas migration to under 180,000 a year over the forward estimates, including by cutting family and international student visas, as part of a push to open up more housing supply.

The shadow housing minister Andrew Bragg will be up at the national press club and says the opposition will strip the 2000 page national construction code, which he says makes it “illegal to build a cheap safe house”, down to an 80-page “basic Australian standard”.

The current permanent migration level is set to 185,000 while the net overseas migration figure has been trending downwards from post-covid peaks and is anticipated to be 245,000 for 2026–27.

Net overseas migration is the total number of people coming into the country against those going out – which means it can be tricky to have total control over.

Bragg will tell the press club that the government has sat over a shortfall of 130,000 dwellings which can be closed if the NOM drops under 180,000 over four years.

double quotation markA NOM reduction on this scale is manageable and in line with reductions we have managed in recent history – for example in 2009-2010 when the NOM declined from 300,000 to 175,000 in around 18 months.

This will be achieved through a higher share of skilled migrant workers linked to jobs that meet Australian industry needs. This includes more reductions in other streams like family, international students and other temporary migrants.

Good morning, Krishani Dhanji here with you for another busy sitting day ahead! The negotiations are continuing between the government and the opposition on gambling, NDIS, and news bargaining incentive reforms – all of which Labor will be hoping to pass this fortnight.

And why milk it for one day when you can milk it – or should I say juice it – for two? The prime minister is still facing pressure to apologise over melon-gate which pretty much took over parliament yesterday.

And the opposition is promising to strip back the housing construction code to help builders build quicker – more on that shortly.

articles.title: At every opportunity, Anthony Fauci hid the truth about COVID, masks, from the American public
articles.excerpt: The 'Outnumbered' panel discusses text messages sent by former NIAID director Dr. Anthony Fauci in January 2021. The communications show Fauci privately discussed miscarriage risks associated with fev...
articles.body_text:
The 'Outnumbered' panel discusses text messages sent by former NIAID director Dr. Anthony Fauci in January 2021. The communications show Fauci privately discussed miscarriage risks associated with fevers from second COVID-19 vaccine doses while publicly stating no safety flags existed for pregnant women.

Six and a half years after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and after years of most in the media and the political class pretending it never happened, our response to the spread of the coronavirus is back in the news. All thanks to the not-so-fearless leader of our pandemic policy making, former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases head Anthony Fauci.

Fauci spent years, starting in early 2020 and beyond, as the center of attention in the United States and beyond. And boy did he know it and revel in it. Promoted by the media as a star "expert," an unbiased keeper of all scientific knowledge, and made into a celebrity thanks to his obvious political leanings and anti-Trump messaging, Fauci became beloved. Just ask him.

The release of his diaries though, revealed some thoroughly discrediting and upsetting details about Fauci's private beliefs.

ANTHONY FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY AND EMAILS SHOW HE KNEW LOCKDOWNS FAILED AND PUSHED MASKS WITHOUT EVIDENCE

Former NIH Director Anthony Fauci is sworn in before testifying to Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on July 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

He knew that lockdowns weren't working, saying that cases seemed to rise and fall regardless of what was closed and when. He knew that there was no justification for masking other than "everyone else is doing it already," and a desire to fit in with the CDC. He knew that COVID-19 vaccines weren't stopping the spread, and even worried about getting infected at an event that required proof of vaccination to attend. He was in communication with important media figures like CNN's Jake Tapper or Dana Bash, or in Tapper's case, described a budding friendship and dinner parties during the early part of the pandemic.

But it's not just his diaries. We now have some texts, released by Sen. Ron Johnson, that indicate he was privately concerned about COVID-19 vaccine side effects and thought they were worth investigating. And alerting his partners in the Biden administration, who concurred.

In one already-infamous newly released text, Fauci said that the COVID-19 vaccine "theoretically could be associated with miscarriage in the 1st trimester."

Sen. Rand Paul, one of Fauci's harshest government critics, addressed that new release in a post on X.

"Once again, Anthony Fauci was saying one thing in public and something completely different in private," he said. "He was willing to put women and their unborn children at risk instead of admitting that he was wrong about the vaccines that he tried guilting Americans into taking."

But even that buries the lede: not only was Fauci saying something different in public and private, he went on television, with his buddies, and described anyone who raised such concerns as dangerous conspiracy theorists.

Thus far, there isn't a lot of high-quality evidence that the COVID-19 vaccine is associated with increased risk of miscarriage. Despite some big numbers being floated around on social media, most research has not found an elevated risk relative to normal rates. That's not the point though. The point is that nobody was allowed to talk about it.

When you limit conversation, when you make public statements of confirmation that everything's safe, effective, and there's nothing to see here, you risk losing trust if there is a legitimate concern to investigate. And there were legitimate concerns, even if not about miscarriages.

Anthony Fauci, the former Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and medical advisor to several U.S. presidents, testifies under subpoena about his role in the national response to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a U.S. Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 29, 2026. (REUTERS/Nathan Howard)

NBA STAR KYRIE IRVING GOT HIS APOLOGY, BUT FOUR COVID-ERA ATHLETES STILL WAITING FOR THEIRS FROM THE MEDIA

Myocarditis was ignored, downplayed, or ultimately dismissed. There were side effects that affected significant numbers of people. Fauci, clearly, privately believed that some of these issues necessitated investigation. While publicly saying something completely different, and implying the public shouldn't even be able to have those concerns or discussions.

Importantly, it wasn't just vaccine side effects that was dishonest about. And one of his emails undermines his later messaging on masking too.

When Fauci joined 60 Minutes in February 2020, he specifically stated that there was "no reason to be walking around with a mask."

Even more importantly, he said that masks do not provide the type of protection people think they do, that they might block a droplet or two, but could even backfire since people touch their faces more when wearing a mask.

That was all true and correct. Masks don't work, they don't provide protection, they do touch their face more frequently, and nobody needed to wear them. Obviously, however, Fauci changed his story months later. Masks become the single most important thing you could do, to the point where "wear a mask" became one of the most important phrases of 2020, according to CBS at the time.

Yet in a rare instance of even moderately difficult questioning posed to the saint-like Fauci, when asked about later, he defended his flip flop by saying he was lying to protect supply for healthcare workers. And didn't know about asymptomatic COVID-19 spread at the time.

"I don't regret anything I said then because in the context of the time in which I said it, it was correct. We were told in our task force meetings that we have a serious problem with the lack of PPEs and masks for the health providers who are putting themselves in harm's way every day to take care of sick people," Fauci said in an interview with Norah O'Donnell.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

"When it became clear that the infection could be spread by asymptomatic carriers who don't know they're infected, that made it very clear that we had to strongly recommend masks," he added.

Putting aside that it's a monumental lie to claim that health providers would order PPE and masks from Amazon, like the public, and that cloth masks are not what health providers use, it's revealing that he claims his flip flop in April 2020 was based on learning about asymptomatic spread.

Except, that's also a lie. And we know it, because of what Fauci wrote in an email.

Former NIH Director Anthony Fauci testifies before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. Fauci was expected to be questioned about his diary entries during his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. (Getty Images)

On January 30, 2020, Fauci wrote, "Another amazing and difficult day." He went on to describe what he'd learned about the spread of the virus, including this important note:

"Mart Cetron who was listening in on the WHO call said that the epidemic was accelerating that this is was clear that the incubation period was shorter (2-5 days than was previously felt and that asymptomatic transmission was occurring.)"

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Ah. Interesting. So in January 2020, Fauci knew that asymptomatic transmission was happening, because he'd been told that by someone listening in on a call with the World Health Organization. In February 2020, he went on 60 Minutes and said that nobody needed to wear masks because they don't work. In April 2020, he changed his mind and says everyone should be wearing masks. Then later in 2020, he tells CBS that he changed his mind on recommending masks because of asymptomatic transmission.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK CULTURE COVERAGE

Spectacular, historic, inexcusable dishonesty. He knew in January that asymptomatic spread was happening. He still said masks didn't work and weren't necessarily the following month. Then when asked to justify his change of heart, he lies again and says it's because he learned about asymptomatic spread, after telling the public not to wear masks. A malicious, vindictive, prolific series of lies.

As always, the more we learn about Anthony Fauci, the worse he looks. His primary goal wasn't serving and helping the public, or accurately communicating risks, trade-offs, or uncertainty. It was promoting himself and misleading Americans to service his own agenda. That's his real legacy, and why trust in public health has never been lower.

articles.title: Bella Thorne says Hollywood treated her like a kid on screen and an adult off camera
articles.excerpt:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Bella Thorne's life as a child star came with a harsh reality: Hollywood expected her to be a kid on screen and an adult everywhere ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Bella Thorne's life as a child star came with a harsh reality: Hollywood expected her to be a kid on screen and an adult everywhere else.

Thorne began working in entertainment as a child, appearing as a model before taking on television roles in shows including HBO’s "Big Love." Her major breakthrough arrived in 2010 when she was cast as CeCe Jones opposite Zendaya’s Rocky Blue in Disney Channel’s "Shake It Up."

"You're ... spending all of your hours a day on set with adults, you know, that is – it's like such a different, the brain's like how do I–" Thorne explained during an appearance on "Call Her Daddy."

GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'

Bella Thorne reflected on the pressures of growing up in Hollywood during a recent appearance on Alexandra Cooper’s podcast. (Getty Images)

"And I'm expected to be this child, but I'm also working like hours like an adult and being in adult conversations," she added. "And when I f--k up it's my bad, not like a child – It's my bad. Like you're an adult, it's your bad."

But navigating those adult expectations while growing up in the public eye didn't come easily for Thorne.

"Well, I think people can see how I've managed it publicly," she told host Alexandra Cooper. "They can see it, they've got photos of it. Oh, they got all the photos. Oh, wow. I don't know that I ever handled it or balanced it out correctly."

"I don't think that I ever had that mental clarity," Thorne acknowledged. "I've worked a lot on the more recent side. I got to a point where I just needed to kind of change things in my life and get better at – I was working so much and yet was leaving very little time for the things that I really, really cared about."

Bella Thorne rose to Disney Channel fame alongside Zendaya after starring in "Shake It Up" as CeCe Jones. (Craig Sjodin/Disney Channel via Getty Images)

FORMER DISNEY STAR MAITLAND WARD SAYS YOUNG ACTORS WERE TREATED LIKE A 'PRODUCT' IN HOLLYWOOD FACTORY

Thorne said she spent the past two years working to prioritize her mental health, a shift that became especially important after "Color Your Hurt" left her feeling emotionally drained. The now 28-year-old actress revealed she finally gave herself "some space to breathe" along with grace.

"I don't think I ever did that when I was younger," she said.

While Thorne struggled to give herself that same grace as a child star, she recalled feeling a dramatic shift when she turned 18.

Bella Thorne said she felt a sense of freedom when she turned 18 after years of working as a child actor. (Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images)

"...I was like, 'I'm free,'" the "Midnight Sun" star recalled.

"Like I'm literally free. Like I'm walking into this house and no one's asking me when I'm like, when I'm gonna be there, when this time or when I'm gonna leave. It ... was such a weird – and you don't know what's weird until someone else tells you it's weird."

Thorne also spoke candidly about being compared to her fellow Disney Channel stars, including Selena Gomez, Miley Cyrus and Demi Lovato.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Bella Thorne said comparisons to fellow Disney stars including Miley Cyrus, Selena Gomez and Demi Lovato began when she was just 12. Pictured with Zendaya. (Craig Sjodin/Disney Channel via Getty Images)

"I didn't so much hang out with people from the network," Thorne recalled. "I hung out with Zendaya, we hung out ... 'Shake It Up' was in a different time when Miley and Selena and Demi and those shows – They were all, I think 16, 17 when we were starting. So the eras are so different, and yet they intersect."

She said people questioned whether she would become Disney's next "bad girl," something she struggled to comprehend at such a young age.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Bella Thorne opened up about the mental-health work she has prioritized over the past two years. (Gary Miller/Getty Images for Glass House Brands)

"And I remember when I was 12, people asking me if I was gonna be – comparing us all, all the Disney girls and with Miley and Selena and this new era – and asking which was gonna be the next bad girl," Thorne claimed. "And, 'Are you gonna be like Lindsay Lohan?' And like all these things at 12, 13 – you're just, your brain is like trying so hard. 'Like am I gonna be like what? Like what? What is the question?' Like, oh my God."

Thorne later moved beyond her Disney image with a steady mix of film and television roles.

Thorne has also made a bigger push behind the camera. In August 2026, she signed on to write, direct and star in "Spring Breakers 2," following her feature directorial debut, "Color Your Hurt."

articles.title: Trump’s Air Force One deception faces scrutiny over ‘decoy’ passengers
articles.excerpt:
Journalists and others were allowed to fly on presidential jet despite security threat while Trump was spirited away

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

Democrats called on Tuesday for...
articles.body_text:
Journalists and others were allowed to fly on presidential jet despite security threat while Trump was spirited away

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

Democrats called on Tuesday for a congressional briefing over a stunning charade in which Donald Trump was secretly spirited to different plane than the one the public and press believed he was travelling on, an episode first reported by the Washington Post and also by the New York Times. Critics now question why reporters and the public had been deliberately misled.

When US intelligence allegedly found a credible threat that Iran plotted to kill him last month, Trump left Air Force One in a catering truck. While the president was reportedly snuck out the side door of the plane, more than a hundred aides, officials and reporters were kept onboard to fly towards Britain, without being told there was a threat to their lives.

“It appears that the idea was we can reduce the danger to President Trump by offering up 100 or so people to be killed by the Iranians in his place,” said Steven Cash, executive director of the Steady State and a former CIA intelligence officer and senior adviser to the Department of Homeland Security’s intelligence branch.

Richard Blumenthal, a Democratic senator for Connecticut, called the operation “unprecedented and surreal” and “downright scary” on CNN. “There has to be a congressional briefing because it involves not just the safety of the president.

“I want to know what precautions were taken to make sure that all of the passengers on that Air Force One, which was judged too dangerous for the president to fly on, what precautions were taken to keep the staff and reporters on that plane safe?”

The White House had publicly said the president would fly to Britain onboard Air Force One – albeit an older version instead of the new Qatari-gifted aircraft. In reality, Trump boarded the presidential jet in full view of television cameras before being spirited away minutes later and transferred to an air force C-32A.

The deception was sufficiently elaborate that journalists travelling with the president – and some White House staff – believed Trump remained onboard Air Force One. Reporters were instructed to keep the shades over their windows closed during the flight.

The C-32A carrying Trump flew to RAF Mildenhall in Britain, arriving at about 10.20pm. The older Air Force One and the travelling press pool arrived minutes later. Photographers subsequently captured Trump descending from the presidential aircraft, apparently after he had been secretly reunited with it.

Trump then greeted troops at the base before boarding the newly refurbished Boeing 747 donated by Qatar and flying on to Washington.

Ned Price, a former deputy to the US ambassador to the UN, said he did not begrudge any White House taking extraordinary measures to protect the president but the current administration had perpetuated an “outright lie” for weeks and turned reporters into “unwitting conspirators”.

Price, an ex-special assistant to President Barack Obama on the national security council, added: “There was a way to do this where they didn’t need to lie. They could have enlisted the travelling press pool, who would have very willingly, I am certain, not reported on certain security arrangements.

“Once all was said and done and the president was safely in the UK or back at Andrews air force base, they could have said, ‘This is what we did and this is why we did it,’” Price added. “But they feel no compunction to the truth. They feel no loyalty to the truth. Instead it’s just an effort over the past month to lie and to mislead.”

Journalists also raised concerns. Jake Tapper, an anchor on CNN, tweeted: “Obviously the life of the president is paramount, and previous White Houses have used deception to protect the president’s life. But no officials I’ve spoken to have ever before heard of using an AF1 full of WH staff and journalists as a decoy during an imminent threat.”

The White House has not directly confirmed the details of the operation. Its communications director, Steven Cheung, instead told the Post the president faced numerous threats and that officials used “every tool at our disposal” to protect him.

The revelation sheds new light on an abrupt decision that had already raised questions about the security of the Qatari aircraft. Trump had flown the newly refurbished jet to the Nato summit – its first international journey – but unexpectedly announced that he would instead use the older Air Force One on the first leg of his return journey.

At the time, Trump said the new aircraft was being flown to Mildenhall so US troops stationed there could inspect it. The New York Times and CBS News subsequently reported that intelligence officials had raised concerns about a possible attack on Trump or his aircraft amid the escalating conflict with Iran.

During the summit, the US military was conducting major strikes against Iran, adding to fears of Iranian retaliation. The new account suggests that the threat was taken more seriously than previously understood.

Not everyone is convinced the threat justified what happened next. “From the Iranian perspective, pulling off an attempted targeting of presidential aircraft at this depth would be extremely implausible; it would require close-in clandestine operators with man-portable anti-air systems,” said Ankit Panda, the Stanton senior fellow in the nuclear policy program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Panda said it was not clear there had been a specific, credible threat within Turkey itself, though presidential security routinely plans around “known unknowns”.

“Iran doesn’t have surface-to-air missiles that could target an aircraft taking off from Ankara,” said Dr Jeffrey Lewis, a distinguished fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute. Iran could in theory strike a plane on the runway with a ballistic missile, he said, “but that seems very unlikely”. His guess: US officials were worried about “a terrorist-like attack using a man-portable air defense system,” such as a Chinese-made QW-12 or FN-16, or a North Korean version of the Russian Igla.

James Jeffrey, a former US ambassador to Turkey and deputy national security adviser under George W Bush who is now a distinguished fellow at the pro-Israel Washington Institute, said the secrecy around moving Trump to another aircraft pointed to serious intelligence behind the threat.

“This is very unusual, and indicates that they had very good intelligence of a threat, and that they did not trust the aircraft that he was in,” said Jeffrey, who has extensive experience traveling onboard Air Force One.

Jeffrey said he believed the intelligence may have come from Israel, which has extensive intelligence capabilities focused on Iran. While Israeli officials sometimes seek to “not only inform but influence” US policy, he said they would not risk fabricating a threat involving the president’s safety.

“They wouldn’t play with something as serious as the president’s safety,” Jeffrey said, adding that any such warning would prompt the US government to verify the intelligence, gather more information about the threat and follow up on it.”

Trump himself appeared to hint at the security concerns when reporters questioned him about why they had been ordered to keep their window shades closed. “You’re probably on a dangerous flight,” he said. “But if I go, you go. Right?”

Asked later whether there had been a credible Iranian threat against Air Force One, Trump said: “Well, I have a threat all the time. I’m number one on their list before you.”

The operation has nevertheless prompted questions about the decision to deceive the press corps and the public, particularly after the White House continued to maintain the cover story.

“The way to mitigate the threat included offering up the remaining people on Air Force One as an unwitting decoy,” Cash said. What was unclear, he added, was the order of operations – whether Trump’s team waited until he was safely away before letting the rest of the plane take off, or sent it up not knowing. If officials had simply announced Trump wasn’t onboard once he had landed safely, he said, they could have accomplished most of what they wanted without anyone remaining in the dark. “It really does sound like they were intended to serve as a decoy.”

Cash pointed to Intelligence Community Directive 191, the government’s “duty to warn” policy, which requires intelligence agencies to alert people who are the specific, credible target of a threat of killing, serious injury or kidnapping – including, he said, journalists and civilians, not just officials.

“If there’s intelligence collected that shows that a human being or a group of human beings are in danger, they need to be warned,” Cash said. “The question is: were the people who remained on the plane warned? If not, it violated ICD 191.” The directive, adopted by the director of national intelligence in 2015, does allow waivers when a warning would compromise sources, methods or operations – but Cash said he knew of no exception written for using people as decoys. “Probably because nobody ever thought that anybody would come up with the idea.”

Others defended the operation. Ari Fleischer, a former White House press secretary under President George W Bush, said that if the report was accurate, the Secret Service, air force and White House deserved credit for protecting the president. “If there’s a credible threat against any POTUS, their job is to protect him,” he wrote on X.

The extraordinary journey echoes an operation carried out by Bill Clinton in 2000, when the former president secretly flew into Pakistan onboard an unmarked executive jet while Air Force One was used as a decoy.

But Matthew Hoh, a senior fellow at the Eisenhower Media Network and Iraq war combat veteran, described the Trump incident as unique. “If it was a credible threat and they allowed Air Force One to take off thinking it was going to be shot down or whatever was going happen, they saw the pilots, the air crew, the White House staff, the journalists as all being expendable, dispensable, meaningless,” he said.

“There’s a lot of implications here with this story that help us understand this administration better or maybe reinforce the understanding we already have of this venal and vainglorious White House.”

articles.title: Trump's Justice Department sues New York, other blue states over tuition for illegal immigrants
articles.excerpt: Colorado Gov. Jared Polis clarifies the state's in-state tuition policy for undocumented students. He emphasizes that these students do not qualify for federal financial aid like Pell grants or studen...
articles.body_text:
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis clarifies the state's in-state tuition policy for undocumented students. He emphasizes that these students do not qualify for federal financial aid like Pell grants or student loans.

The Department of Justice under the Trump administration announced Monday that it plans to file lawsuits against New York, Connecticut and Vermont over laws that it claims provide in-state tuition and other financial incentives to illegal immigrants.

"These laws unconstitutionally discriminate against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rates or scholarships, create incentives for illegal immigration, and reward illegal aliens with benefits that U.S. citizens are not eligible for, all in direct conflict with federal law," a statement from the department read.

According to the legal complaints, the Department of Justice is seeking to enjoin enforcement of laws that provide financial assistance to illegal immigrants or provide tuition rates to any immigrants "who maintain in-state residency, regardless of whether they are lawfully present."

NEBRASKA ENDS IN-STATE TUITION BENEFITS FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS UNDER DOJ DEAL

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong spoke out against the Department of Justice's lawsuit targeting his state. (Ryan Caron King/Connecticut Public via Getty Images)

"This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens," Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division said in a press release. "This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country."

In a comment to Fox News Digital, the Department of Justice expressed confidence in its latest lawsuits, boasting legal wins in five other states with similar complaints.

"Under the leadership of Attorney General Todd Blanche, the Department’s efforts have already delivered wins for the American people, as five similar lawsuits in Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska and Illinois have resulted favorable orders permanently enjoining and declaring unconstitutional analogous laws that gave reduced tuition to illegal aliens, including an order from the Fifth Circuit," the statement read.

OVER 100 CALIFORNIA COLLEGES ACCUSED OF DISCRIMINATING AGAINST US-BORN STUDENTS IN NEW DOJ COMPLAINT

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong pushed back on the lawsuit against his state in a comment to Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

The Department of Justice under President Donald Trump filed lawsuits against 17 states targeting in-state tuition laws for illegal immigrants. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)

"Note to Trump — stay out of Connecticut. How we run our schools and teach our kids is none of your business, and you have no authority to force the sovereign state of Connecticut to deny our kids a future," Tong said. "I fought for this bill as a legislator when it passed in 2011, and I’ll fight to defend Connecticut families now from this cruel attack. Connecticut offers in-state tuition and financial aid to all eligible Connecticut students because all kids deserve the opportunity to learn, to advance, and to achieve their dreams. Donald Trump doesn’t run UConn or any of our state colleges, and we’re not about to let him start."

FLORIDA BOARD VOTES TO BAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS FROM PUBLIC COLLEGE ADMISSIONS

Fox News Digital also reached out to New York and Vermont's attorneys general for comment on the developing lawsuits.

As of Monday, the Department of Justice has filed 17 lawsuits targeting laws that the Trump administration has claimed provide reduced tuition for illegal immigrants. The other states sued included Minnesota, Virginia, California, New Jersey, Kansas, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Maryland and Colorado.

A federal judge ruled last month that Illinois' in-state tuition policies for illegal immigrants were unconstitutional. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Last month, a federal judge provided a win for the Trump administration's Justice Department after ruling that Illinois' in-state tuition policies, the RISE Act and the Illinois DREAM Act, were "unconstitutional and invalid." The department originally sued Illinois in September 2025.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

articles.title: Dethroned Miss North Carolina USA threatens legal action over title removal
articles.excerpt:
Brittany Boltinhouse’s attorney says removal of title and crown ‘another troubling example of cancel culture’

A lawyer for beauty queen Brittany Boltinhouse, dethroned as Miss North Carolina USA last...
articles.body_text:
Brittany Boltinhouse’s attorney says removal of title and crown ‘another troubling example of cancel culture’

A lawyer for beauty queen Brittany Boltinhouse, dethroned as Miss North Carolina USA last week, is threatening legal action, claiming the actions of pageant organizers were “wrongful and unjustified”.

The attorney, Patrick Mincey, described the removal of her title and crown “another troubling example of cancel culture”.

Boltinhouse, 27, was stripped of the title after event organizers said her conduct had violated Miss USA standards “over an extended period of time” – but did not specify how she had violated its policies.

The North Carolina news outlet NCBeat reported that Boltinhouse’s resurfaced social media posts showed her freely using the N-word under the username Sosa the Stallion between 2017 and 2019.

Boltinhouse won the title in June and was preparing to represent North Carolina at the 75th annual Miss USA pageant in Miami later this month.

Organizers said in a statement that the decision to remove Boltinhouse “was not made lightly”. The first runner-up, Myla Hadley, has been named Miss North Carolina USA 2026.

“It followed a thorough review of recently surfaced information and was based on the totality of the circumstances and our responsibility to preserve the integrity of the Miss North Carolina USA title and the values of our organization.”

Thom Brodeur, president and CEO of Miss USA, said that the brand “does not tolerate racism, homophobia, transphobia, nor language that strips any person of their dignity – whoever they are”.

Mincey said in an Instagram video on Monday that his firm had evidence his client, who is Mormon, was “targeted because of her Christian faith and her conservative political views”, Mincey said.

Mincey said his firm had obtained recorded statements of pageant officials acknowledging there was no “legitimate or legal basis” for the decision to strip Boltinhouse, who would have been the third Latina and first Honduran woman to represent North Carolina at Miss USA, of her state title.

Mincey, who did not lay out specific allegations of religious or racial bias, called Boltinhouse the “very best of the American dream” and pointed to her background as a daughter of immigrants who grew up in rural North Carolina and how, as a pageant newcomer, she won four of five awards at the June Miss North Carolina USA.

Boltinhouse told the Carolina Journal: “I believe I was stripped of my title because of my political stance and my belief system as a conservative Christian woman.

“I’m proud of my faith, I’m proud of my standards, I’m a proud conservative woman, but Christian woman, a God-fearing woman,” she said.

“Every teenager has made a mistake; every person has made a mistake,” she added. “I’m here to talk about the woman I am today, things may have happened a decade ago, but I am the hardworking woman who stood up there and won Miss North Carolina USA fair and square.”

Boltinhouse claimed pageant organizers had not offered her a clear reason for being dethroned: “Honestly, I don’t know; I wasn’t really given anything.”

A Blaize Productions, license holder for Miss North Carolina USA, told The News & Observer that the reasons “were clearly shared and expressed” to Boltinhouse.

Mincey said Boltinhouse had “earned the respect and admiration of millions who support her. And one thing is for certain: Brittany Boltinhouse will not be canceled.”

articles.title: Anguish of Colombian brother at rubble of building being searched for earthquake survivors
articles.excerpt:
At the scene of the rescue, workers and volunteers hold their hands in air in a symbol for silence, allowing survivors to be heard

Efraín Gallego does not lose faith that his brother will be found al...
articles.body_text:
At the scene of the rescue, workers and volunteers hold their hands in air in a symbol for silence, allowing survivors to be heard

Efraín Gallego does not lose faith that his brother will be found alive, although when he speaks about him, trapped beneath the rubble of a building, his voice breaks and he swallows hard until he regains his composure.

"You feel anguish. Every time there is an alert about someone being alive, hope is reborn that we will find him," Gallego tells me emotionally.

His 80-year-old brother was buried along with his wife when the Torres del Limonar building collapsed in Cali.

This city in south-western Colombia is one of the hardest hit by the earthquake.

The building has become a symbol of the tragedy in the country's third most populous city.

Cali has more than two million inhabitants. According to Mayor Alejandro Éder, there are at least 95 dead.

Under the scorching heat on Tuesday morning, Torres del Limonar is a shattered mountain of rubble, with mattresses, furniture, and belongings peeking out from the concrete.

On top of the remains are rescuers and volunteers: "Silence! We are firefighters. If you can hear us, shout or make any noise."

The phrase is repeated every time the teams dig deep enough to believe they may be close to a survivor.

These are the moments when Gallego regains hope, but the seconds pass and no answers come from below.

Efraín Gallego spoke to BBC Mundo at the scene of the collapse

Torres del Limonar is one of more than 50 collapsed buildings in Cali.

It is located in its south, in the Capri neighbourhood. The four-storey building held dozens of apartments. The exact number of tenants who were inside when it collapsed is unknown.

Around it, apart from some cracks, the rest of the buildings seem to have escaped the fate of the Torres.

Rescuers, military personnel, volunteers, paramedics, firefighters, humanitarian workers, and journalists have come here.

There are more than 100 people waiting for news. According to Mayor Éder, as of Monday night, it was estimated that 25 people were trapped under the rubble.

Éder declared a nighttime curfew to speed up rescue operations.

The night passed. Excavations continue. A rescuer at the site said about 10 people had been saved since the collapse.

Reports in local media, such as one from Blu Pacífico radio, spoke of six survivors up until a few minutes before my arrival, including an infant only a few months old.

In the midst of tragedy, figures are often closer to estimates than definitive data.

"What I can tell you is that right now there are at least two people detected alive. Tunnels are being made to get them out. One of them has to have his leg freed," rescuer James Velasco tells me.

Some rescuers are clearing debris from the structure using handsaws

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck Colombia on Monday, 10 August, is the worst in this century, according to the National Geological Service.

In addition to Cali, it left destruction and death in other regions such as Chocó, in the north-west.

Around the remains of Torres del Limonar, unlike Gallego, many residents choose not to speak. They are visibly affected.

Some sleep exhausted on the ground or on a sofa placed in the street. Others gather together under the shade for support.

The hours are long, increasingly so, and the anguish grows.

In shattered Cali, residents search for loved ones

"In the past I have participated in operations where we have pulled out survivors after seven days trapped."

"Those who are meant to survive, survive. Nothing is written," he adds.

"I wanted to help from the very beginning."

Amid his anguish, Gallego wants to acknowledge the work of ordinary citizens.

"We must mention all the people who have come to help with water, supplies, tools, equipment; there is a lot of collaboration. Volunteers are plentiful," he says.

Alejandro Mahecha, 19, is one of those volunteers. He decided to come after spending the night safely with his family and overcoming the initial shock.

"I wanted to help from the very beginning. The earthquake affected my city and the homes of people I know. I came to this site because there has been a lot of talk about this building and the need for help here," the young man explains.

Alejandro Mahecha arrived to help from the morning when the building collapsed

Together with several friends, Mahecha helps remove rubble, bring water to rescuers, and clear the street to facilitate evacuation efforts.

In the background, hammers and saws can be heard creating escape routes through the destruction.

They stop only when those present raise their arms.

That means everyone must remain silent. Gallego waits. This time, too, there was no news of his brother.

Rescuers scramble for survivors with 180 dead in Colombia earthquake

articles.title: A combination of bad coaching hires and subpar quarterback play is the culprit for SEC's recent swoon
articles.excerpt:
Dan Dakich reacts to Greg Sankey saying the SEC is exploring options outside of the NCAA.

It has been a hotly debated topic in college football circles as to whether the SEC's reign of dominance has ...
articles.body_text:
Dan Dakich reacts to Greg Sankey saying the SEC is exploring options outside of the NCAA.

It has been a hotly debated topic in college football circles as to whether the SEC's reign of dominance has ended after a nearly 20-year run, and while I'm not here to bury the league just yet, it's hard to argue they've taken a step back.

From 2006 to 2023, an SEC team won a staggering 13 of a possible 17 national championships during the era of both the BCS and College Football Playoff.

However, the once-dominant Southeastern Conference hasn't won a championship in three years despite adding two traditional powers to its ranks (Oklahoma and Texas) and hasn't even reached the title game since Georgia won it all in January 2023.

PERCEPTION IS REALITY, AND THE SEC NEEDS TO START WINNING AGAIN BEFORE IT CONTINUES TO PUFF OUT ITS CHEST

Many people like to point to the advents of NIL and the transfer portal as the boogie men responsible for the SEC's downfall, but to me, it's a far more nuanced conversation than just saying "paying players is legal now, therefore the SEC sucks."

While there may not be a single issue that is easily identifiable, I can think of two reasons as to why the SEC has experienced its recent CFP swoon.

Georgia quarterback Stetson Bennett (13) gestures to the crowd during the trophy presentation the Southeastern Conference Championship football game Saturday, Dec. 3, 2022 in Atlanta. (AP Photo/John Bazemore)

First, and perhaps most importantly, the coaching hires at several top-flight SEC programs have left much to be desired.

Some coaching changes were flat out downgrades from their predecessors while others, while not necessarily poor coaches in their own right, were terrible fits and never should have been considered in the first place.

Let's start with the two tentpole programs of the conference since the league went to a championship game format, Alabama and Florida.

Since the SEC expanded to 12 teams in 1992 and implemented the SEC Championship Game, both the Tide and Gators are first and second in league titles, with 11 and seven, respectively.

When the conference was in its early stages of ascending to dominance in the late 2000s, two of the greatest coaches of their era called Tuscaloosa and Gainesville home.

Nick Saban won six national championships while coaching the Crimson Tide, but when he called it quits in 2024, Alabama needed to find someone to fill his shoes.

DID ALABAMA DOOM THEMSELVES TO MEDIOCRITY WITH KALEN DEBOER EXTENSION?

Now, DeBoer isn't a bad coach, per se, but he isn't Saban, and Bama has failed to live up to its legendary status from the decade prior since he arrived.

For the Gators, it's been way worse since Urban Meyer left.

A program like Florida, with all its resources and in-state talent available, should never bottom out like it did in 2025, but the crazy thing is they've experienced three separate four-win seasons since the legendary coach Meyer walked out the door in 2010.

A run of subpar coaching hires culminated in the Billy Napier tenure, who was, by every metric, the worst coach in Gator football history since World War II.

A fan wears a Fire Billy Napier bag over their head between the Florida Gators and Mississippi State Bulldogs during the second half at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium on Oct. 18, 2025. (Matt Pendleton/Imagn Images)

His arrival coincided with the steady decline of the SEC starting with the 2023 season, and although Florida wasn't a perennial contender from 2010-2022 before hiring Napier, his destruction of the program has left a void where a once-proud national power used to be.

For another SEC powerhouse in LSU, it's a bit more complex.

If we are talking purely from an X's and O's standpoint, I believe Brian Kelly is a better coach than former Tigers head man Ed Orgeron, so I understood and even joined in the optimism for the Bayou Bengals when they hired the former to replace the latter in November 2021.

BY ADDING ED ORGERON TO STAFF, LANE KIFFIN AND LSU ADDRESS KEY FLAW FROM PREVIOUS REGIME

Coach O had won a national title while in Baton Rouge, so surely Kelly could do the same, right?

There are two main differences separating Kelly and Orgeron that made one more successful than the other: willingness to delegate and culture fit.

The culture fit piece is perhaps more nebulous but equally important, and while Orgeron fit LSU like a glove, Kelly stuck out like a sore thumb.

Kelly's inability or unwillingness to accept the "LSU way" doomed him from day one, and it's a big reason he was ousted as unceremoniously as he was while Coach O has been welcomed back with open arms.

Florida head coach Billy Napier, left, talks with LSU head coach Brian Kelly before an NCAA college football game, Saturday, Nov. 16, 2024, in Gainesville, Fla. (AP Photo/John Raoux)

What Orgeron lacked in game-day coaching acumen he more than made up for in recognizing talent and delegating, both on the field and with his coaches.

Having Dave Aranda and Joe Brady (along with Steve Ensminger) orchestrating the Tigers' defense and offense, respectively, led to the record-breaking 2019 season that saw quarterback Joe Burrow win a Heisman and guide LSU to a historic national championship.

Speaking of Burrow, let's transition to the other half of the equation regarding the SEC's steady decline.

Talent has started to equalize at the top, particularly between the SEC and Big Ten, and when talent is equal, coaching and quarterback play act as the tiebreaker.

We touched on coaching, but what about quarterback play?

There's no question that when the SEC was ripping off their run of national championships that the quarterbacks were outrageously talented.

Players like Tim Tebow, Cam Newton, Tua Tagovailoa, the aforementioned Burrow, and even a guy like Mac Jones were all Heisman winners or finalists who elevated the play of the team around them and ultimately captured college football's biggest prize.

Since the Big Ten started their own run of dominance in the sport, the balance of power under center has shifted heavily away from the SEC.

Even during Georgia's run of back-to-back national championships in 2021 and 2022, the Dawgs had a player like Stetson Bennett, a Heisman finalist in his own right whose stats were otherworldly despite his relative obscurity and circuitous path to becoming a starting QB.

It's not like the SEC has missed out on talented signal-callers, but it seems like all the best quarterbacks are playing for the lower-level teams in the league that have no shot at winning the title.

Hopefully for the league's sake, that changes this year with players like Arch Manning and Trinidad Chambliss leading Playoff-caliber teams near the top of the league, but it seems like whenever the league gets a quarterback that is capable of winning a championship, he ends up on either a flawed team like Jayden Daniels with LSU in 2023 or a team that just isn't talented enough like Diego Pavia on last year's Vanderbilt team.

Sometimes, transcendent quarterback play can even lift a mediocre coach to glory, as we saw with Cam Newton at Auburn in 2010.

ESPN analyst Cam Newton appears on the set of "First Take" in San Francisco, Calif. (Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images)

With all due respect to Gene Chizik, he had no business winning a national championship, especially with that 2010 Auburn team, but Newton's superhero performance that season elevated them to a dream ending.

Obviously, there are way more factors that go into the shift of the balance of power in college football, and these theories are neither exhaustive nor foolproof, but they're a good start and way more in depth and nuanced than just pointing at NIL and the transfer portal.

The SEC still has the talent for a team from its ranks to win it all, and there are still plenty of great coaches and quarterbacks within the Southeastern Conference to perhaps break the drought in 2026.

Coaches like Kirby Smart, Lane Kiffin, and Steve Sarkisian have the chops to make a run this season and will have great teams with talented, veteran quarterbacks to boot.

Whether they put it all together or cede to the Big Ten once again remains to be seen, but I think I speak for everyone when I say I can't wait to see how it all plays out.
