articles.title: In Gaza’s tents, widows face war’s harshest realities alone
articles.excerpt:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Under the scorching heat inside a displacement tent in northern Gaza, Mona al-Masri tries to plan for each day as it comes.

Mona is a widow, and the mother of four children, r...
articles.body_text:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Under the scorching heat inside a displacement tent in northern Gaza, Mona al-Masri tries to plan for each day as it comes.

Mona is a widow, and the mother of four children, ranging in age from nine to two. Her husband, Mohammed, was killed in an Israeli strike in September 2024.

Between fabric walls that provide little protection, Mona carries the responsibilities of a family burdened by displacement brought on by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and the accompanying loss of security.

Mona begins each morning trying to secure her family’s basic needs, searching for water, arranging food, and attempting to protect her children from a reality that no longer resembles the life they knew before the war began in 2023. She says that what hurts her most is not only the harshness of their living conditions, but also the feeling that she has been forced to confront every detail of daily life alone.

“There is no normal life inside the tent. Every day begins with the same questions: how will we secure our needs, and how will we get through another day surrounded by this exhaustion?” Mona says. “The war did not only take away our homes; it took away our sense of safety and stability and made even the simplest things require enormous effort.”

Mona is one of thousands of women in the Gaza Strip who have found themselves facing new roles imposed by the war, taking care of their families by themselves.

According to data from the Ministry of Social Development in Gaza, the total number of widows in the Gaza Strip has risen to more than 50,000. The figure includes 28,224 women who became widows as a result of the war, in addition to more than 22,500 widows who were already registered with the ministry before the war.

Aziza al-Kahlout, spokesperson for the Ministry of Social Development in Gaza, says the number is expected to rise further because not all widows have yet been registered.

“The war has left these women facing a difficult reality, including the responsibility of supporting their families without a provider, amid widespread destruction and the collapse of the basic conditions needed for a decent life,” al-Kahlout says.

“This requires effective programmes for economic empowerment, job creation and strengthening self-reliance to help lift them out of poverty and deprivation,” she says.

Al-Kahlout stresses that widows’ needs extend beyond financial assistance. They also require psychological and social support, healthcare, and legal assistance related to guardianship, custody, financial rights and inheritance.

“Protecting and empowering widows in the Gaza Strip has become a shared national and humanitarian responsibility that requires an urgent and sustainable response,” al-Kahlout says.

She explains that widows need regular financial assistance, emergency relief, psychosocial and healthcare services, legal support and educational opportunities, in addition to vocational training and support for small and family businesses.

The loss of a husband during the war has not only deprived thousands of women of their life partners, but has also been accompanied by displacement, the destruction of homes, and the loss of stability.

Aseel Abu Shaweesh, a psychologist, explains that losing a husband during war represents a traumatic experience with profound psychological and social impacts on widows and their children. She notes that many women who lost their husbands have found themselves facing new and increasing responsibilities while simultaneously dealing with their other troubles.

“A widow in Gaza faces the pain of losing her husband, the responsibility of supporting her family, and caring for her children in an environment filled with fear and instability,” Abu Shaweesh says.

She adds: “Many women are forced to hide their grief and emotional collapse so they can carry on in front of their children, while the accumulation of daily pressures and the lack of space to express their pain increase levels of anxiety and psychological exhaustion.”

Abu Shaweesh explains that children in families who have lost one parent are also deeply affected, especially when the loss of the father is accompanied by displacement and deteriorating living conditions.

“A child loses their father and their sense of safety and stability. They may show signs of constant fear, sleep disturbances, and behavioural changes as a result of the difficult experiences they have endured,” Abu Shaweesh says.

The psychologist emphasises that widows’ needs include financial assistance as well as psychological and social support services to help them adapt to the new roles imposed by the war.

“These women need continuous support that helps them regain a sense of safety and the ability to manage their lives and their families under these difficult circumstances,” she says.

articles.title: Fishermen face deadly dangers as Yemen’s Red Sea becomes a warzone
articles.excerpt:
Al-Makha, Yemen – Mazhar works on a sea that has long been a front line in Yemen’s conflict.

The fisherman, based in the city of al-Makha (also known as Mocha) on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, has long stru...
articles.body_text:
Al-Makha, Yemen – Mazhar works on a sea that has long been a front line in Yemen’s conflict.

The fisherman, based in the city of al-Makha (also known as Mocha) on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, has long struggled to make a living since war arrived in the region in 2015.

Fuel is expensive, and so is renting a boat. But Mazhar, who is in his 40s and has a family that solely relies on the income from his fishing, has a bigger problem: whenever he sets out for the sea, he might not return home.

“Recently, a fishing boat in al-Khawkhah was fired on, and we lost two colleagues,” Mazhar said. “No one knows why, and the authorities haven’t announced the cause of the incident.”

Venturing beyond the shoreline is a dangerous gamble since the sea turned into a battlefield – Mazhar knows fishermen who have gone missing without a trace. But when there’s no food left at home, he decides to risk it anyway.

Yemen’s Red Sea coast is one of the main hubs of the country’s fishing industry, which before the war was the country’s second-largest source of export earnings after oil.

The Red Sea fishing industry has been impacted since the early years of the war, with fish exports from the region falling by about 70 percent, according to a 2018 study.

The region is strategically important for other reasons, too. Yemen’s principal port of Hodeidah sits about 160 kilometres (100 miles) up the coast from al-Makha, and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait lies at its southern entrance, controlling entry into one of the world’s most vital waterways. All of that means that the coastline has been heavily contested since the early days of the war.

Currently, the Houthi rebels control most of the territory from Yemen’s border with Saudi Arabia down to Hodeidah, with pro-government forces, largely the Guardians of the Republic force, operating south of the port city. The front line had been quiet in recent years, but recent Houthi attacks against pro-government forces across the country have also targeted al-Makha.

But it is events in the waters of the Red Sea that have drawn the most attention internationally. The Houthis began regularly striking shipping passing through the region after the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, and have also recently attacked Saudi shipping. The attacks have prompted the United States, the United Kingdom, Israel and Saudi Arabia to strike Houthi targets in Yemen at various times, including on the Red Sea.

Mazhar explained that fishermen now face strict boundaries at sea that they cannot cross. That is not only the case in al-Makha, but also in neighbouring al-Khawkhah district and large parts of the entire Red Sea coast.

“We pay money to buy scrap barrels and car bodies to dump into the sea to form artificial reefs. However, with every escalation in the Red Sea, we are denied access to our reefs for military reasons and are forced to fish near the shore,” Mazhar said.

“I cannot name the party restricting us right now because I am a fisherman, and speaking out could put me at risk,” Mazhar said. “But both warring sides have prevented us from sailing at different times. We are the victims of every faction fighting in our area.”

Before 2018, local fishermen say that the National Resistance Force (which the Guardians of the Republic forces later emerged out of) prevented fishermen from venturing into deep waters and reaching their reefs. Although restrictions were later eased, the fishermen say that both the Houthis and pro-government forces have placed restrictions on sailing since 2023.

“In the end, it is the fishermen who suffer to provide for their families,” Mazhar said. “We have no hand in this war, yet we bear its worst consequences.”

He added that several of his fellow fishermen have been arrested after being accused of smuggling or aiding one faction against another – claims he says are completely unfounded.

Akram, who also works as a fisherman in al-Makha, describes another danger: sea mines.

“Last year, I left home alongside two of my neighbours, and a sea mine exploded under their boat near the shore in al-Khawkhah,” he recalled. “It’s a sea mine; how can we avoid it? I can say with certainty that the Red Sea is no longer safe, and we have to move elsewhere.”

“We are witnessing the worst days in the Red Sea,” Akram added. “To be a fisherman in the Red Sea, you must carry your shroud on your shoulders.”

Fouad Doubla, head of the Fishermen’s Association in al-Khawkhah, told Al Jazeera that more than 30,000 fishermen have been affected by the conditions on the Red Sea coast and are struggling to provide basic necessities for their families, as fishing is their sole source of income.

Doubla noted that 113 fishermen have gone missing in the Red Sea since 2023, with their families receiving no information about their whereabouts. He added that the presence of sea mines is a direct consequence of the war that continuously threatens fishermen’s lives.

“Sea mines have killed 264 fishermen and maimed 215 others, forcing many to stop fishing and look for alternative work,” Doubla said, adding fishermen had also been detained by pirates in the Red Sea.

Doubla explained that the difficulties and dangers encountered by fishermen have many looking for a different way to make money.

“When fishermen realised they could no longer sail safely and that their families lacked food, they were left with no choice but to either risk their lives at sea or find another job – and many chose the latter to stay safe,” Doubla said.

For Akram, that means relocating to Aden, where he believes fishing on Yemen’s southern coastline will be safer.

“Nothing is worth risking our lives for. The families of those who were lost are now struggling just to find enough food. I encourage my colleagues to join me and move to a safe area.”

Ismail, a 48-year-old who comes from a long line of fishermen, decided to leave the profession behind entirely last year, selling the gear he had collected over 20 years and using the proceeds to buy a minibus instead.

“Danger surrounds fishermen from every direction, and we never know when we will meet our fate at sea,” Ismail told Al Jazeera while holding the steering wheel of his minibus. “I don’t think any wise man would continue fishing amid such danger.”

Ismail’s wife supported his decision to quit fishing and sold some of her jewellery to help him start his new business, relieved to end the constant anxiety she and their five children felt whenever he went out to sea.

“Sometimes we stayed at sea for four days, which was completely normal under regular circumstances,” Ismail said. “But nowadays, it isn’t safe. When I stayed out for more than a day, my family would panic, and I think they had every right to be worried.”

Today, Ismail earns a modest income driving his minibus, but he is content knowing he is safe and able to share every meal with his family without constant fear.

Mazhar, who continues to fish close to their shore, believes those who transitioned to new jobs have made the right choice.

“I’ve thought more than once about leaving this dangerous profession, but I have no alternative,” he said. “As soon as I find one, I won’t hesitate for a second.”

articles.title: Luigi Mangione murder trial to have anonymous jury and overflow seating
articles.excerpt: The judge overseeing the state trial of Luigi Mangione, accused of killing UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson, has laid down the ground rules for court public and media access to the high...
articles.body_text:
The judge overseeing the state trial of Luigi Mangione, accused of killing UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson, has laid down the ground rules for court public and media access to the high-profile case.

Mangione returned to court on Tuesday ahead of his murder trial, which begins next month in New York. Dressed in a charcoal grey suit with his hair clipped short, Mangione sat silently at the defence table while his attorneys conferred with the judge.

In Tuesday's hearing, Judge Gregory Carro decided that the 12-person jury would remain anonymous to the public due to the spotlight on the case, and that there would be an overflow room to meet media demand.

The case has attracted national attention, and has also created an online frenzy, with both his backers - many of whom see Mangione as a symbol of the backlash against US healthcare costs - and his critics analysing everything from his intentions to his appearance.

The spectacle is likely to intensify when jury selection for the trial begins on 8 September.

Mangione, if found guilty, could face decades behind bars. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges, including second-degree murder and weapons-related offences.

He faces a separate federal trial next year, in which he has also pleaded not guilty.

Much of what is expected at the state trial – the prosecutor's case, Mangione's defence, and obstacles both parties face – were previewed in months of court filings and arguments.

Here's what to know about the upcoming trial, and what questions remain.

In recent weeks, Mangione's lawyers and prosecutors have traded terse court filings debating just how much access the public will have to the trial.

The trial is expected to generate significant coverage across traditional outlets, social media, and streaming platforms. Mangione's supporters have demanded more transparency, and frequently post and broadcast from outside court.

On Tuesday, Carro said the court would open an overflow room during the trial, which will allow more members of the public and press to attend in person.

Listen to The Mangione Podcast: How a murder case fuelled a culture war

Judge rules gun and writings are admissible in Luigi Mangione's New York murder trial

In earlier court filings, Mangione's lawyers had questioned the court's press procedures, and why the court had not yet established an overflow room to meet public demand. They also implied – and later walked back – that prosecutors were influencing the court's media policies, which the Manhattan District Attorney's office denied.

Carro took to the bench to rebuke Mangione's attorneys for their filings, saying "any suggestion the district is involved is simply incorrect".

He also chastised prosecutors for raising security concerns about an overflow room, telling them it was not the court's "first rodeo" with blockbuster cases.

While the public can be admitted to court in New York, space is often limited at high-profile trials.

The court and its press office "remain firmly committed to providing the greatest possible access for both the media and the public", spokesman Al Baker said, adding that the court is "evaluating the complex logistical and safety considerations involved".

One of the most crucial elements of the Mangione case was decided earlier this summer, after a multi-day hearing in December where the judge weighed which evidence prosecutors could present during trial.

Mangione's team mounted an aggressive bid to exclude evidence recovered from his Pennsylvania arrest. It alleged that state police improperly seized and searched Mangione's possessions, and did not properly advise him of his constitutional rights before questioning him.

Public spectators leave Mangione's hearing, one of them wearing a shirt that demands officials "open the courtroom".

The defence succeeded in excluding some items, including a gun magazine, cell phone, passport, wallet and computer chip found in Mangione's backpack.

But Judge Gregory Carro allowed at trial a gun and notebook with Mangione's purported writings, viewed as vital to the prosecution.

Prosecutors have unveiled surveillance footage showing the moment Thompson was shot from behind by a hooded individual. They also used footage to piece together Mangione's alleged movements after the shooting, and ballistics and fingerprint evidence they claim bolsters their case.

As trial approaches, Mangione's team has yet to unveil its full strategy. So far, his lawyers have not offered a robust alternative theory to the one prosecutors have put forth.

"We do not have, like in 'The Fugitive,' the idea of the one-armed man who's the real killer," said former federal prosecutor Mitchell Epner, referencing a 1993 thriller about a man wrongly convicted of killing his wife.

Earlier this summer, Mangione's lawyers proposed, then quickly withdrew, an  "extreme emotional disturbance" argument.

In such a defence, New York law requires lawyers to show a defendant "acted under the influence of extreme emotional disturbance for which there was a reasonable explanation or excuse". Extreme emotional disturbance would allow the jury to consider the less severe charge of manslaughter, rather than second-degree murder. But jurors would have to be convinced of the accused's state of mind at the time.

Mangione's defence team leave court. Pictured from left to right: Marc Agnifilo, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, and Jacob Kaplan.

Some experts wondered if Mangione would argue a full insanity plea - different from emotional disturbance, but his lawyers have not proposed it.

"Short of being delusional, or having no understanding of the nature of what one is doing, an insanity defence is not likely to be successful," said Cheryl Bader, who leads the Criminal Defence Clinic at the Fordham University School of Law.

Mangione's team did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As in every US criminal trial, the burden rests on the prosecution to prove its case to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt, a high legal bar.

"The more his case is about the question of who killed the victim, the easier it is for the prosecution," said Epner.

Epner cited other themes, including healthcare in America, as potential narrative threads that could sway a jury in Mangione's favour.

"The more it's about the other peripheral issues, the harder it is for the prosecution," he said.

How the six-day hunt for New York shooting suspect unfolded

articles.title: Rescuers scramble for survivors with 180 dead in Colombia earthquake
articles.excerpt:
Watch: Moment powerful earthquake shakes Colombia and crumbles buildings

Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Mon...
articles.body_text:
Watch: Moment powerful earthquake shakes Colombia and crumbles buildings

Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Monday's powerful earthquake.

More than 180 people have been confirmed dead - most in the cities of Cali and Pereira.

The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) on Monday and was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia - with fresh aftershocks still being felt on Tuesday.

While the official death toll remains 181, an aggregated figure gathered from local officials puts it higher - potentially at more than 240. A state of emergency has been declared by President Abelardo de la Espriella.

Giving an update on Tuesday from Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, President Espriella said as well as those killed, almost 2,600 had been injured, and almost 200 people remain missing.

He also reported that more than 1,100 homes had been destroyed, and more than 8,000 had been damaged.

Overnight on Monday into Tuesday, several people several people spent the night outdoors in cities like Pereira and Cali - either due to their homes being destroyed, or fear of further collapses.

Across the country, dozens of larger buildings have also collapsed.

In Cali, a city of 2.2 million people where there have been 95 deaths, a unified command post has been set up to co-ordinate the rescue effort.

On Tuesday, Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said that 239 people remained trapped, with 949 injured and 45 buildings which have either completely or partially collapsed.

Several of the upper floors of one of the city's hospitals, some dedicated to paediatric care, collapsed, leaving some patients trapped.

In Calima, a neighbourhood in the north of Cali, four children died after a section of the Gimnasio Calima school collapsed.

The mayor of the municipality, Antonio Cadavid, stated that other children ended up with serious injuries, with a total of 30 children were referred to care centres.

To combat threats of looting, he has also ordered a curfew, coming into effect at 20:00 local time, and lasting until 06:00 on Wednesday morning.

Firefighters in Cali have worked to pulled survivors free from rubble

Rescuers searched for survivors at the site of a collapsed building in Cali

Further tremors were felt in Cali on Tuesday - part of a pattern of aftershocks across the country, with more than 70 having taken place since Monday's earthquake, according to Colombia's geological service.

According to the agency, two earthquakes of magnitude 3.6 occurred early on Tuesday. The first was in San José del Palmar and the second in Santander.

In Pereira, 79 people have died according to the city's fire department.

The city has implemented a car-free day to allow the search to go ahead, with citizens urged to comply.

Footage from the city has shown the massive scale of the rescue effort, with hundreds of volunteers working to remove rubble and free trapped survivors.

Large numbers of volunteers joined the effort to free survivors in Pereira

Hours after the earthquake hit Pereira, a resident of the Parque Industrial neighborhood, near the city's airport, told BBC Mundo about the shock being experienced in the area.

"It's impossible to get around the city center. In Bolívar Square (the city's main square), at least one building collapsed. Furthermore, there are structures where buses and trucks are trapped, and people are afraid those structures will collapse as well," he said.

"We're all in shock. It was really awful."

Jorge Eduardo Rojas, mayor of Manizales, said five people had been killed in the city.

Sixty buildings in Manizales had partially or totally collapsed.

Cautioning about further aftershocks, Rojas urged the public not to share chain messages or social media posts from unknown sources, as they "may contain false or unverified information... which could cause greater concern and alarm among the public".

On Tuesday, help and support continued to be offered to Colombia from the international community.

A statement from a spokesperson for UN Secretary-General, António Guterres, stated that he "expresses his solidarity with the people and government of Colombia" and that it working to support the government's response.

Spain's Foreign Minister, José Manuel Albares, reported that 164 Spaniards were still missing.

At the moment, he added, there are no reports of injuries or deaths of its citizens.

The Donald Trump administration, which backed President Abelardo de la Espriella in his successful election earlier this year, announced this afternoon a donation of $15.5m (£11.5m) to Colombia.

Offers of help have also come from Ecuador, Brazil, El Salvador, and Venezuela.

articles.title: Former Wisconsin Gov Scott Walker warns Hong ‘undermining one of her strengths’ with campaign backtracking
articles.excerpt:
The former Wisconsin governor says gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong should have stuck to her guns on her controversial views because voters liked when she bucked the Democratic establishment.

E...
articles.body_text:
The former Wisconsin governor says gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong should have stuck to her guns on her controversial views because voters liked when she bucked the Democratic establishment.

EXCLUSIVE — Former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker shared his concerns about politics in the state amid the rise of democratic socialist Francesca Hong, while also arguing she's "undermining" her own campaign in a Fox News Digital interview on Tuesday.

Hong, a Wisconsin state representative, is leading the field heading into Tuesday's Democratic primary, according to recent polling. The far-left, 37-year-old former chef and single mother has courted controversy in recent weeks for her progressive platform and past rhetoric about abolishing the police, as well as her hot take on Thanksgiving.

"Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621," Hong wrote in a now-deleted November 2020 post to X. "If it takes a worldwide pandemic for us to realize we should stop celebrating colonialism and the original superspreader event that killed indigenous folx [sic] and women, so be it," she added. She has since said her views have "evolved," telling Politico Thanksgiving is actually her "favorite" holiday.

"Well one, I think it’s a sign she’ll say just about anything to get elected," Walker, who is now the president of Young America's Foundation, told Fox News Digital ahead of Tuesday’s primary. "And finally, as she’s getting close, thinking she might actually be the nominee, people are telling her you cannot have outrageously outlandish ideas."

WISCONSIN DEM SOCIALIST GUBERNATORIAL HOPEFUL DODGES WHETHER SHE STILL WANTS TO 'ABOLISH POLICE'

Former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker speaks during the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in National Harbor, Maryland, Feb. 23, 2017.  (Joshua Roberts/Reuters)

"Not only on Thanksgiving. Doesn’t care for Christmas. Heck, in Wisconsin, doesn’t like Culver’s cheese curds," Walker said, in reference to another of Hong's old social media posts. "Those are all things that are wildly out of touch with the people that she’s going to need if she’s got a shot for the general election."

Walker warned Hong, however, that she could be hurting her campaign because primary voters had been attracted to her, in part, because of her bucking of the Democratic establishment.

"But I think she’s undermining one of her strengths," Walker said. "One of the reasons why she’s going to win today’s primary is because Democratic primary voters view her as not the establishment, not the traditional politician. Someone who will just tell it like it is, even if people don’t agree with her. So the more she backtracks on things she didn’t even say as a kid — she’s actually posted as an elected official — the more I think she starts to undermine her own base, and the typical voter can see right through her."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Hong campaign for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Walker is the most recent Republican to serve as Wisconsin governor. He was elected in 2010 and 2014 — and also survived a recall in 2012 — before losing to Democrat Tony Evers during a bid for a third term in 2018.

SOCIALIST FRONTRUNNER IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER 'CANCEL THANKSGIVING' POST EMERGES ONLINE

Wisconsin state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist candidate for governor, poses for a portrait at St. Paul Baptist Church on July 19, 2026, in Racine, Wisc. (Sara Stathas/For The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Establishment Democrats have been hoping to stop Hong in her tracks, but she's the clear polling favorite going into Tuesday night. David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive who earned the endorsement of outgoing Gov. Evers, told Politico that Republicans wanted Hong to be their opponent.

"You know, it’s the only time that I know that the governor — Tony Evers — the Republican Governors Association and Turning Point USA have ever been on the same page: in thinking that Francesca Hong is the best candidate to lose this race," Crowley said.

Whoever wins Tuesday's Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary will face Trump ally Tom Tiffany, who is heavily favored in the Republican primary.

Hong has pushed back on the narrative that she’s too extreme, although she has conspicuously failed to win the endorsement of even far-left darling Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.

"We have to take this moment, a movement moment, and be bold with transformative change, and build the actual big tent that we can, and we must be as Democrats," Hong told a crowd at a senior community center in Siren.

"It’s common sense versus dangerously crazy," Walker told Fox News Digital of the recent rise of democratic socialism in the U.S. "When you talk about abolishing the police, when you talk about a world without prisons, no consequences for criminals, no push for public safety."

SCOTT WALKER: DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ARE COMING FOR MY STATE. THIS IS HOW WE BEAT THEM

Wisconsin Gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong waves as she acknowledges the crowd during a campaign rally on Aug. 2, 2026 in Milwaukee, Wisc. (Joshua Lott/Getty Images)

SCOTT WALKER: DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ARE COMING FOR MY STATE. THIS IS HOW WE BEAT THEM

Walker said it is intriguing timing that next year will be the 40th anniversary of President Ronald Reagan’s "Tear down this wall" speech at the Berlin Wall.

"In all the years since, I think we’ve kind of lost a sense in America, of why there was a wall there in the first place, why did it have to come down," he said. "That’s because communism and democratic socialism are barriers to freedom. They’re barriers to economic freedom, political freedom, even religious freedom. That’s why Ronald Reagan, Pope John Paul II, Margaret Thatcher and others fought so hard to bring that down. We have to remind anyone, but particularly young people, that democratic socialism has failed in Venezuela, just like communism failed in the old Soviet Union. And it’s a really important reminder."

Walker said the newfound popularity of democratic socialism is in part due to primary voters shifting to the left, particularly under President Donald Trump. Second, he said, is the "years of liberal indoctrination on college campuses." The third, he argued, is due to a strong frustration over housing prices and the feeling that young adults' "piece of the American dream is slipping away," so they are drifting toward the extremes on either side of the aisle.

Fox News Digital's Alba Cuebas-Fantauzzi contributed to this report.

Cortney O'Brien is an Editor at Fox News. Twitter: @obrienc2

articles.title: Costco employee fatally rammed car into co-worker on motorcycle after seeing hug: DA
articles.excerpt: Seattle police say a 15-year-old has been charged in connection with food festival shooting that killed three people. Mayor Katie Wilson and police chief Shon Barnes announce a manhunt for a second su...
articles.body_text:
Seattle police say a 15-year-old has been charged in connection with food festival shooting that killed three people. Mayor Katie Wilson and police chief Shon Barnes announce a manhunt for a second suspect.

A Costco employee in a Seattle suburb allegedly rammed his car into a co-worker riding a motorcycle, killing him out of anger and jealousy, according to reports citing statements made to investigators.

Tyler Sorensen, 22, is charged with second-degree murder in connection with the July 31 death of 20-year-old Jonathon Langdon in Issaquah.

Sorensen allegedly followed Langdon out of a Costco parking lot before swerving into his lane and striking his motorcycle, according to court documents obtained by PEOPLE.

SILICON VALLEY DEVELOPER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER INVESTIGATORS SAY TESLA REACHED 142 MPH BEFORE FATAL CRASH

Security video showing the moments before Tyler Sorensen, 22, allegedly rammed 20-year-old Jonathon Langdon in Issaquah. (King County Prosecuting Attorney's Office)

Langdon was thrown from his motorcycle into a metal signpost, authorities said. Sorensen fled the scene but returned an hour later with a family member to speak with investigators, according to the Issaquah Police Department.

"The defendant, however, continued on his way without hesitation, only stopping to make sure his vehicle was okay to drive home," states the affidavit obtained by PEOPLE.

Sorensen allegedly told investigators that he became jealous after seeing Langdon hug a female co-worker whom Sorensen claimed was his girlfriend. After seeing the hug, he texted friends that his "blood is boiling."

SEATTLE POLICE CHIEF SNAPS OVER CHICAGO HOME QUESTIONS, ABSENCE FROM CITY AFTER MASS SHOOTING

The female co-worker denied that she and Sorensen had ever dated, stating she had previously told him he was "crossing boundaries," PEOPLE reported.

Sorensen allegedly told law enforcement that his actions were "stupid" and that he only wanted to "spook" Langdon, claiming he did not intend to hit him with his vehicle.

"Our hearts go out to the family and friends of the victim as they process this tragic loss of life," said Issaquah Police Chief Steve Mylett.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the King County Prosecuting Attorney's Office.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: NYPD’s legendary ‘Hip-Hop Cop' Derrick Parker, who investigated rap’s biggest stars and murders, dead at 65
articles.excerpt: Former NYPD rap unit investigator Derrick Parker joined 'Fox & Friends' to discuss his reaction to the embattled artist's apology after he took full responsibility for the alleged assault on his forme...
articles.body_text:
Former NYPD rap unit investigator Derrick Parker joined 'Fox & Friends' to discuss his reaction to the embattled artist's apology after he took full responsibility for the alleged assault on his former girlfriend caught on surveillance video.

Derrick Parker, the former NYPD detective known as the "Hip-Hop Cop" for his work in the city's rap-related intelligence unit in the 1990s, has died. He was 65.

His brother, Ralph, told Fox News Digital Monday he died unexpectedly on July 24 at a hospital in New York's Nassau County. He did not give a cause.

A funeral is scheduled for Thursday at the J Foster Phillips Funeral Home in Jamaica, New York.

Derrick J. Parker was the former head of the NYPD's rap intelligence unit when the city's hip-hop scene exploded in popularity in the 1990s. His work included monitoring high-profile artists and their entourages as they came and went from the Big Apple. He said he shared his strategies to reduce violence in the music industry in other parts of the country, including in Miami and Atlanta.

TUPAC SHAKUR MURDER SUSPECT TAKES CENTER STAGE AT TRIAL NEARLY 30 YEARS AFTER SHOOTING SHOCKED MUSIC WORLD

Longtime NYPD Detective Derrick Parker pictured in New York in 2024. He was part of an intelligence unit that focused on hip-hop artists and their entourages during the 1990s. (Stefano Giovannini)

He also served as a homicide and cold case detective during a career that spanned more than 20 years and worked alongside the US Marshals, the ATF, the DEA and the FBI, according to his website.

"You have to watch and see who's coming to your city. Who's there and who's what," he told Fox News Digital in a 2024 interview. "We can't track everybody, but when certain people come to the city, you should know who, especially certain people that are on your radar. That's the way I look at it."

Much of the job, he said, involved keeping law enforcement and nightclub management aware of who was going where in order to avoid potential confrontations between rival groups.

CASSIE VENTURA FLED THE UNITED STATES AFTER TESTIFYING AGAINST DIDDY IN SEX CRIMES TRIAL: DOCS

Sean "Diddy" Combs, the Notorious B.I.G. and Lil Kim — three of rap music's biggest '90s stars. (Getty Images)

He played a role in the 1999 investigation into the Club New York shooting where music mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs was charged but later acquitted. Pop superstar Jennifer Lopez was also briefly detained and released.

Parker said his approach to policing the hip-hop world wasn't to come down hard on its stars.

"I was the law, so he was always friendly," he later said of Combs. "I'm never hard on these guys. They know what they get into. They know what trouble they have."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Parker wrote a book about his experiences, "Notorious C.O.P.: The Inside Story of the Tupac, Biggie and Jam Master Jay Investigations from the NYPD's First 'Hip-Hop Cop.'" The book chronicled his involvement in investigations surrounding three of hip-hop's most notorious killings: Tupac Shakur, Christopher Wallace, who performed as the Notorious B.I.G. and Jam Master Jay, the Run-DMC DJ whose real name was Jason Mizell.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Tupac Shakur in Poetic Justice. (Columbia/Kobal / Shutterstock)

It would be decades before Mizell's killers went on trial. Parker was on the witness stand.

After Parker retired from the NYPD in 2002, he worked in security for large events and executive protection applying the same philosophy of knowing who would be going where to avoid conflicts.

He also became a frequent media commentator on high-profile cases involving figures and venues he had encountered during his NYPD career, including Combs' sex-trafficking trial last year and even the wedding between Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce at Madison Square Garden.

He had also told Fox News Digital that he hoped to write a follow-up book.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"I want to really tell a big, big story about a lot of stuff," he said.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis enters a courtroom in Clark County District Court for a trial readiness status check at the Regional Justice Center on June 17, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Steve Marcus-Pool/Getty Images)

Days before his death, he said he was closely following the Las Vegas murder case against Duane "Keffe D" Davis, who is charged with playing a role in Tupac Shakur's 1996 murder. Jury selection began Monday.

"We were supposed to go out to dinner for my birthday," Ralph Parker told Fox News Digital. "He's like, ‘Oh, we're gonna go out and eat. Your birthday's coming, don't worry about it.’ Well, I won't be able to go eat with him."

The Department of Justice said that officials are monitoring polling sites in Hennepi...
articles.body_text:
Approximately 20 staff sent to polling sites in Hennepin and Ramsey counties during Minnesota’s primary elections

The Department of Justice said that officials are monitoring polling sites in Hennepin and Ramsey county – Minnesota’s largest – throughout the state’s primary elections on Tuesday.

In a press release, the justice department said that it has deployed approximately 20 staff from the Civil Rights Division’s Voting Section and Minnesota’s US attorney’s office to continue “its nationwide effort to ensure free and fair elections”.

Minnesota has long been a target of the Trump administration since the president returned to the White House last year.

The North Star state was the sight of a deadly immigration crackdown that killed two US citizens earlier this year, and the administration has paused more than $500m in Medicaid payments to Minnesota to clamp down on alleged fraud over the last year.

In the year since the Donald Trump sent a wave of federal law enforcement to Washington DC – including the deployment of the national guard and the administration’s temporary takeover of the DC police department – officials have touted a reduction in crime.

The newly confirmed attorney general, Todd Blanche, claimed on social media that “in just one year” the capital “is safer than it has been in years”.

However, data from the Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) tells a different story.

While certain types of crime, like homicide, have decreased since this time last year, others are actually significantly higher. There has been a 40% increase in assault with a dangerous weapon in 2026. Overall, total violent crime in Washington DC is up by 3% compared to the same point in 2025.

The Trump administration claims regularly that the federal takeover has led to record-breaking dips in crime, but the drop in violent crime between 2025 and 2024 – when Joe Biden left office – was 29%.

There was also a consistent 32% decrease in the number of homicides in DC year-on-year, between 2023 and 2025.

We’re also chasing new reports that Donald Trump left Turkey last month on a secret military flight to Britain amid an Iranian assassination threat. ABC News reporter Michelle Stoddart, who traveled with the president and senior officials from Ankara in July, noted today that before the press corps departed the summit, they were given no additional guidance on the president’s movements or flight plans beyond his publicly posted Truth Social post. More here

The state department has revoked more than 175,000 visas of foreign nationals who officials say have “violated the terms of their visas, committed crimes, called for violence against US citizens”. These include people who allegedly “celebrated” the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, according to officials. The state department noted an instance of online comments which included: “when fascists die, democrats don’t complain” and another who said Kirk “died too late”.

Donald Trump said he is exploring to see if the federal government has any way of stepping in to try to end Zohran Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax in New York City.

“This dangerous political ‘experiment’ in New York will destroy what was once a great City and State,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

On Monday, a state judge temporarily blocked the tax, which would place a surcharge on second homes, after homeowners filed a lawsuit against the mayor and city officials. The tax would apply to people who own, but do not reside full-time in, any house worth more than $5m, or a condominium or cooperative unit worth at least $1m.

Trump said today that the policy is actually costing New York more – by forcing “tens of thousands” of people to leave the city “never to return”.

“It is pure Amateur Hour, and it’s hard, as President of the United States of America, to sit back and watch it happen, especially to a place I once loved,” he added. “Financial, and then Social, RUIN, is a 100% certainty … This doesn’t work in America, and must be stopped, NOW!”

The United States will sponsor a new round of talks between Israel and Lebanon in early September in Rome, a state department official announced today.

“The political track will reconvene in Rome in early September, and conversations will continue in Beirut, Jerusalem, and Washington in the interim,” the official told AFP on condition of anonymity, adding: “We feel good about the trajectory.”

The US has been facilitating talks between Israel and Lebanon aimed at putting an end to hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militant group based in Lebanon, with Beirut seeking Israel’s phased withdrawal from the swathes of southern of Lebanon it currently occupies, while Israel wants the disarmament of Hezbollah.

In June, Israel and Lebanon agreed to a framework deal that involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon’s south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in test areas known as “pilot zones”.

The seventh round of US-mediated talks between the two countries concluded last week. One of the days of discussion was cut short after Israel resumed heavy strikes on Lebanon, accusing Hezbollah of violating the truce. But really there has been continued intermittent Israeli strikes and shelling, as well as detonations and demolitions in southern villages, since the ceasefire agreement was signed on 26 June.

The US official today gave an update on the last round of talks in Rome, telling AFP: “The framework is being implemented, the first zones are live, and the working groups have aligned their language, maps, and procedures.”

At the next round of technical talks, they added, “Lebanon will present detailed roadmaps for securing new areas as implementation proceeds in the current zones.”

Israel’s bombing campaign and ground invasion has killed more than 4,300 people in Lebanon, injured over 12,200 and displaced over 1.2 million.

Further to that, Donald Trump has said the agreement came about after he spoke to Vladimir Putin about releasing Robert Gilman “on a humanitarian basis” and that Gilman will land back in the US at Joint Base Andrews tonight.

“I just spoke to him, and he had one request – A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands. I will take care of that!” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

The US president also confirmed that this was not a prisoner exchange, adding: “We appreciate this decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return – No exchange took place.”

Trump’s post included this photo of Gilman traveling back to the US, alongside his mother, Nancy, and officials.

Russia has freed a former US marine who had been in jail since 2022, after Vladimir Putin granted the ailing American a pardon on humanitarian grounds.

Robert Gilman, 32, an English teacher who briefly served in the US Marines, was travelling by train when he was arrested in the southern Russian city of Voronezh in January 2022 for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk, according to Russian state media. He was later sentenced to four and a half years in prison, though his family has consistently denied the allegations against him.

His father, Vladimir Gilman, who emigrated to Massachusetts from Russia, wrote in an October 2024 Boston Globe op-ed that his son had fallen ill when the incident occurred and had accidentally kicked the police officer.

Concerns over Gilman’s health had grown sharply in recent weeks, and the White House and the state department had urged Moscow to release him so he could receive medical treatment in the US.

Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer at Global Reach, an advocacy group representing Gilman’s family, told Reuters last week that he had been transferred in late June from a prison hospital to the psychiatric ward of a civilian emergency hospital in a catatonic-like state that doctors assessed as a “dissociative stupor”.

“While this news is deeply welcomed, it is long overdue,” Massachusetts senator Edward Markey wrote on X. “Approximately 50 days ago, Robert was diagnosed with a dissociative stupor – a condition where he could not interact or eat. He was essentially catatonic and also suffered a severe case of pneumonia. We do not know his current condition or the long-term impact on his recovery.”

US officials told Reuters that Gilman was already on a state department plane carrying him ‌from Russia to Washington Dulles airport, adding that Gilman would be greeted on arrival by US envoy Steve Witkoff and Sebastian Gorka, a deputy assistant to Donald Trump.

The official who spoke to Gilman said he was walking and talking.

“All things considered, he seems to be in good ‌shape,” the official said.

The move to release Gilman is likely to be a signal of Moscow’s eagerness to improve relations with the Trump administration, after several weeks in which the US president has appeared to take a more supportive position towards Ukraine.

Supreme court justice Samuel Alito gained up to $2.9m from his fossil fuel interests between 2005 and 2024, a new review of financial disclosures shows.

The analysis from the non-profit advocacy group and judicial watchdog Court Accountability, shared exclusively with the Guardian, found that even at the lowest range of estimates, Alito gained almost $400,000 from his oil and gas interests since being tapped for the high court by George W Bush in 2005.

The findings come as the supreme court prepares to take up a case in which the oil companies Suncor Energy and Exxon asked the justices to find that federal law prevents subnational governments from filing lawsuits against fossil fuel producers for the climate-warming effects of their products.

The supreme court said this month it will hear oral arguments in the case on 5 October, the opening day of its new term. The Trump administration, which is siding with the oil companies, has asked for 10 minutes of argument time. Court Accountability and other groups have called for a Senate committee to investigate Alito, the sole supreme court justice with holdings in energy companies, and said he should recuse himself.

Supreme court ethics rules focus specifically on investments in companies named in court cases. In May, a supreme court spokesperson told NBC News that Alito is not required to recuse himself from the Suncor lawsuit as his holdings do not include the companies directly named in the case, Suncor and ExxonMobil.

But Lisa Graves, co-founder of Court Accountability who authored the new analysis, said Alito’s oil-tied wealth provides grounds to question whether Alito can impartially weigh in on cases affecting the entire fossil fuel sector.

“You might have real appreciation for how that industry has helped make it possible for you to perhaps buy a second home on the water, or live a [certain] lifestyle,” she said.

The advocacy group Free DC has held a rally in Washington DC today to mark one year since Donald Trump declared a “crime emergency”, despite violent crime being at a 30-year low, and deployed national guard troops to the capital.

One of the most controversial measures of Trump’s second term so far, the deployment – currently at more than 4,600 personnel – was recently quietly extended through January 2029, to a cost of about $1.4bn. It marks the longest and largest of Trump’s extraordinary mobilizations of military personnel on US soil.

The lawsuit in my last post is the latest example of organizations pushing back on what they call the Trump administration’s efforts to undermine international law and prevent efforts to combat impunity by governments around the world.

“The fact that so many leading human rights and humanitarian organizations have come together to challenge Trump’s unlawful executive order demonstrates the widespread harm it is causing across civil society groups dedicated to bringing those responsible for grave crimes to justice,” Andrew Loewenstein of Foley Hoag LLP, the lead counsel representing the plaintiffs, told the Associated Press.

The groups assert that the financial and legal penalties against the ICC have forced them to “curtail a wide range of human rights and legal work in violation of their First and Fifth Amendment rights under the US Constitution and under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act.”

“The Trump administration seeks a get out of jail free card for whomever it chooses. And with this case, we say no,” Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch, told a press conference this morning.

Four prominent US human rights organizations have accused the Trump administration of using its “crippling” sanctions regime against the international criminal court (ICC) to undermine global efforts to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity.

In a lawsuit filed in federal court today, the groups – the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch and the Open Society Institute – argued that the administration’s targeting of the ICC, as well as of groups and individuals affiliated with it or assisting its work, amounts to a “blatantly illegal attack on international justice”, the groups said.

The suit challenges Donald Trump’s February 2025 executive order, which authorized sanctions on ICC officials, judges and others working to support its investigation of Israeli crimes in Palestine – one of 18 investigations into war crimes and crimes against humanity the Netherlands-based tribunal is overseeing.

The US state department and justice department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The US government has long opposed and sought to impede the work of the court – of which it is not a party – but those attacks escalated after the ICC prosecutor issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant over crimes committed in Gaza. The US responded by sanctioning ICC prosecutors, judges, three leading Palestinian human rights groups and Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Palestinian territory.

Earlier this summer, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, also escalated efforts against the ICC, announcing a campaign aimed at “dismantling” it by pressuring member states to leave the court.

Those attacks, and Trump’s executive order, undermine access to justice for victims of major human rights violations and criminalize the work of those seeking to combat impunity by collaborating with the court – including the plaintiffs in the case – in violation of both constitutional protections for free speech and association and US obligations under international law, the lawsuit argues.

“The Trump administration took the extraordinary step to not only deny Palestinians and victims of US torture equal access to justice, but to criminalize and punish them, their lawyers and advocates, and their partners,” said Katherine Gallagher, a senior attorney at the Center for Constitutional Rights who represents victims before the ICC. She added:

double quotation markAll victims of international crimes – from Sudan and Ukraine to Palestine and Afghanistan – need and deserve to have an independent and strong ICC able to fulfill its mission of ending impunity, without fear or favor.

In response to the Washington Post’s reporting that Donald Trump took a clandestine flight on a military jet to avoid an Iranian assassination attempt, Ned Price, a former state department official, said that while “subterfuge is sometimes a necessary safeguard” the decision to mislead reporters “in the moment” and continue “to lie to the American people weeks later is never acceptable”.

Price, who noted that he’s traveled overseas with multiple presidents said that as far as he’s aware, this decision making is “unique to this White House”.

We’re also chasing new reports that Donald Trump left Turkey last month on a secret military flight to Britain amid an Iranian assassination threat – despite the White House saying he was aboard the old Air Force One – and that he briefly hid in an airport catering truck to move from one aircraft to another.

ABC News reporter Michelle Stoddart, who traveled with the president and senior officials from Ankara in July, noted today that before the press corps departed the summit, they were given no additional guidance on the president’s movements or flight plans beyond his publicly posted Truth Social post.

Stoddart said the press pool’s movements were not unusual once they boarded the old Air Force One. But she added that the pool was instructed to keep window shades closed. Another ABC News journalist said a Secret Service agent returned to the press cabin to remind reporters to keep the shades down. At one point, a photographer seated behind Stoddart opened their shade and was quickly told to close it. When they asked a White House aide why, the aide said only that it was a request from Secret Service.

A 71-year-old lifeguard and park manager in Maine had an encounter with a great white shark off the coast over the weekend. He initially thought his rescue can got caught on a boat after he was dragged underwater.

But it wasn’t a boat. Greg Wilfert, who has worked at Scarborough Beach for 55 years and looks like a guy who should have his own reality show, was pulled five to six feet under the water by a great white.

He was swimming around the buoys at the time with a few other lifeguards. Luckily, he was able to remove the strap from the rescue device then swim back to shore to safety without any further interactions with the shark.

SHARK WEEK SHOCKER AS GREAT WHITE BREACHES JUST YARDS FROM OBLIVIOUS BOOGIE BOARDER

"I thought a boat had come by and grabbed my rescue can because I got pulled under, and I realized right away that it was not a boat, that it had to have been a great white," Wilfert told WHDH.

Veteran lifeguard in Maine dragged underwater by great white shark. (Getty Images)

"I just swam as fast as I could to the surface, and then I just was hoping it wasn't behind me. I could've beaten Michael Phelps."

Once he made it back to shore, his duty as a lifeguard took over. He warned the beachgoers, had them get out of the water, then shut down the beach for an hour.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Lifeguard who has worked at a beach in Maine for 55 years had a close call with a great white shark over the weekend. (Getty Images)

FISHING CONTENT CREATOR WHO FILMED HIMSELF BEING BITTEN BY A SHARK WHILE SPEARFISHING LUCKY HE STILL HAS LEG

Since his encounter, Wilfert has had jet skis and drones keeping an eye on the water for other great white sharks. While he wasn’t hurt, he is taking his encounter seriously.

There's been an increase in great white activity in the area recently and this veteran of the beach isn't taking any chances.

Great white shark sightings are up in the area and this 71-year-old lifeguard isn't taking any chances. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

articles.title: Burnham’s prison plans could raise risk of mistaken releases, union warns
articles.excerpt:
Concerns raised over proposed changes to early release scheme as probation staff vote to strike over workloads

Andy Burnham’s plan to stop the early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers and other se...
articles.body_text:
Concerns raised over proposed changes to early release scheme as probation staff vote to strike over workloads

Andy Burnham’s plan to stop the early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers and other serious offenders could increase the risk of some more dangerous prisoners being released by mistake, unions have warned.

In another blow to the proposals announced by the prime minister, probation staff have voted overwhelmingly to go on strike, warning of already unrealistic workloads.

While the vote by members of Napo was not directly connected to the early release plans, the probation officers’ union has previously criticised the proposals as rushed. The union said the 91% vote in favour of a strike would come as a blow to ministers.

Burnham said earlier he recognised “the depth of public concern” about the proposed early release of Harper’s killers and announced a change to the early release scheme. The scheme is designed to free up urgently needed spaces in overcrowded prisons across England and Wales.

After an uproar about the proposed release of Harper’s killers Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, Burnham said on Tuesday morning that he had instructed the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to find more prison spaces so the pair and other serious offenders would not be freed.

Writing on Facebook, Burnham said places could be provided by removing foreign offenders more quickly, finding a way to release lower-risk prisoners stuck in jail on indeterminate sentences, and “making greater use of the entire prison estate including using the female estate for male offenders”.

Downing Street had said on Monday that there was no feasible way of exempting just a handful of prisoners from the scheme to block the release of Cole and Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for Harper’s manslaughter. Under the scheme, they were due to be freed in January.

Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors’ Association, said further changes to the scheme could lead to prisoners being wrongly released. “Mistakes are more likely due to having to recalculate sentences against a very tight deadline,” he said.

Wheatley said removing overseas prisoners was likely to be difficult as many would resist this and a number did not have proper documentation. He said victims would also want to be sure that anyone sent back to home countries would properly serve their sentence there.

Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the Prison Officers’ Association, said placing men in women’s prisons would require investment and retraining. “Repurposing women’s prisons to accommodate male prisoners is not something that can simply be achieved by changing the sign above the door,” he said.

“There would inevitably be additional staffing, training, security and operational requirements. “The physical design and facilities of women’s prisons are not necessarily suitable for a male population, and those differences would need to be properly assessed before any decision was taken.

“You cannot create safe prison places simply by finding additional buildings. You need the staff, training, infrastructure and resources to operate them safely.”

The Ministry of Justice said it was disappointed by the Napo strike vote and it would continue to engage with the union. Officials in Norris’s department are understood to be working at full speed on preparing detailed and workable plans to free up spaces by September.

When the early release scheme was announced, there were exemptions for prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences but not manslaughter, prompting pressure to block the release of Harper’s killers, including from police and his family.

Officials initially said it would be unrealistic to just block the release of Cole and Bowers and that exempting all manslaughter cases risked not creating enough prison spaces to ease the crisis. But in his Facebook post, and speaking to reporters on a later visit to Derbyshire, Burnham said he was aware of the strength of public feeling about the plans.

“It’s my job to speak up for the public on this issue,” he said during the visit. “I take that duty very seriously indeed, and I’m confident that there’s more that can be done, and will be done to address public concern.”

He said on Facebook he understood “the depth of public concern about the potential early release of those involved with the killing of PC Andrew Harper – and I share it”.

He wrote: “I am increasingly confident that a more focused approach along these lines will allow us to reduce the number of people released early and, in the case of the most serious offenders like those convicted of the killing of PC Harper, prevent their early release altogether.

“In advance of the justice secretary’s proposals being presented to parliament, we will seek to engage other political parties in discussions with the aim of gaining the widest possible public and political consensus on the approach being taken.”

Last week, Napo warned that ministers seemingly did not “have a clue about how ill-equipped the probation service is to take on this additional work” connected to early release, such as informing victims that a perpetrator was being released.

Announcing the result of the strike ballot, Ben Cockburn, the Napo national chair, said the vote was “professionals warning they cannot protect the public properly when there are not enough people to do the work”.

A union statement said: “The result should come as a blow to government as it prepares to expand early release from prison and implement Sentencing Act changes, increasing the number of people managed in the community while probation is already struggling to cope.”

Harper, 28, was fatally injured when he got caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and was dragged down a country road as the killers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in 2019.

Cole and Bowers, two of three men sentenced over the police officer’s death, are due to be released halfway through their 13-year sentences, having been convicted of manslaughter in 2020. A petition demanding an intervention has nearly 900,000 signatures.

The early release changes were part of the Sentencing Act passed earlier this year that cut the minimum amount of time many offenders would have to spend in prison.
