articles.title: Elite rock climber's cause of death revealed after horrific accident at national park
articles.excerpt:
High-performance psychologist Michael Gervais explains the mental demands of elite climbing following the death of accomplished rock climber Jake Whisenant.

Authorities have revealed the cause of dea...
articles.body_text:
High-performance psychologist Michael Gervais explains the mental demands of elite climbing following the death of accomplished rock climber Jake Whisenant.

Authorities have revealed the cause of death of Jake Whisenant, an elite rock climber who recently died in an accident in California's Sierra Nevada, shocking many.

Whisenant died of "blunt force trauma injuries, sustained as a result of a fall," the Tulare County Sheriff’s Office told Fox News Digital. He was just 30 years old.

The spokesperson also disclosed that the incident took place at Sequoia National Park.

RECORD-SETTING EL CAPITAN ROCK CLIMBER DIES AT AGE 30 IN SIERRA NEVADA ACCIDENT

Whisenant’s death was first announced by his friend, Bailee Moore, who remembered him as her "lifelong friend and confidant."

"Our family is absolutely devastated by this news but find solace in the fact that Jake died doing what he loves in the beautiful Sierra Nevada," said Moore.

Accomplished rock climber Jake Whisenant died at age 30 after an accident in California's Sierra Nevada. (jake.doubleyew via Instagram)

"I will look for you in every life, my brother. Now go rest high up on that mountain."

Whisenant had established himself in Yosemite's climbing community through a series of impressive feats on El Capitan, one of the world’s most challenging rock-climbing destinations, as Fox News Digital previously reported.

NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING'

In May, Whisenant teamed up with fellow climber Noah Fox to climb El Capitan's Nose route twice in one day, completing the feat in 14 hours and 38 minutes, according to the Yosemite Climbing Association.

In October 2024, Whisenant and another climber named Brant Hysell set a speed record on El Capitan's Lurking Fear route, completing the climb in 2 hours, 55 minutes and 32 seconds.

Rock climber Jake Whisenant, age 30, died Aug. 3 after an accident in California's Sierra Nevada, according to authorities. (@jake.doubleyew via Instagram)

At the time, Whisenant described it as a "truly magical day that I’ll never forget."

YELLOWSTONE OFFICIALS DECIDE FATE OF BISON THAT LAUNCHED GRANDFATHER 8 FEET IN AIR

"We both tapped into a flow state, fully committed to our plan, and most importantly had an absolute blast on our favorite rock," he wrote on Instagram.

"That type of incredible psychological and technical skill is rare, and it is special."

It takes an "incredible commitment" to excel at climbing, Michael Gervais, a high-performance psychologist and founder of Finding Mastery, said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Gervais, based in California, said becoming an elite climber requires an extraordinary level of mental and physical commitment. (He did not advise or work with Whisenant.)

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"The consequences are so high, because the thrill is so wonderful," said Gervais. "It requires an all-in full commitment to be elite in this consequential sport."

Sequoia National Park sits in California's Sierra Nevada, where Jake Whisenant died following a climbing accident. (iStock)

"They’re able to override that reflexive brain dictum and focus all their attention on the task at hand: the next placehold, the next foothold, the next challenge in front of them to be able to solve," added Gervais.

"That type of incredible psychological and technical skill is rare, and it is special."

Friends remembered Jake Whisenant as a kind and genuine person following news of the 30-year-old climber's death. (@jake.doubleyew via Instagram; George Rose/Getty Images)

He cautioned against viewing elite climbers as thrill-seekers or "adrenaline junkies."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"From the inside, spending the last 25 years working with the best athletes in the world ... we have a very different perspective," said Gervais.

Authorities said the accomplished rock climber died after a fall at California's Sequoia National Park. (Paul Bersebach/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register)

"Elite climbers, in this case — they are not adrenaline junkies. They have developed the full capacity to become incredibly present in environments where full command of themselves is required," he added.

"So, it's that state of being fully present that I think is incredibly compelling."

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

articles.title: HHS bureaucrats accused of 'sabotaging' RFK Jr's efforts to expose Fauci records
articles.excerpt:
Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., warned that longtime HHS employees were standing in the way of revealing more corruption during the pandemic as his probe into Dr. Anthony Fauci gains steam.

FIRST ON FOX: A...
articles.body_text:
Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., warned that longtime HHS employees were standing in the way of revealing more corruption during the pandemic as his probe into Dr. Anthony Fauci gains steam.

FIRST ON FOX: A Senate Republican leading a dive into Dr. Anthony Fauci’s old government iPhone alleged that "career bureaucrats" within Fauci’s old agency are sabotaging the senator’s and others’ quest for information from the pandemic era.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., told Fox News Digital that he believed longtime employees of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) were putting up roadblocks to his own probe and other information trawling expeditions pushed by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

"Again, we don't know what we don’t know," Johnson said. "We don't know what HHS has. Bobby Kennedy doesn't know what HHS has."

FAUCI HELD IN CONTEMPT AS COVID CELLPHONE LANDS IN HANDS OF SENATE INVESTIGATORS

Kennedy said Fauci is to blame for Americans’ lack of trust in public health and added that "they shouldn’t" because they were "lied to." (Alex Wong/Getty Images; Kent Nishimura/Getty Images)

Johnson, along with Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., received a copy of Fauci’s personal work phone from HHS as part of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee’s broader investigation into the former head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID). On Monday, Johnson’s panel, the Senate Homeland Security Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, released the first tranche of private messages found on the device, which included over 34,000 text messages and 522 voicemails.

The first batch of texts, exchanged between Fauci and former Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Dr. Rochelle Walensky and Dr. Vivek Murthy, who would become surgeon general under the Biden administration, revealed that Fauci had concerns about the effects of the second dose of mRNA vaccines on pregnant women in the first trimester.

FAUCI'S HHS IPHONE TURNED OVER TO SENATE INVESTIGATORS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

"I asked around a bit more and another issue came up that you need to be aware of," Fauci wrote. "Since many people have significant cytokines storm and fever after the 2nd dose, this theoretically could be associated with miscarriage in the 1st trimester."

The lawmaker believed that the revelation was just the "tip of the iceberg," but has remained cautious with his investigation and what information dumps come next, particularly to protect the personal information of others who may be included in the communications.

FAUCI IN THE HOT SEAT AS GOP SENATOR TEARS INTO 'TRULY SICK' VACCINE TEXTS: 'TIP OF THE ICEBERG'

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations hearing in the Hart Building on July 11, 2023. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

He argued that releasing the first batch of texts was based on public health and safety concerns, said that Fauci’s concern "immediately impacts public safety, immediately impacts informed consent."

As he waded through the rest of the information on the phone, Johnson believed that there was more to find about the HHS’ handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, and charged that even though Kennedy was at the helm, not even he had full knowledge of the information that could be lurking within the agency.

"I mean, fortunately, now we have Bobby Kennedy, I think gaining a little bit more control over the agency," Johnson said. "Remember, most of the people serving in these agencies have been there a long time, and they were involved in the cover-up. They were supposed to be surveilling for vaccine injuries and they weren’t."

"So, you know, Bobby Kennedy has people in those agencies sabotaging his efforts at radical transparency," he continued. "So this is like pulling teeth. So, I mean, I did not know they had government-issued phones. They've been sitting there, locked away somewhere."HHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

articles.title: Former judge removed by Orbán elected Hungarian president
articles.excerpt:
András Baka served for 17 years as the Hungarian judge at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg

Hungary's parliament has elected András Baka, 73, a respected judge and former head of the S...
articles.body_text:
András Baka served for 17 years as the Hungarian judge at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg

Hungary's parliament has elected András Baka, 73, a respected judge and former head of the Supreme Court, as head of state.

The Hungarian president is a largely figurehead role, but Baka's rule promises to be tempestuous.

His task will be to monitor Prime Minister Péter Magyar's efforts to dismantle the interlocking economic and political powerhouse established by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. He will also oversee the writing of a new constitution, to replace Orbán's constitution of 2011.

"We cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," András Baka told Parliament, after he was elected by 140 votes to 6.

"The majority of society now feels a sense of liberation and hope. Others feel disappointment and uncertainty," he said. "In a democratic society, this is not an anomaly, but a natural state of affairs."

All 51 MPs belonging to Orbán's party Fidesz walked out of the chamber before the vote, in protest against the ousting of their favourite, Tamás Sulyok, from the post last month.

In his speech, András Baka promised the broadest possible debate on the creation of a new constitution.

Since taking office in early May, the new Magyar government has lost no time attacking Orbán's legacy.

Twenty-seven laws have been passed, and two amendments to the constitution.

The states of emergency - migrants, Covid, and war in Ukraine - which Orbán used to govern by decree, were all cancelled.

The Sovereignty Protection Office, which the Fidesz government used to attack critical journalists and NGOs, was abolished, and an National Asset Recovery and Protection Office was established, with sweeping powers to investigate and prosecute individuals accused of stealing state funds under the former government.

Fidesz accuses the Tisza government of establishing a "tyranny". Ironically, they removed Baka from his post as president of the Supreme Court in 2011, for attempting to stop them undermine the rule of law.

Public service radio and TV have been off air since 9 July, as news programmes are revamped. The stated aim is to restore their independence, from their Fidesz-era role as government propaganda organs.

Other key changes came under Amendments 16 and 17 of the constitution, limiting the prime minister to two terms in office, and MPs to three. The ability of the Constitutional Court to oversee acts of parliament, taken away by Fidesz, was also restored.

If the Tisza majority expects Baka to be a tame president, they may get a rude awakening.

In a BBC interview before he was asked to take the post, he made clear he opposes the limitation of MPs' terms as an intrusion on the right of voters to freely choose their representatives.

Baka served for 17 years as the Hungarian judge at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.

"I am not a political man," he told the BBC last month. "I got involved in politics through my professional, legal way of thinking."

Baka was elected today as a transitional figure.

Under the constitutional amendment which made his presidency possible,  the new president will likely only be in place until the new constitution comes into force - or for maximum of five years.

Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, Baka made it clear that he intended to push back against the Hungarian tendency to trust in powerful leaders.

"The state is not there for itself," he said, at the end of his speech. "It is there for the people."

What does new Hungarian PM Péter Magyar stand for?

Orbán era swept away by Péter Magyar's Hungary election landslide

articles.title: Paramount CEO may remove operations from California over stalled merger
articles.excerpt: Paramount CEO David Ellison may pull his operations out of California if the state does not end its attempt to block the company’s merger with Warner Bros Discovery and agree to settlement talks as so...
articles.body_text:
Paramount CEO David Ellison may pull his operations out of California if the state does not end its attempt to block the company’s merger with Warner Bros Discovery and agree to settlement talks as soon as October.

The rumours were first reported by the publication Variety on Tuesday. They signal Ellison may be willing to leverage economic pressure on California’s ailing film industry in order to push through the merger.

Al Jazeera was not able to independently confirm the validity of the report.

In July, California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced that he was leading a coalition of 12 state attorneys general in an antitrust lawsuit to block the consolidation.

Should Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery combine, Bonta warned that the resulting company would control 27 percent of theatrically released films in the United States and a third of the country’s basic-cable output.

“Consolidation here not only leads to higher prices,” Bonta said. “It also leads to fewer opportunities for important stories to come to life, and fewer ways for audiences to encounter stories, ideas, and perspectives beyond their own experiences.”

But Variety reported that Ellison told Paramount’s senior executives that he would begin the process of moving the company out of California on October 1 if Bonta does not agree to settlement talks.

There could be downstream effects as well. The report also alleged that Ellison would pull Warner Bros Discovery out of California, too, if the $110bn merger goes through.

Variety indicated that Paramount is considering relocating to the US states of Tennessee, Texas or Georgia — none of which are involved in the ongoing antitrust lawsuit.

The dispute over Warner Bros Discovery’s fate stretches back to late 2025, when the company’s sale was first announced.

Critics quickly observed that the sale had the potential to shift the balance of power in Hollywood, with Warner Bros Discovery wielding influential properties including the news channel CNN, the production company New Line Cinema and the television-streaming service HBO.

The streaming giant Netflix initially emerged as a frontrunner to take over Warner Bros Discovery, but by February, Paramount succeeded in inking an agreement.

It was the second major merger Paramount had lined up in less than a year. In 2025, it had also succeeded in consolidating with the media production company Skydance, in a deal that generated scrutiny about the editorial independence of its subsidiaries.

Paramount’s decisions that year to cancel The Late Show with Stephen Colbert and enter into a $16m settlement with US President Donald Trump were widely perceived as efforts to curry government favour for the merger.

Paramount is considered a titan in US filmmaking and media production, as one of the oldest studios in the country. Its portfolio includes CBS News and Paramount Pictures.

The impending merger with Warner Bros Discovery has led to a fresh round of scrutiny for Ellison and the Paramount leadership.

Last week, Ellison addressed some of those concerns in an opinion column in The New York Times.

In it, he questioned whether the states’ antitrust lawsuit was “really about market share”, speculating that it was instead about control over major news outlets like CNN. He also sought to portray himself as politically independent.

“I have regularly voted for candidates of both parties; I hold some views that would be called conservative and others that would be called liberal, just like most Americans,” Ellison wrote.

“When it comes to our news operations, I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views.”

But the states have argued that combining Warner Bros Discovery and Paramount would create a monopoly, stifling competition.

If the merger succeeds, the states say that only four distributors would control 86 percent of the country’s films.

The merger could also mean job losses. As of the end of 2025, the headcount at Paramount stood at 17,600, while Warner Bros Discovery had 35,500 employees.

A day after the 12 states filed their lawsuit, the Writers Guild of America (WGA) followed suit.

In its July 14 complaint, the guild argued that the merger would mean fewer jobs and more pressure on writers to accept less favourable working terms, owing to reduced competition in the media market.

“Writers will be paid less and have fewer employment opportunities,” the WGA complaint said.

In Los Angeles County alone, the merger could result in a loss of nearly 2,500 jobs, according to an analysis by the Los Angeles County Department of Economic Opportunity, published in June.

As many as 6,000 employees around the world could also see their positions cut.

By comparison, when the Paramount and Skydance merger was completed in 2025, the company laid off roughly 2,000 people.

On July 24, Paramount Skydance agreed to pause the merger until a ruling in the states’ case is ultimately made or until June 1, 2027 — a move the WGA celebrated.

“It remains our view that this merger is unlawful, and we will continue the fight to block it,” WGA said at the time.

The WGA did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Slowing the merger could be costly for Paramount Skydance. Under the terms of the merger, the company would have to pay a so-called ticking fee of $7m per day, or $650m per quarter, if the deal does not close by September 30.

But the standoff with Ellison could also be costly for California, which is experiencing a downturn in the number of productions filmed in the state. New York, another state involved in the lawsuit, could see a backlash, as it houses studios for CBS News and Paramount’s executive offices.

Representatives for the state of California and Paramount Skydance did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Paramount Skydance’s stock is trending upward on the heels of Tuesday’s report. The stock was up 0.4 percent in midday trading, while Warner Bros Discovery was up 1.1 percent.

Fire rages after drone strikes Libya’s largest oil refinery

Firefighters in Libya are battling a massive blaze at the Zawiya refinery following a drone attack, with the country’s national oil company...
articles.body_text:
Fire rages after drone strikes Libya’s largest oil refinery

Firefighters in Libya are battling a massive blaze at the Zawiya refinery following a drone attack, with the country’s national oil company warning it may declare a force majeure and shut down operations if attacks continue.

Libya’s Ambulance and Emergency Service said in a statement on Tuesday there were no “serious injuries” from the fire, with most patients treated for smoke inhalation.

Footage verified by Al Jazeera showed huge flames and thick black ‌smoke billowing over the facility, the largest operating refinery in Libya with a refining capacity of 120,000 barrels per day.

It is located about 40km (25 miles) west of the capital, Tripoli.

The National Oil Corporation (NOC) said in a statement on Facebook that the fire broke out on Monday evening at tank number 402-T, belonging to the Brega Oil Company.

It said the tank, which contained about 4.5 million litres (1.2 million gallons) of gasoline, was “directly targeted, resulting in a severe fire before the tank completely collapsed”.

The NOC said the attack followed drone strikes on a water desalination plant at the refinery on Sunday and on a naphtha reservoir on Saturday.

The company declared a “maximum emergency” in the region and urged authorities to launch an investigation and bring the perpetrators to justice.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attacks, and the company did ‌not say who they believed was behind them.

In a statement hours later, the NOC said the refinery was “still being subject to sabotage attacks” with a drone targeting an oil blending and filling ⁠plant operated by the Zawiya Oil Refining Company.

It said the drone fell near its main oil tank and a pipeline network used to produce oils for the domestic market, without causing any casualties or damage.

“The company’s board of directors also confirms that if these attacks continue, it will have to declare a state of force majeure and suspend operations at the refinery,” it warned.

The Brega Oil Company, meanwhile, appealed to “all parties to stop the fighting and stay away from oil facilities and depots”. It said “oil facilities are vital infrastructure and owned by all Libyans” and that “protecting them is a national responsibility that does not tolerate any negligence”.

The attacks highlight the continuing security challenges in Libya, where rival administrations and armed groups have retained influence despite a ‌2020 ⁠ceasefire that halted major warfare. The country split in 2014 after a NATO-backed uprising that toppled longtime leader Muammar ⁠Gaddafi in 2011.

Two governments are currently vying for power: the United Nations-recognised administration in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and a rival in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.

In a statement, the Tripoli-based government said Dbeibah held a meeting earlier in the day with key officials, including the interior minister and the chiefs of some armed groups in the capital, “to follow up on the latest security developments”.

Dbeibah “stressed the need to deal firmly with any transgressions or actions that threaten security or harm vital facilities and installations”, the statement said.

Separately, a Libyan parliamentary panel condemned the attack and called for stronger protection of oil installations.

“The House of Representatives’ Energy and Natural Resources Committee condemns in the strongest terms the criminal attack targeting the Zawiya Refinery, one of the most vital facilities in the oil and gas sector that is a cornerstone of the national economy,” it said in a statement.

articles.title: Alan Jones trial: alleged victim told brother indecent assaults weren’t ‘too bad’ but involved broadcaster grabbing his penis, court hears
articles.excerpt:
Former 2GB and 2UE radio host, now 85, has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email...
articles.body_text:
Former 2GB and 2UE radio host, now 85, has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An alleged victim of Alan Jones told his older brother, after the broadcaster was arrested, that his indecent assaults weren’t “too bad” but involved Jones grabbing his penis, a Sydney court has heard.

The witness on Tuesday was asked by the trial prosecutor Georgina Wright to describe what his younger brother, known as complainant J, told him during a meeting at a McDonald’s.

Last week, J, a former student athlete, told the court he reported the indecent assaults to police in 2024 after Jones was arrested because he wanted his child to know “right from wrong”.

Jones has pleaded not guilty to 20 charges of indecent assault and two of sexual touching against six complainants.

J’s brother said J told him at McDonald’s words to the effect of: “This is the hardest thing that I’ve ever had to tell you. You’ve probably seen the news about the defendant. I’m one of the people who have come forward.”

The witness then asked his younger brother: “How bad was it?”

The witnesses told the court that J replied: “Nothing too bad, he didn’t try to fuck me or anything like that. He would grab me on the cock, he would kiss me, those sort of things.”

Complainant J told his older brother that Jones would “grab me on the cock and ask me if it was OK” and he would tell Jones he was “uncomfortable” and the older man would change the subject and become “a different person”, the court heard.

Asked by his sibling why he hadn’t told him about the abuse decades ago, J said, according to the witness: “It was hard. I didn’t want things to stop, the money, the support.”

J’s brother agreed that he told police the complainant disclosed to him that the hugs would get longer and “one time he put his hands on my shoulders and told me he loved me”.

The brother, the first of more than 70 witnesses other than the alleged victims to appear at the trial, said he met Jones on several occasions in the early 2000s, at the broadcaster’s homes at Circular Quay and Fitzroy Falls, and at the 2GB studios. He told the court he had never seen the broadcaster acting inappropriately towards his younger brother.

The witness said the first time he met Jones was when he drove his younger brother to 2GB in 2003. He said they talked about J’s athleticism and horse racing as they sat around a boardroom table.

He told the court that Jones was generous and they shared a love of sport. J’s older brother said Jones offered to help him buy his fiancee an engagement ring and later gave him a Villeroy & Boch dinner set as a wedding gift.

The witness said during a family visit to Jones’s Fitzroy Falls farm he went for a drive with Jones and his brother to “put some bets on”, played tennis and toured the property.

Under cross-examination by Jones’s barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC, the witness said his brother had never told him he was frightened of Jones.

Last week, J told the court he watched Jones’s arrest on television almost two years ago and decided to make a statement to NSW police.

Asked on Tuesday why he didn’t tell his mother about the abuse, J said he wasn’t prepared for that at the time, and she would have pushed him to report it to police. “I would be crushed in court and no one would believe me,” J said.

The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

articles.title: RBA interest rates: Reserve Bank holds cash rate at 4.35% as house prices continue to fall
articles.excerpt:
In a widely expected decision, the Reserve Bank of Australia holds interest rate after three hikes earlier this year

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news emai...
articles.body_text:
In a widely expected decision, the Reserve Bank of Australia holds interest rate after three hikes earlier this year

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Reserve Bank has held the cash rate at 4.35% but threatened to hike again if needed, as it warned falling house prices will slow income growth.

The widely expected decision comes after a steep decline in property values in Sydney and Melbourne arrived in Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide following three rate hikes earlier this year.

Economists and financial markets were unanimous in predicting no change following the latest two-day RBA board meeting.

The board in a statement accompanying the decision said that after this year’s three rate hikes “the economy appears to be slowing as expected”, but warned that it “will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if upside risks materialise”.

Board members all voted in favour of holding the cash rate, even as they acknowledged that “inflation is still too high”.

At 3.8% in the year to June, headline inflation would not return towards the targeted 2.5% until late 2027 and “there are upside risks to this projection”, the board said.

“With monetary policy judged to be somewhat restrictive, the board decided to leave the cash rate target unchanged while it assesses how the economy is evolving,” the statement said.

The RBA released its latest assessment of the economy’s health in new forecasts on Tuesday.

It predicted economic growth would hold at about 1.4% over 2026, with slightly higher population growth offset by a surprisingly heavy drop in home prices, in its statement on monetary policy.

The RBA predicted household spending would be weaker than expected in 2026, as falling house prices would reduce household wealth and lead to fewer home sales.

It cited research suggesting the federal budget’s tax reforms would leave house prices up to 5% lower in the long term. It noted prices had risen about 5% in the last year and were up 50% since 2020.

New home loans have already begun to slow. Investor loan commitments in June had fallen by roughly a quarter compared to the start of the year, as a share of total housing credit, the RBA reported.

Westpac on Monday reported a 20% fall in home loan applications since mid-May, blaming interest rate rises rather than the federal budget.

As the housing market slows, some banks have started cutting advertised mortgage rates by as much as the equivalent of an interest rate hike. The RBA said this demonstrated “continued strong competition and could reflect efforts to maintain market share”.

Mortgage holders have kept ahead on repayments as rates rise, with seven in eight borrowers holding almost a year or more worth of repayments in their offset and redraw accounts.

The RBA predicted a recovery in house prices, along with falling interest rates, could push per person economic activity back up again by 2028.

Australia’s economic growth is expected to be supported by a boom in datacentre investment. The RBA has previously warned the rapid build-out could add to inflation but its Tuesday statement said businesses were reporting no issues getting workers and materials for datacentre projects.

Underlying price pressures had risen in construction materials costs and groceries, including fruit and vegetables. Service industries like hospitality have also continued to report rising costs, with a tight jobs market adding to pressure on business.

Carol Kong, an analyst at Commonwealth Bank, said in a note on Tuesday that the RBA could afford to wait and see how severely its past hikes were affecting the economy,.

“Softer inflation and the weakness in the housing market give the RBA scope to assess the lagged effects of earlier tightening,” Kong said.

Bullock will hold her regular press conference at 3.30pm, Sydney time.

articles.title: Clover Moore unveils 4,500 sq metre Sydney plaza design after more than 40 years of planning
articles.excerpt:
Lord mayor says Town Hall square will be ‘fantastic’ – but business advocate says project’s scale of demolition presents ‘unwanted disruption’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

...
articles.body_text:
Lord mayor says Town Hall square will be ‘fantastic’ – but business advocate says project’s scale of demolition presents ‘unwanted disruption’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Sydneysiders have been given a first glimpse of a new public square set to “unify” the CBD, more 40 years after the project was initially conceived.

The City of Sydney on Tuesday released new renders of a plaza that will be built opposite Sydney town hall after the council began finalising discussions with the owners of the last of seven buildings that need to be acquired and bulldozed for the project.

The square’s design, demolition and construction is expected to cost $150m but the lord mayor, Clover Moore, has said the proposal presents a “once-in-a-generation opportunity”.

“I’ve sat in squares in Vienna and Rome and Greece and Spain – it’s where people gather, it’s the centre of city life and it’s quite fantastic,” she said.

“This isn’t going to be like that – it’s going to be just as grand as one of those squares, but it’s going to be very Sydney and it’s going to be very Australian.”

Councils have been acquiring the land needed to build the 4,500 sq metre plaza since 1982. Demolition is expected to start in 2028, with a completion date set for 2031.

Renders of the space, created by lead design consultant and architect, JPW, and landscape architects Aspect Studios, show a semi-circular clearing with a water feature flanked by movable tables and chairs, and a grove of native trees.

The fountain will provide a misting effect to help passersby cool off on summer days, the designers said.

The surrounding trees are expected to provide shade to about 50% of the site.

“It will draw together the disjointed public places around here and gather our wonderful Victorian sandstone buildings together into a unified place,” the JPW director and lead design consultant, Matthew Morel, said.

“It will be comfortable for two friends gathering to share lunch, or for thousands coming together for a civic celebration.”

But the Business Sydney executive director, Paul Nicolaou, said the demolition of seven buildings would create “unwanted disruption” in the heart of the city.

“The area involved needs to remain a commercial hub for our city when the CBD is still recovering post-Covid,” he said.

Moore has said the council will do all it can to help businesses find other places to operate.

“These are the consequences of doing these big city projects – which the city needs, the people need – but also other people have to accommodate themselves to changed circumstances,” she said.

articles.title: Jackie, the famous California bald eagle, dies after weeks of intensive care
articles.excerpt:
Wildlife organisation describes Jackie's condition before her death

Jackie, a bald eagle in California who became an online star, died on Monday after receiving weeks of veterinary treatment.

Jackie...
articles.body_text:
Wildlife organisation describes Jackie's condition before her death

Jackie, a bald eagle in California who became an online star, died on Monday after receiving weeks of veterinary treatment.

Jackie was being cared for by Ojai Raptor Center, a wildlife rehabilitation organisation, after she was attacked by other eagles. The bird had underlying health issues that caused anaemia and weight loss.

"Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists," Ojai Raptor Center said in a statement.

A livestream featuring the Big Bear Valley nest of Jackie and her partner, Shadow, has hundreds of thousands of subscribers.

The Big Bear Eagle Nest Cam, run by the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley in California, amassed a loyal following and Jackie was frequently spotted in the area since she hatched in the spring of 2012.

Jackie and Shadow had been mates since 2018, the Friends of Big Bear Valley website said.

"Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her," the Ojai Raptor Center said.

"We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her.

"We are working closely with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and will provide a more comprehensive statement including additional information on her treatments and test results."

Jackie's remains have been transferred to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the Ojai Raptor Center said.

articles.title: Nvidia gets $500bn from major investors to develop AI infrastructure
articles.excerpt:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has seen his company's value soar amid the AI boom in tech.

Nvidia has teamed up with some of Wall Street's largest banks and investors to raise $500bn (£370bn) in capital for...
articles.body_text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has seen his company's value soar amid the AI boom in tech.

Nvidia has teamed up with some of Wall Street's largest banks and investors to raise $500bn (£370bn) in capital for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

The chipmaker said it had struck deals with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR, and that the investors were for the first time treating AI hardware and infrastructure, often referred to as "compute", as an asset class.

"In AI, compute is revenue", Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, said. "We are bringing the world's leading long-term capital providers together to independently underwrite AI infrastructure."

The financing will go towards Nvidia's own projects and those being built by its partners.

Infrastructure projects backed by this fund will likely include the construction of new data centres to house, operate, and cool miles of stacked computer chips that process AI data and actions.

It will also back new factories to manufacture the AI chips needed to power these systems and increase their availability to buyers.

"Compute has become a critical infrastructure asset", Joe Bae and Scott Nuttall, co-chief executives of KKR, said in a joint statement. "As we've scaled our approach to digital infrastructure, we've learned that delivery, not ambition, is the hard part."

Essentially every major technology and AI company uses Nvidia's computer chips, or graphics processing units (GPUs), to power their services, AI platforms and AI chatbots.

Companies using Nvidia's popular chips or GPUs include Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic.

Such companies have collectively spent over $1tn, external in just three years on AI projects and infrastructure, with much more spending expected. And their demand for Nvidia's chips and services has driven the stock market value of the company up five fold in three years.

In a statement on Monday, Huang referred to Nvidia's role as a chip-maker as the company's beginning.

"Today, we are helping create a new class of productive, investable infrastructure: AI factories," he said.

With a new ability to tap some funding from the banks and investors partnering with Nvidia, they will be able to finance more of the AI boom.

Jim Zelter, president of Apollo, a lender which manages more than $1tn in assets, said: "Modern compute has emerged as a scarce, mission-critical asset class."

It is also "positioned to drive significant long-term economic growth and productivity gains", Zelter added.

BlackRock last month entered into an individual deal with Meta, external to finance and take a majority ownership stake in one data centre in Texas.

Anthropic also recently entered into a deal with Macquarie Asset Management and GIC, a sovereign wealth fund in Singapore, for its own investment in AI infrastructure.

The company did not specify the size of the deal, but said more financing was needed as its popular chatbot Claude had become so popular that the "demand requires significant new compute".

Preliminary reports reveal South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham died at 71 from an aortic dissection due to arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, breaks down the fatal condition and the emergency response timeline at Graham's home. Additionally, Dr. Siegel warns about a spike in Cyclosporiasis cases across 31 states, offering crucial safety tips for prevention.

A 22-year-old passenger who died after a medical emergency aboard a Southwest Airlines flight bound for Los Angeles has been identified as officials investigate what may have led to his sudden death.

Rain McMillan Walmsey died Aug. 7 after becoming unresponsive aboard Southwest Flight 958 from Dallas to Los Angeles, prompting desperate attempts to save him before the plane landed at Los Angeles International Airport.

Newly released records from the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner reveal the investigation into Walmsey’s death remains open, and exactly what led to the young passenger’s death remains unclear.

The medical examiner identified Walmsey as a 22-year-old man and listed his place of death as "LAX Southwest plane."

CO-PILOT BECOMES SICK MIDAIR AS CREW ILLNESS REPORTS EMERGE AFTER OVERNIGHT LAYOVER

Portland, Oregon, USA - February 9, 2026: A Southwest Airlines 737 comes in for landing at Portland International Airport. (iStock)

His cause of death was listed as "deferred," which the medical examiner’s office says means the determination is pending additional investigation. No manner of death has been listed.

Walmsey became unresponsive after experiencing a medical emergency while Flight 958 was en route to Los Angeles, law enforcement sources told NBC Los Angeles. CPR was administered to Walmsey aboard the aircraft, and paramedics responded when the flight arrived at LAX, according to the outlet. He could not be revived and was pronounced dead at the scene.

It remains unclear what type of medical emergency Walmsey experienced.

DELTA FLIGHT FORCED TO DIVERT AFTER PASSENGER GOES INTO LABOR AND DELIVERS BABY MIDAIR

The device’s lithium battery was larger than the permitted limit, causing the delay. (iStock)

Southwest Airlines confirmed to Fox News Digital that a "medical incident involving a customer" occurred aboard Flight 958 from Dallas to Los Angeles on Friday but did not provide additional details, instead referring further questions to local authorities.

The incident follows other recent cases involving passengers who suffered fatal medical emergencies aboard commercial flights.

A Southwest passenger flight takes off from San Diego International Airport in San Diego, California, U.S., February 3, 2023. (REUTERS/Mike Blake)

In January 2025, 53-year-old Barbara Dipoli of Kansas died aboard an Air France flight from Paris to Boston, with authorities saying preliminary information pointed to a medical episode during the flight.

In June 2024, 8-year-old Sydney Weston became ill and unresponsive aboard a SkyWest flight before the plane diverted to Peoria, Illinois.

That same month, a 41-year-old American passenger died after suffering a severe medical emergency aboard a Fiji Airways flight bound for San Francisco.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides
articles.excerpt:
Watch: Chinese man targeted by 'flash wedding' scams

At 37, Wang Zhuang had almost given up hope of finding a wife, until he saw the glossy matchmaking adverts.

They promised he wouldn't have to was...
articles.body_text:
Watch: Chinese man targeted by 'flash wedding' scams

At 37, Wang Zhuang had almost given up hope of finding a wife, until he saw the glossy matchmaking adverts.

They promised he wouldn't have to waste years on building a relationship that had no future. They offered to introduce him to a demure, devoted woman.

"The matchmakers said that girls from Guizhou are frugal," Wang says. "They told me they are good at running a household, able to do housework, and their families are very poor, so after marrying into your family, they would settle down and live a life with you."

So Wang travelled to Guiyang, a city in the southwestern province of Guizhou, in the hope of finding his soulmate.

He thought he had, when he was matched with a woman who seemed to tick every box. They had only met a few times before they married.

Then, almost as quickly as his new life had begun, it was over.

"My whole family has been thrown into chaos," he says, shaking his head.

He is still picking up the pieces more than a year after he discovered that everything he had been told by his wife was a lie.

She was a former karaoke hostess who'd been married three times, had three children, a serious sexually transmitted disease and was deeply in debt. She had even lied about her age.

He is fighting for a divorce and cannot return home to his old life - at least until he can recoup some of his life savings, which he says he paid to the agency within hours of being introduced to several potential matches.

"My parents blame me. I have insomnia and anxiety. I can't focus on work."

Chinese brides are in huge demand because of a steep gender imbalance

Wang's story is an extreme symptom of a demographic crisis that has long been in the making in China.

For decades, China's Communist Party decreed that couples could have only one child. They reversed course in January 2016 but by then the "one-child" policy, coupled with a preference for boys, had produced a shrinking pool of women and a stark gender imbalance.

There are now 30 million more men than women in China – that's more than the male population of the UK, or the entire population of Australia.

This has left men like Wang, who are in their late 30s and who live in smaller cities or far- flung, rural areas, with few options. Women in these places can afford to be choosy as they know they are in demand.

"The requirements for men are very high in my city. You need to have a car, a house and your family should preferably run a business," he says.

Many families also demand a high "bride price", a longstanding Chinese custom where the groom's family gives money to the bride. In parts of China, where men far outnumber women, this has become a significant financial burden.

Hence the appeal of matchmaking agencies like the ones in Guizhou, which are proposing a one-stop, quick solution - or "flash marriages".

Matchmaking agencies are hardly new in China, but many seem to be finding vulnerable targets in men who are struggling to find partners as they grow older.

So much so that state media recently reported that the industry had seen "rapid growth" which  had "bred illegal practices and chaos".

The "flash marriage" market is now on Beijing's radar

It's hard to determine the scale of such fraud across China but it has grown enough to draw the attention of Chinese officials. Between January 2024 and March 2025, prosecutors handled cases involving 1,546 individuals for crimes related to the matchmaking industry.

This month, five separate authorities jointly launched a nationwide crackdown on the matchmaking industry after the issue generated "widespread public concern".

In one case, a matchmaking agency reportedly used karaoke waitresses as bait to defraud 128 victims of more than 2.5 million yuan (£274,000, $371,000).

"I think the government could introduce industry-specific regulations targeting flash marriage scams," Fan Binghe, from the Nanjing Office of the Beijing Jingshi law firm, told the BBC.

Although Guiyang has become synonymous with this booming "flash marriage" market, there is little to suggest it is a romantic hub.

The agency offices sit in a dense warren of buildings above a shopping precinct, where vendors sell local fruit and workers queue for takeaway sour soup rice noodles.

Wang, however, was convinced he could trust them after the company told him they would do a full background check and that he would be entitled to compensation if he was the victim of fraud.

So he paid up and the introductions began.

Wang was drawn to Guiyang by the promise of a demure spouse

He met seven women in various "blind date" rooms over a few days while being carefully supervised by agency staff. He asked questions about where they came from, if they'd been married before and if they had any kids.

He set his heart on the eighth woman he met. He was hoping to meet someone who hadn't been married before, with no children and who was just a little younger than him.

"She also dressed very simply," he recalls. "She looked introverted and honest."

They met four or five times for just eight to ten minutes each time. He says they had been under strict instructions not to exchange phone numbers or any details on private messages, or they would be fined.

After two or three days he decided she was the one and he agreed to pay her a substantial bride price. "I spent more than 300,000 yuan ($44,000)," he says, with a pile of well-thumbed legal papers in hand to prove it.

"If you include the wedding banquet and everything else, I spent around 400,000 to 500,000 yuan."

The whole process was documented by the matchmaking agency in a series of glossy photos, which they also use to advertise their services on Chinese social media.

In the video the couple are holding hands on a red carpet and smiling while romantic music plays in the background.

Wang with his ex-wife in a photo taken soon after their wedding

Just months into the marriage, debt collectors started calling, alleging she owed them money.

Wang grew suspicious and wanted to know what else she had kept hidden. He checked her phone and found details of her former life, her birth certificate and former marriage documents.

When he confronted her, she offered him a divorce, but refused to return a single penny of the bride price.

He says he tried to hunt down the agency responsible for his marriage, but when he returned to their offices, they had packed up and disappeared.

From his rented flat in Guiyang, just across from the main district which houses most of these agencies, Wang now spends his time making social media videos trying to warn other men about what can go wrong.

In Guiyang, it is difficult to find an agency where the staff is willing to talk. One agency boss agreed to talk to us in their offices – although his business partner later asked us to leave.

Inside there was a red carpet littered with fake petals ready for a proposal. He told us a couple had pledged to marry just hours before we arrived.

"There's a huge market for flash marriages in China. It only really emerged over the last two or three years," he told us.

The agencies claim families here did not strictly adhere to the one-child policy, which means the area has a larger pool of women. "Even if a family had two or three daughters, they would keep trying for a son," one of them told the BBC.

They say they are now trying to match these women with men from central provinces – like Wang who lives in Hebei – who are relatively wealthy but have few women around them.

"Our clients are free to choose whoever they like. The purpose of our business is to help people find someone they genuinely want to be with."

One of the advertisements assures their prospective clients that "Three days with the right introduction can beat three years of dating".

It was in a room like this where Wang met his bride

Wang now spends his time trying to help other victims of similar spiels.

His rented flat is full of men who are either searching for the owners of the agency who scammed them, or are trying to recoup their losses from their wives who ran off after only a few weeks of marriage.

On a fold-up bed by the window, 59-year-old Xu Rulin from Jiangxi province pulls his carefully collated evidence out of a red plastic shopping bag.

He spent nearly 500,000 yuan trying to find his son a wife through a "flash marriage" agency.

Together they travelled to Guiyang - more than 1,000km away - and his son wed just seven days after he first met his bride in a "blind date" room.

Xu says after the marriage was registered, she demanded they buy her an iPhone and transfer around 20,000 yuan to help her with her business. She also asked for 120,000 yuan for a wedding dress and jewellery, he claims.

"All I wanted was for her to genuinely settle down and live with us," he told us. "She said she wanted a house and I agreed to buy one for them. It was all agreed."

But he says she ran away after living with them for less than two weeks. She has been detained by the police, and the couple have been able to get divorced.

He says the owners of the matchmaking company were also arrested in January this year, but he is still in Guiyang trying to recover some of the losses.

The bride Xu Rulin spent a fortune finding for his son ran away within two weeks

The agency manager the BBC spoke to admitted there were no formal background checks on their clients.

"The women are introduced by local matchmakers who already know them very well. They know their family background because they're often from the same village. The male's matchmaker also usually knows the man very well."

They would not say how much their services cost because that information was "confidential".

He did say that if the information provided by either side is not truthful, then the client is entitled to get their money back.

"I'd say more than 90% of what our clients tell us here is true," he claimed.

"We have a saying here in China. One rotten mouse dropping spoils the whole pot of soup. That's exactly what it's like. We regularly attend meetings with the local police. If a matchmaking agency is found to be involved in marriage fraud, it will be held legally responsible."

This matchmaker says most people in the industry are genuine

This brings little comfort for those who have lost whatever money they had saved.

"I never imagined that with the agency charging such a high service fee, a local matchmaker in her hometown checking her background and the company offering so many guarantees, that the women's information would turn out to be completely fake," Wang says.

He is almost resigned now to his losses. And he blames himself for falling for the scam: "Only women with problems would agree to these kind of flash marriages."

He has kneeled at the police offices in Guiyang pleading for them to help him get his money back and he has even travelled to Beijing to urge the authorities to do more to combat this type of crime.

These cases are difficult to prosecute, says Fan Binghe, the lawyer who has handled many.

For one, Chinese law has no specific criminal offence which covers this kind of marriage fraud, and so to bring criminal charges, a victim has to establish that the aim of their spouse was always to take their money.

"In cases I've handled, suspects often argue that they genuinely intended to marry and live a good life but realised they were incompatible, had conflicts, and decided to end the relationship," he says.

"In situations like that, the line becomes blurred. Relationship issues are difficult to disprove."

Wang's apartment has turned into a refuge for scammed men

Even harder is getting money back from sham matchmaking agencies which often shut up shop as soon as they have made enough cash.

Wang has managed to get some money back, but not all.

"After going through something like this, I don't even know if I can still get married. It was already hard for me to find someone. And now I've spent so much money. I won't consider it now."

Wang's life, and the life of the men in the apartment, all appear to be in limbo.

"It has taken almost two years, and even now I still don't know when I can divorce her," he says, surrounded by his legal paperwork.

"I don't know when this will be resolved, so I can restart a normal life. It feels endless."

articles.title: Fauci texts raising theoretical miscarriage concern after COVID vaccine dose spark backlash
articles.excerpt:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier discusses newly revealed text messages involving Dr. Anthony Fauci and his concerns about COVID-19 vaccine-related miscarriages on 'America Reports.'

Multiple ...
articles.body_text:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier discusses newly revealed text messages involving Dr. Anthony Fauci and his concerns about COVID-19 vaccine-related miscarriages on 'America Reports.'

Multiple officials erupted on social media after a Senate committee released text messages Monday showing Dr. Anthony Fauci privately raised a theoretical concern that fever and other reactions after a second COVID-19 vaccine dose could be associated with miscarriage in the first trimester.

The January 2021 conversation, obtained from Fauci's government-issued cellphone, shows the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) discussing concerns about fever and other symptoms following a second vaccine dose. Fauci wrote that the reaction "theoretically could be associated with miscarriage in the 1st trimester."

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., who released the conversation with Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., blasted Fauci on social media.

FAUCI DISCUSSED COVID MRNA VACCINE CONCERNS FOR PREGNANT WOMEN IN TEXT CHAIN RELEASED BY SENATE COMMITTEE

Rand Paul accused Fauci of saying one thing publicly and another privately, and claimed Fauci downplayed vaccine risks to pregnant women rather than admit he had been wrong about the shots. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Once again, Anthony Fauci was saying one thing in public and something completely different in private," Paul said in a post on X. "He was willing to put women and their unborn children at risk instead of admitting that he was wrong about the vaccines that he tried guilting Americans into taking."

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also blasted the former top health official, accusing him of withholding information that could have put pregnant women and their unborn children at risk.

"Pregnant women were told it was safe! How many women lost babies due to Dr. Fauci's lies," Uthmeier said in a post on X.

Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., took a step further, calling for Fauci's arrest in an ordeal she called "the most infuriating thing."

"Fauci knew Covid shots cause miscarriages. And still forced the shots. Fauci belongs in prison," Greene said in a post on X.

FAUCI'S HHS IPHONE TURNED OVER TO SENATE INVESTIGATORS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

James Uthmeier accused Fauci of withholding information about potential vaccine risks to pregnant women and questioned whether his guidance may have contributed to miscarriages. (Amy Beth Bennett / South Florida Sun Sentinel)

"If a Covid vaccine can kill a baby and cause a miscarriage, then imagine all the other things it can do to you. And Fauci knew it and still told people to take it," she added in a separate post.

Johnson's press release on the text messages said the findings "could have an immediate impact [on] public health and the principle of informed consent."

In addition, Fauci had previously acknowledged that there were "no data or theoretical reason" to believe vaccination earlier in pregnancy should be preferred over vaccination later in pregnancy.

He also noted that more than 10,000 pregnant women had already been vaccinated with "no issues" reported.

FILE - Dr. Anthony Fauci testifying on Capitol Hill on Jan. 11, 2022. (GREG NASH/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Around that time, Dr. Vivek Murthy, who was part of the conversation and would later serve as former President Joe Biden's surgeon general, flagged a World Health Organization recommendation against Moderna's vaccine for pregnant women due to limited data.

Murthy said issuing a strong recommendation against vaccination based on a lack of data could be "potentially quite damaging to public confidence among pregnant women."

Fox News Digital's Eric Mack contributed to this report.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

articles.title: DiJonai Carrington responds to 'White privilege' post, but leaves meaning of it still unclear
articles.excerpt:
DiJonai Carrington went to Threads to claim "white privilege" following her takedown flagrant foul of Sophie Cunningham despite her intentionally clotheslining her in the face.

Chicago Sky’s DiJonai ...
articles.body_text:
DiJonai Carrington went to Threads to claim "white privilege" following her takedown flagrant foul of Sophie Cunningham despite her intentionally clotheslining her in the face.

Chicago Sky’s DiJonai Carrington finally responded to those criticizing her for posting "WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever" after being ejected for clotheslining Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham.

But her response still doesn’t explain why she chose those specific words to post on her Threads account, presumably from the locker room, following her ejection during Saturday’s loss to the Fever.

Carrington quote tweeted a retort to ex-NFL player and sports personality Emmanuel Acho, who said on his "Speakeasy" show that Carrington could not call her foul on Cunningham "White privilege."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

DiJonai Carrington of the Chicago Sky looks on during a game against the Las Vegas Aces on Aug. 1, 2026, at Wintrust Arena in Chicago, Ill. (Getty Images)

"I’ve never once claimed that the assessment of the foul was white privilege (that was your assumption)," Carrington’s reply to Acho read on X. "Try exercising your critical thinking skills, I know you studied psych.

"Furthermore, I’m the LAST thing from ignorant or asinine when it comes to speaking on 'white privilege,' do ya research on that one. I actually went to school, one of the top universities might I add, to educate myself on this exact subject," Carrington, who attended Stanford for four years before grad-transferring to Baylor, added. "I would never use that term as a rhetorical weapon knowing the historical and social weight it holds without having the proper evidence to substantiate it."

FORMER NFL PLAYERS CALL OUT DIJONAI CARRINGTON FOR BLAMING EJECTION ON 'WHITE PRIVILEGE'

So, if Carrington’s Threads post wasn’t about the assessment of the foul, then what exactly did her Threads post refer to on Saturday night following her ejection?

Fox News Digital didn't immediately receive a response from Carrington’s rep after asking that exact question.

Does Carrington’s post refer to Cunningham, though she didn’t accuse her by name and there was no evidence the foul has any connection to the Fever star’s position on transgender athletes in women’s sports? Does it refer to the Fever organization, or the WNBA as a whole?

Carrington took time to reduce the list of possibilities by one, but for whatever reason, continues to remain vague and mysterious about the controversial post.

The WNBA has yet to announce any discipline for Carrington’s actions in the loss to the Fever, which occurred late in the first quarter when she was hawking Cunningham, who had a breakaway layup. When Cunningham went up, Carrington jumped and smacked her in the face.

DiJonai Carrington of the Chicago Sky fouls Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever during the first half Aug. 8, 2026, at the United Center in Chicago, Ill. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Cunningham was livid, getting up from the hardwood and confronting Carrington face-to-face. As she was being held back by teammates, she shoved Carrington slightly before officials stepped in as well.

After official review, Carrington’s foul was upgraded to a Flagrant 2, and she was ejected from the game.

Cunningham has been at the center of a widening political debate about biological men in women’s sports, as supporters of her stance held a fourth rally outside the Fever road game at the United Center in Chicago on Saturday, while counterprotesters also gathered near the venue.

WHO IS DIJONAI CARRINGTON? WNBA STAR WHO SMACKED SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM, GOT EJECTED AND BLAMED 'WHITE PRIVILEGE'

Cunningham has stated she does not harbor any hatred toward transgender people, but she believes protecting girls and women in sports is "common sense." She has received backlash for her belief, and the debate has spilled inside and outside of WNBA venues, while discourse continues online.

Meanwhile, this isn’t the first time Carrington has been at the center of controversy involving Fever players. During the 2024 campaign, where she was playing with the Connecticut Sun, Carrington mocked then-rookie Caitlin Clark for what she believed was flopping and later called Fever supporters "the nastiest fans in the W" after receiving racist abuse from online users.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Then, Carrington struck Clark in the eye while defending a pass during the 2024 WNBA playoffs, leading to the latter having a black eye. Both players said that the contact was accidental, though Carrington drew some renewed criticism after she appeared to joke about the controversy during an Instagram Live video.

Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington commits a flagrant 2 foul against Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham. (Kamil Krzaczynski/Imagn Images)

Beyond basketball, she has drawn attention for wearing an explicit anti-President Donald Trump sweatshirt and urging WNBA players to oppose Trump administration policies affecting women and the LGBTQ community.

Carrington is in her sixth WNBA season, her first with the Sky, where she is averaging 9.8 points and 2.2 rebounds across her five games in a depth role for Chicago.

Fox News' Jackson Thompson and Matthew Reigle contributed to this report.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: President Trump warns FIFA will pay a massive price if it ousts chief Gianni Infantino
articles.excerpt:
DiJonai Carrington went to Threads to claim "white privilege" following her takedown flagrant foul of Sophie Cunningham despite her intentionally clotheslining her in the face.

President Donald Trump...
articles.body_text:
DiJonai Carrington went to Threads to claim "white privilege" following her takedown flagrant foul of Sophie Cunningham despite her intentionally clotheslining her in the face.

President Donald Trump is handing out a big red card to FIFA’s bosses, warning soccer’s top execs they’d be out of their minds to dump embattled president Gianni Infantino.

Taking to Truth Social, Trump went to bat for Infantino, who faces an all-out revolt from global soccer leaders after a disastrous scheme to sell off a chunk of the men’s World Cup to private equity investors.

"FIFA would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing President Gianni Infantino," Trump posted.

TRUMP ADMIN TAUNTS LEFT FOR ‘PRAYING’ FOR WORLD CUP DISASTER AS DOT TOUTS RECORD NUMBERS

"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented. If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again!"

Trump has is on the money concerning, well, the money.

US President Donald Trump and FIFA president (Fédération Internationale de Football Association) Gianni Infantino talk in the Oval office of the White House after signing an executive order for a task force related to the FIFA World Cup, in Washington, DC, on March 7, 2025 (Jim WATSON / AFP)

President Donald Trump speaks alongside FIFA President Gianni Infantino at a FIFA reception at Trump Tower in New York City on July 17, 2026. (Andrew Harnik/Reuters)

The 2026 World Cup across America was a total monster as it packed stadiums and smashed revenue records. Say what you want, but nobody puts on a sports spectacle quite like the USA.

Yet the president's defense comes as Infantino’s internal trouble reaches a boiling point.

EUROPEAN SOCCER'S GOVERNING BODY FLIPS SPORT UPSIDE DOWN WITH BOYCOTT OF FIFA, FUTURE WORLD CUPS

The Swiss-Italian soccer boss ignited a firestorm by proposing a commercial entity dubbed FIFA Forward Enterprise, which would sell private investors a 20% stake in World Cup commercial rights for a $4.2 billion payday.

Soccer's power brokers wanted no part of it. Leaders across Europe, Asia and North America rejected the deal, accusing Infantino of trying to quietly sell off the sport's crown jewels. He quickly scrapped the proposal and apologized, but the revolt was already rolling.

UEFA, the AFC and CONCACAF then unloaded on the FIFA boss, accusing him of deception and abandoning his duty. European leaders have even floated a boycott of FIFA events, while execs behind closed doors are plotting rival tournaments that could leave Infantino on the outside looking in before the next election cycle.

FIFA REPORTEDLY WILLING TO LET TRUMP HAND WORLD CUP TROPHY TO WINNING CAPTAIN AT METLIFE STADIUM

Could Infantino’s close relationship with the president be adding even more fuel to the revolt?

UEFA General Secretary Gianni Infantino gives a press conference following a UEFA Executive meeting on October 15, 2015 at the European football's governing body headquarters in Nyon. UEFA President Michel Platini will get a strong indication of the level of support from the organisation he heads after he was suspended for 90 days by FIFA's ethics committee looking into corruption at the global football body. AFP PHOTO / FABRICE COFFRINI (Photo credit should read FABRICE COFFRINI/AFP/Getty Images)

Trump, who was firmly in Infantino’s corner throughout the World Cup, clearly sees the fight through a dollars-and-cents lens.

Whether Infantino survives the red cards flying from every direction remains to be seen.

But Trump has picked his side — and he’s warning FIFA that dumping Infantino could come with one hell of a price tag.

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

articles.title: Colombia’s far-right government recognises Israeli claim over Golan Heights
articles.excerpt:
Colombia has become only the second country to recognise Israel’s claim of sovereignty over the occupied Syrian Golan Heights, just days after far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took power.
...
articles.body_text:
Colombia has become only the second country to recognise Israel’s claim of sovereignty over the occupied Syrian Golan Heights, just days after far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took power.

Colombia’s Foreign Ministry made the announcement on Monday, joining the United States as the only other country to recognise Israel’s annexation of the territory in 1981.

“The Government of Colombia recognises Israeli sovereignty over this territory, as well as that State’s right to protect itself against external threats,” read a statement published on X.

“Colombia recognises that maintaining Israel’s control and sovereignty over the Golan Heights is an essential component of its national defence,” it added.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar thanked his “good friend” de la Espriella for the “historic” recognition.

He said the pair had agreed on the move in the Colombian city of Barranquilla a day before de la Espriella’s inauguration.

Israel captured most of the Golan Heights from Syria during the 1967 Six-Day War, before illegally annexing the territory in 1981. The move was rejected by most of the international community, although the US formally recognised Israel’s claim in 2019 during President Donald Trump’s first term in office.

The United Nations recognises the region as a part of Syria, and last month, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres reiterated that stance, describing Israeli occupation as “totally unacceptable”.

Syria tried to regain the Golan in the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, but was thwarted. Israel and Syria signed an armistice in 1974, and the Golan has been relatively quiet since.

Colombia’s recognition of the Israeli claim comes as Israel expands its military footprint in Syria following the collapse of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024. Israel has moved troops into a UN-monitored buffer zone and seized strategic territories, including the Syrian side of Jabal al-Sheikh (Mount Hermon), which overlooks the capital, Damascus.

De La Espriella, the new Colombian president, ran a bombastic campaign during which he promised close relations with the US and Israel as a way to combat armed groups in his country.

The US-backed millionaire has promised to restore Bogota’s ties with Israel after his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, criticised Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, severed diplomatic relations and halted Israeli arms imports.

De La Espriella has also cancelled Petro’s plans to open an embassy in Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.

articles.title: Trump demands compensation from Iran as talks on Strait of Hormuz continue
articles.excerpt:
Trump to demand compensation for Tehran’s ‘conflicts’

United States President Donald Trump has demanded compensation from Iran for those he claimed were killed by the country after Tehran conditioned...
articles.body_text:
Trump to demand compensation for Tehran’s ‘conflicts’

United States President Donald Trump has demanded compensation from Iran for those he claimed were killed by the country after Tehran conditioned the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz on receiving war reparations from Washington.

Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday that his administration was going to seek payment for “50 years” of damages caused by Iran, framing the move as a direct response to Tehran’s claims.

Tehran has said it will not open the Strait of Hormuz – through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas flowed before the US-Israel war on Iran – unless Washington agrees to pay war reparations and end sanctions. The Iranian demands were largely in line with the terms of an interim peace agreement signed in June, which has since broken down over a dispute on control over the strait.

Talks between Iran and Oman over the waterway, which separates the two countries, are ongoing, but Trump’s new demands risk complicating efforts to reopen the maritime passage.

“They asked for reparations, you might say. Or they asked for money for the damage that we’ve done. I said that’s a good idea,” he told reporters. “Well, we’re going to ask for money for the damage they’ve done over a 50-year period.”

The payments would cover deaths among US forces in the region as well as civilian protesters in Iran, he said, claiming that 52,000 people have been killed in Iran in the past four months. Tehran says some 3,117 people died in antigovernment protests that swept the country in January, prior to the launch of the US-Israel war.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) in February reported about 7,000 deaths, including 6,500 protesters.

Trump also said Tehran should compensate families of the 17 US sailors killed in an October 2000 attack in Yemen on the USS Cole naval vessel, which has been blamed on al-Qaeda, not Iran.

“Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!” he wrote in a Truth Social post.

Since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, Trump has repeatedly oscillated between threats of escalation and claims that a peace deal is imminent.

He threatened last week to “hit” Iran “very hard”, only to pull back, hinting a peace deal was near. This weekend, he said he was “low-keying” his approach to the conflict, suggesting that he was prepared to let economic pressure mount in place of further military strikes.

Charles Kupchan, a former special assistant to ex-US President Barack Obama, described Trump’s remarks about requiring compensation as “banter” and said both sides have strong incentives to reach a deal.

“Unfortunately, we are just looking at some back-and-forth banter here, where neither the Iranians nor the Trump administration is being serious,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Iran cannot survive if it won’t be able to export its oil”, he said, and Trump doesn’t want to go into the US midterms with high gas prices. There is also pressure on the Pentagon in light of reports that US munitions stockpiles are low, he added.

Iran earlier said it was nearing a final pact with Oman defining new shipping lanes between them through the Strait of Hormuz, but repeated that the US must meet its conditions, including an end to military threats.

The strait has been effectively blocked since the war began, pushing up oil prices and inflation.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told state media on Monday that talks with Oman were “progressing smoothly and constructively”, with an agreement reached on a shipping route map, while some technical issues remained unresolved.

Baghaei said the discussions also covered services that would normally involve payment, such as safe navigation, environmental protection, maritime services and combating crime.

He added that the US’s continued “hostile actions” in the Strait of Hormuz have made the passageway unsafe and that Tehran considers Washington’s naval blockade of Iranian ports an “act of aggression”.

US Central Command said on Monday that it has redirected 55 commercial vessels since reinstating the blockade in July and “disabled” at least two. According to Windward, a maritime intelligence firm, the blockade has resulted in a “complete halt” to Iranian oil exports from Kharg Island, located in the Gulf.

Trump on Monday described the blockade as a “steel wall” and said that “the only one that has control of the Strait of Hormuz right now is the United States Navy”.

He also claimed the waterway was open and that the US military has cleared it of mines.

Shipping data firms, meanwhile, said traffic in the waterway had dropped sharply over the weekend, with MarineTraffic reporting that crossings had gone down from 15 on Friday to 11 on Saturday, and six on Sunday.

The data showed that 17 vessels passed through the Iran-designated route, while 10 others took a route classified as “undetermined”, it said.
