Melissa Donnelly, t...
articles.body_text:
Melissa Donnelly, the national secretary of the Community and Public Sector Union, will replace the outgoing ACTU head

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Melissa Donnelly, the national secretary of the Community and Public Sector Union, will take on the role as the next head of the trade movement in Australia, after the resignation of Sally McManus.

The Australian Council of Trade Unions’ secretary and its president, Michele O’Neil, revealed last month they would be stepping down after eight years together as the first all-female leadership team in the ACTU’s 99-year history, playing a major role in shaping the Albanese government’s workplace agenda.

On Monday, the ACTU executive met to elect 44-year-old Donnelly, who will be among the peak body’s youngest secretaries.

In a statement, Donnelly said it was a “tremendous honour” to take on the “important role”.

“Following in the footsteps of Sally is no easy task,” she said. “She has dedicated her life to fighting for fairer, safer and more secure workplaces.

“I am eager to get to work delivering real outcomes for working people and advancing the interests of workers across the country.

“Most of all, I am looking forward to meeting union members from every corner of Australia and serving alongside you as we work to lift living standards and secure a better future for all.”

Donnelly, who started her career as a lawyer in private practice, has led the CPSU for seven years, rising through the ranks after spearheading the union’s federal court case enabling public servants to participate in the nationwide “Your Rights at Work” campaign, which opposed the Howard government’s WorkChoices legislation.

In a statement, the CPSU said membership had grown by 23% during her tenure, with Donnelly pursuing flexible working arrangements, including a removal of caps on the number of days staff can work from home, delivering 18 weeks’ paid parental leave for both parents and leading the campaign to reverse the government outsourcing work to private consultancy firms.

Under her leadership, the CPSU has recently taken the tax office to the Fair Work Commission over alleged violations of the Albanese government’s “same job same pay” laws.

In a statement, the public service minister, Katy Gallagher, congratulated Donnelly and said the pair had worked “closely together” to rebuild “the public service and strengthened its capacity and capability to deliver for Australians”.

“Melissa has been a tireless advocate for public servants,” Gallagher said. “I know she’ll bring that same determination and experience to standing up for workers across Australia.”

McManus said Donnelly had “overwhelming support” across the union movement, describing her as “smart, strategic and completely focused on the needs of working people”.

“The average union member is a 44-year-old working mother and so is Melissa. She’s a year younger than I was when I took up the office and represents generational change,” she said.

“With two school-age children and having led a large union, she well knows the pressures working people are under. She has my full support, and I look forward to assisting her as she steps into the role.”

articles.title: Kurdish hunger striker says ICE force-feeding ‘mentally broke me’
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Film-maker Gabar Choli describes how he endured coercive treatment over eight months in detention in Texas

A Kurdish man who was force fed over the course of eight months while on hunger s...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Film-maker Gabar Choli describes how he endured coercive treatment over eight months in detention in Texas

A Kurdish man who was force fed over the course of eight months while on hunger strike in US immigration detention has spoken out about it for the first time, describing how much the process harmed him physically and psychologically.

Gabar Choli, a film-maker and activist now living in Canada after being deported, described how he endured the coercive treatment – a practice widely considered torture by international human rights groups – often twice a day after being detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) when his asylum application was denied.

“It just broke me, mentally broke me,” Choli said in an exclusive interview with the Guardian. “It came to a point that I decided to write my body an apology letter.”

ICE officials force-fed Choli at the Port Isabel federal detention center in Los Fresnos, south Texas, from late May 2025 until he was deported in January of this year, a Guardian investigation found. Choli had resorted to a hunger strike to protest conditions at the facility and to push for a resolution to his immigration case.

He described how a team of detention center guards would physically restrain him while ICE medical staff forcibly inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his esophagus and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach.

“I was respectful. I just told them I am protesting for humane treatment, nothing else,” Choli said. “But they were determined to break me.”

Much of what happens in ICE detention has been hidden from public view over successive administrations.

An investigation by the Guardian last week found that the second Trump administration used court orders in plans to subject at least 10 hunger strikers in ICE detention to involuntary medical procedures.

However, it has since emerged that the number is even higher. DHS sources told the Guardian over the weekend that between January 2025 and 4 August, 2026 ICE obtained court orders for involuntary medical treatment for 18 hunger strikers. The Guardian has previously found that while some people are force-fed, some give in and eat at the last minute when presented with a court order.

DHS sources also said that ICE “provides involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death”.

In court records reviewed by the Guardian in relation to Choli’s case and other hunger strikers, “involuntary medical treatment” is used as an umbrella term that includes the option of force-feeding.

According to court records related to Choli, ICE requested the court give the agency permission “to conduct routine physical examinations and routine laboratory testing, administer hydration, and if necessary, use restraints to accomplish this involuntary monitoring, treatment and administration of nutrients, fluids and medication(s), by way of intravenous measures and/or a nasogastric tube”.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), its parent agency, did not respond to specific questions about Choli’s case and had not responded to questions about force-feeding for the prior articles in the investigative series, but on Friday night sent a statement by email in response to the Guardian’s reporting and requests for comment.

“ICE respects an individual’s right to refuse medical treatment where appropriate,” an unnamed DHS spokesperson said. “However, when an individual’s medical condition presents a serious risk of death or permanent harm, or when other compelling legal or operational interests are implicated, ICE may seek judicial authorization for appropriate medical interventions consistent with applicable law. Any involuntary medical treatment is undertaken only pursuant to legal authority and under the direction of qualified medical professionals.”

“ICE is committed to ensuring the safety, security, and well-being of all individuals in its custody,” the spokesperson added.

Dozens of pages of federal court records verify that Choli was subjected to force-feeding, including declarations by ICE doctors and officers. Combined with interviews with medical and legal experts and an interview by phone with Choli himself , much of the secretive process is revealed. His case could be the longest documented case of force-feeding in ICE detention to date.

Choli arrived in Blaine, Washington state, in 2022. He had been living in Vancouver where he was a film-maker and activist campaigning for an independent nation of Kurdistan, having come to Canada from what he considers occupied territory in Iran. He said he requested asylum in the US due to death threats for his political activism while in Canada, and lived in Los Angeles with a work permit while his case was in process. But he was arrested during an ICE check-in on 25 February 2025 – the month after Donald Trump returned to the White House – after his asylum case failed.

He began a hunger strike in detention in California and was transferred to Texas. DHS and ICE then requested an emergency court order from a federal judge to force-feed him and perform other medical procedures, such as involuntary intravenous hydration, involuntary blood draws and urine analysis tests through forced catheterization, documents from the southern district of Texas federal court seen by the Guardian show.

“I am not suicidal,” Choli wrote in a letter to the federal judge overseeing his proceedings. “I am using hunger strike as the only available option to protest the abuse and mistreatment.”

DHS and ICE said in court records that force-feeding Choli was necessary for his health, but also that his prolonged hunger strike posed “a serious threat to the security and good order” of the detention center. They further accused Choli of attempting to “manipulate the immigration system” by striking.

During his first force feeding sessions, he recalled in an interview occasions where a nurse working for ICE “shoved the tube so hard” that “he tore my nose from the inside.” After such sessions “they would take me to solitary cell and I would just choke on my blood and drink the blood from inside [my throat],” he added. Many of his court records are sealed, so the Guardian is not able to corroborate some details in Choli’s account.

He did not have legal representation throughout the eight month ordeal. The federal judge presiding over his case, Rolando Olvera, denied Choli’s request for legal assistance and extended the force-feeding order several times at ICE’s request, according to records filed in the southern district of Texas federal court.

Choli suffered injuries and medical complications, including swollen sinuses, damage to his esophagus and stomach problems, court records show.

“That is just not medical care, that is torture,” Dr Chanelle Diaz, an assistant professor of medicine at Columbia University’s medical center, told the Guardian. Diaz has reviewed cases of other detained immigrants subjected to force-feeding and advocated for their release.

articles.title: Embattled Smithsonian director brought 'Marxist' activism, political agenda to roles through career: historian
articles.excerpt:
Historian Dr. Jody Edward Ginn joins ‘Fox News Live’ to discuss the Trump administration and House’s push to rid the Smithsonian museums of ‘woke’ exhibits.

Smithsonian Institution Director Dr. Anthe...
articles.body_text:
Historian Dr. Jody Edward Ginn joins ‘Fox News Live’ to discuss the Trump administration and House’s push to rid the Smithsonian museums of ‘woke’ exhibits.

Smithsonian Institution Director Dr. Anthea Hartig has spent decades promoting what one historian described as an activist and Marxist-inspired approach to history, raising questions about whether the nation's premier museum system is being led by an activist rather than an objective historian.

Dr. Jody Edward Ginn argued that Hartig has worked to pivot traditional historical organizations toward activist missions, including during her time as president of the Organization of American Historians (OAH) and her leadership role at the California Historical Society.

"She's asserting herself as a historical scholar who should get the last word on these things," Ginn told Fox News Digital. "Well, there's more than one problem with that. And it starts with the fact that I don't think she's really ever been a historian, she has been an advocate, an activist."

Ginn said his research into Hartig's professional background yielded accounts from her former associates indicating that she has "long been known for" pushing such agendas.

HISTORIAN BLASTS SMITHSONIAN'S ACTIVISM SHIFT AFTER FIRST VISIT IN OVER A DECADE: 'COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PLACE'

Dr. Jody Edward Ginn told Fox News Digital the Smithsonian has shifted from its educational mission toward activism after visiting the museum for the first time since 2012. (Fox News Digital ; Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

One early example Ginn cited was Hartig's 1995 research article, "In a World He Has Created," published by the California Historical Society, where Hartig later served as an executive director for seven years beginning in 2011.

In the article, Hartig drew on the economic and social theories of Karl Marx to analyze the success of California's agricultural citrus industry, arguing that a wealthy "ruling class" had manipulated the Southern California landscape to reinforce and validate its own class power, including by physically concealing cheap labor.

By the second paragraph of the article, Hartig referenced photographs depicting the nearby estates and characterized them as "the standard paternalistic, elitist, racist, sexist promotional fare of the age."

Ginn argued that the article is significant because it "doesn't read as a historical examination" but instead as a "political treatise."

"The whole thing does not read as a scholarly historical examination," Ginn said. "It reads as advocating that for a particular point of view, a Marxist-informed point of view, and not an objective historical analysis."

WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ IN RESURFACED 2025 CLIP

Anthea Hartig, director of the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History, testifies during a hearing titled "Rewriting American History: Examining the Smithsonian's Efforts to Reshape the Past" at the Rayburn House Office Building in Washington, D.C., on July 21, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

In 2023, Hartig assumed a one-year presidency at the Organization of American Historians, an organization Ginn said is "well on the record for advocating for people's activism."

According to the organization’s website, "The OAH actively collaborates with advocacy partners to support history and advance our mission."

Hartig's 2024 presidential address, published in the Journal of American History, was titled "Where Have All the Women Gone? Let's Bring Them Back before It's Too Late."

In the address, Hartig asserted that despite decades of activism and historical research, women's "lives, accomplishments, bodies, and futures matter less."

Ginn also criticized Hartig's recent Capitol Hill testimony in July, in which she said the Smithsonian's work is governed by nonpartisanship and "does not take sides in America's political debates."

Ginn said he found the account dishonest, arguing that Hartig's research background and resurfaced video footage directly contradict her testimony.

The resurfaced video shows Hartig asserting that history should be used as a "tool of social justice."

"She's denying it. That's the most perplexing thing for me," Ginn said.

"That's kind of the first frustrating thing for me as a scholar," he added. "It's kind of hard to have an honest conversation about this, when they won't acknowledge the obvious."

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

articles.title: A quiet rush for gold is sweeping the globe — here's why countries are stockpiling it
articles.excerpt: NYPD warns of a devastating gold scam targeting seniors after victims lose millions of dollars. Fox News' Nate Foy outlines how scammers pose as government agencies to coerce elderly victims into liqu...
articles.body_text:
NYPD warns of a devastating gold scam targeting seniors after victims lose millions of dollars. Fox News' Nate Foy outlines how scammers pose as government agencies to coerce elderly victims into liquidating their assets into untraceable gold bars. Authorities report over $100 million stolen in New York City alone, with one victim losing $9 million.

As wars spread, trade tensions escalate and inflation remains stubbornly high, governments around the world are quietly buying more gold, a sign many are preparing for a future they believe will be more uncertain.

A new World Gold Council survey found that 89% of central banks expect global gold reserves to grow over the next year, while a record 45% plan to add to their own holdings. Central banks are the institutions that manage a country's money and financial reserves.

For everyday Americans worried about rising prices, growing government debt and what comes next for the economy, the trend is worth paying attention to.

A SINGLE TRUMP ANNOUNCEMENT SPARKS BILLIONS IN LOSSES ACROSS GOLD AND SILVER

Some experts say central banks buying more gold is a sign they expect today's economic and geopolitical uncertainty to stick around.

That's because gold has long been considered a safe place to put money during wars, market turmoil and periods of high inflation because it isn't tied to the economy or policies of any one country.

Gold has long been viewed as a safe-haven asset during periods of war, inflation and market volatility because, unlike currencies or government debt, it isn't tied to the financial health of any single country. (Matt Jelonek/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

For decades, central banks have invested heavily in U.S. Treasurys — government debt backed by the U.S. and considered among the world's safest investments.

But Cavatoni said many countries are now adding gold because they want another layer of protection against inflation, global instability and economic turmoil.

WHAT TRUMP’S NEXT PICK TO LEAD THE FEDERAL RESERVE MEANS FOR YOUR WALLET

"They're looking at diversifying," Cavatoni said. "And gold fills that need because it provides liquidity, diversification and protection against inflation and geopolitical uncertainty."

The World Gold Council survey backs that up.

About 90% of central banks said gold's performance during times of crisis is one of the main reasons they hold it. Another 84% cited its role as a long-term store of value and inflation hedge, while 83% said it helps diversify their reserves.

Those reasons have fueled a global buying spree.

A person walks past a poster showing 'American Eagle' gold and silver bullion coins at a gold dealer's window in Madrid, on January 30, 2026. (Oscar Del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images)

While China has received much of the attention, it isn't alone. Central banks around the world have been steadily increasing their gold reserves.

According to Cavatoni, Poland, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, the Czech Republic, Chile, Jordan and Ghana have also been among this year's biggest buyers.

While the United States still owns more gold than any other country, much of today's buying is coming from developing economies looking to rely less on foreign currencies they don't control.

"The U.S. has no natural need to continue to accumulate more reserves in the form of gold," Cavatoni said.

The survey also found that nearly three-quarters, or about 74%, of central banks expect the U.S. dollar's share of global reserves to be lower five years from now, while they expect gold's share to increase.

Gold is often viewed as a financial safe haven because, unlike currencies or government debt, it isn't tied to the economy or policies of any one country. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

The same concerns driving governments to buy gold are also attracting individual investors.

One trend that surprised Cavatoni is that even with gold trading near record highs, people aren't rushing to sell.

"It tells me a couple of key things," Cavatoni said. "People are less likely to let go of their gold."

For everyday investors, the trend doesn't necessarily mean they should rush out and buy gold. But it does offer a window into how some of the world's largest financial institutions are preparing for uncertainty, with central banks placing greater value on diversification and protection against economic and geopolitical risks.

And individual investors appear to be showing a similar mindset.

Instead of cashing in, both investors and many central banks are holding on to or building their gold positions, a sign that they see gold less as a short-term investment and more as long-term financial insurance in an increasingly unpredictable world.

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

articles.title: Descendant of slaves shames Smithsonian’s woke ‘indoctrination’ against the ‘greatest nation on earth’
articles.excerpt:
Bishop E.W. Jackson Sr., a senior pastor, founder and author, voices his disgust at the anti-American "indoctrination" at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History.

Black bishop and author ...
articles.body_text:
Bishop E.W. Jackson Sr., a senior pastor, founder and author, voices his disgust at the anti-American "indoctrination" at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History.

Black bishop and author Earl Walker Jackson, a descendant of enslaved ancestors, is criticizing the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for what he said amounts to anti-American "indoctrination" against the "greatest nation on earth."

Although his great-grandparents were enslaved, Jackson believes that "if you were born an American, you hit the proverbial lottery because you have more opportunity and hope than any people living anywhere else on the planet."

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Jackson said the latest controversy over what the White House described as the Smithsonian’s woke "ideological capture" angered him because of what he views as smears against the U.S.

"It makes me angry when people do this to our country, but it's sad too because what it tells me is that the indoctrination machine is hard at work convincing people [of] this narrative," he said. "This is a wonderful country; it's the greatest nation on earth. And you've got people so indoctrinated into seeing our country sliced and diced into race and ethnicity and class and income and so forth that they fail to understand the blessing of the United States of America."

SMITHSONIAN'S TAXPAYER FUNDS FACE CHOPPING BLOCK AS GOP DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY FOR 'WOKE' HISTORY

Nondenominational Bishop Earl Walker Jackson, a descendant of enslaved ancestors, criticized what he described as anti-American "indoctrination" at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History. (Nikki Kahn/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

The Smithsonian National Museum of American History (NMAH) has faced scrutiny over what the White House described as the museum’s promotion of woke ideology. In July, the White House Domestic Policy Council released its 162-page "Saving America's Story" report, concluding that the NMAH has undergone "ideological capture." The report included images of exhibits and placards and information about museum curators and leaders.

After the report was released, congressional hearings brought additional scrutiny to NMAH leadership. NMAH Director Anthea Hartig, who has led the museum since 2019, drew particular attention. A resurfaced video of a presentation by Hartig shows her calling "history as a practice" a "prime tool of social justice."

In a presentation to University of California, Los Angeles, students in February 2025, Hartig asserted that the "United States’ long and violent racial history continues to be present in our reckoning, if you will" and said that "redress in the form of reparation, of course, goes beyond acknowledgement of wrongdoing; it should leverage responsibility, it should think about the act of correction, as we pursue restorative justice and, for us [on the call], restorative justice through history."

In response, Jackson said, "She talks about how history should be a tool of social justice. No, history should be facts about what has happened in the past and leave others to draw their own conclusions about what those facts mean."

"But no, she wants to use history to try to get people to think a certain way and respond a certain way and, namely, to be somewhat angry and bitter and resentful of our country because of our past," he continued.

WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ AFTER EXPLOSIVE HEARING

National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig appears at a House Oversight subcommittee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington on July 21, 2026. The hearing, titled "Rewriting American History: Examining the Smithsonian's Efforts to Reshape the Past," followed a White House report criticizing the museum’s presentation of American history. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Though the White House report was released less than a month ago, Jackson said he has been warning for years about what he describes as woke ideology at the Smithsonian.

In 2015, he confronted the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery over the inclusion of Planned Parenthood founder Margaret Sanger in its exhibit on civil rights leaders. He took issue with Sanger’s inclusion because he said, "She was an elitist, she was a eugenicist, she was racist, she admired Adolf Hitler [and] she spoke for the Ku Klux Klan."

Jackson believes much of what he describes as ideological capture at the Smithsonian, as well as in the broader education system, entertainment industry, journalism and sports, stems from the influence of Howard Zinn’s book "A People's History of the United States."

Jackson said Howard Zinn "was a professed anarchist" who "wrote that book as a polemic against America."

He said he is "amazed at how few Americans understand that book has been more influential in teaching American history than any other book that the public schools or colleges have ever used," emphasizing, "And it's still being used."

As an example, Jackson pointed to materials currently promoted by the Zinn Education Project that draw a line between deportation operations today and Great Depression-era deportations, which the materials say derived from "a program of ‘racial expulsion,’ rooted in racism."

Fox News Digital reached out to Planned Parenthood, the Margaret Sanger Papers Project at New York University, the Zinn Education Project and the Zinn Trust for comment.

SPEAKER JOHNSON WARNS STUDENTS ARE 'INDOCTRINATED' TO SEE US THROUGH 'WRONG LENSES' AS NATION CELEBRATES 250TH

People walk on the National Mall near the Smithsonian Castle in Washington, DC, on May 10, 2021. President Donald Trump ordered signs installed outside the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History directing visitors to a White House report criticizing the museum's portrayal of American history. (MANDEL NGAN/AFP via Getty Images)

"If you're learning that from the very beginning of your education, my goodness, by the time you're an adult and you've been through 20,000 hours of that, no wonder we've got people protesting outside of ICE facilities, and no wonder you've got people at the Smithsonian talking about America as if we're the worst place on earth to live," he said. "They frankly have been brainwashed and indoctrinated into it."

Jackson countered, "There is no place on earth that has been more affirming of human dignity, offered more opportunity for human flourishing. And frankly acknowledged in spite of the apparent differences that we have, that we are ultimately one nation under God."

"I think loving America is easy because, you’re right, I'm the great-grandson of slaves, I am a product of a broken home and foster care, and yet my life has just been wonderfully blessed," he concluded. "First, of course, by the grace of God, but also because I live in a country where anything is possible, where you're free, where you can dream, you can strive to fulfill your God-given gifts and talents and abilities."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Smithsonian Institution, National Portrait Gallery and NMAH for comment.

Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Tupac Shakur murder suspect takes center stage at trial nearly 30 years after shooting shocked music world
articles.excerpt:
Duane "Keffe D" Davis tells the cop he's being arrested for "biggest case in Vegas history." (CREDIT: Las Vegas police/FOIA)

Nearly 30 years after rapper Tupac Shakur was fatally shot in Las Vegas, t...
articles.body_text:
Duane "Keffe D" Davis tells the cop he's being arrested for "biggest case in Vegas history." (CREDIT: Las Vegas police/FOIA)

Nearly 30 years after rapper Tupac Shakur was fatally shot in Las Vegas, the only person ever charged in his killing is set to go on trial.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, is scheduled to stand trial beginning Monday on a murder charge in the 1996 drive-by shooting that killed Shakur, one of hip-hop’s most influential artists.

Davis has pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors do not accuse him of firing the shot, but allege he helped plan the attack and provided the gun used in the shooting.

Shakur was shot Sept. 7, 1996, while riding in a BMW driven by Death Row Records founder Marion "Suge" Knight near the Las Vegas Strip. He died six days later at age 25.

LAWYERS FOR SUSPECTED TUPAC SHAKUR KILLER CLAIM HIS WORDS WERE TWISTED, WANT HIM RELEASED FROM JAIL

Tupac was born in New York and raised in Baltimore and Oakland before claiming Los Angeles as his home. (Raymond Boyd)

Hours before the shooting, Shakur, Knight and others were involved in a fight at the MGM Grand with Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, Davis’ nephew and a member of the South Side Compton Crips.

Prosecutors say Davis, Anderson, Deandrae "Freaky" Smith and Terry "Bubble Up" Brown were later riding in a white Cadillac that pulled alongside Shakur’s car and opened fire.

Davis is the only one of the four still alive.

Tupac Shakur and his East Coast rival, Biggie, were killed six months apart. (Getty Images)

Authorities long suspected Anderson was the gunman, although evidence presented in the case has also raised the possibility that Smith fired the shots.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

According to the Associated Press, prosecutors hope to prove that Davis called the shots in and provided the gun used in the crime. Gunfire came from the Cadillac that Davis was in, and he's one of the only people there that night who is still alive.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Davis has acknowledged being in the Cadillac and discussed the killing in interviews and in his 2019 memoir, "Compton Street Legend." Prosecutors say those statements help establish his role in the attack.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis enters a courtroom in Clark County District Court for a trial readiness status check at the Regional Justice Center on June 17, 2025, in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Steve Marcus-Pool/Getty Images)

His attorneys, meanwhile, have argued that some of Davis’ public statements were exaggerated and have challenged whether statements he made during a 2008 police interview could be used against him.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

A Nevada judge ruled that Davis' police interview, as well as portions of his memoir, will be allowed during the trial.

Tupac Shakur was killed in a 1996 shooting in Las Vegas. (Associated Press)

The trial is expected to last about four weeks. In November, Davis' attorneys unsuccessfully sought to dismiss the charges.

"Think of it this way: Shakur’s murder was essentially the entertainment world’s JFK assassination — endlessly dissected, mythologized, monetized — so it’s not hard to see why someone in Davis’s position might falsely place himself at the center of it all for personal gain," his attorneys said in a petition to the Nevada Supreme Court that was denied.

Shakur's legendary rap career was highlighted by more than 75 million records worldwide with hits including "California Love," "Changes" and "Dear Mama."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department for comment.

Fox News Digital's Brie Stimson and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Sarah Rumpf-Whitten is a U.S. Writer at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to sarah.rumpf@fox.com and on X @s_rumpfwhitten
