articles.title: Two workers were temporarily stood down after near-miss collision at Sydney Airport
articles.excerpt:
Transport minister says improved staff rostering will be in place from next month after ‘unacceptable’ delays and incident involving Qatar Airways and Jetstar planes

Follow our Australia news live bl...
articles.body_text:
Transport minister says improved staff rostering will be in place from next month after ‘unacceptable’ delays and incident involving Qatar Airways and Jetstar planes

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The transport minister, Catherine King, has said improved staff rostering will be in place at Sydney airport from next month after “unacceptable” delays and a near-miss collision that resulted in two workers being stood down.

King called in the Airservices Australia chief executive officer, Rob Sharp, for a meeting in Canberra on Monday, the day after a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided hitting a Qatar Airways plane that was pulled across the runway in front of it.

Two staff involved in the incident – an Airservices Australia air traffic controller and the tug driver who was towing the Qatar plane – were stood down while they completed standard post-incident drug and alcohol testing.

The temporary loss of an air traffic controller only exacerbated delays at Australia’s biggest airport, where staff shortages had already resulted in days of disruption.

Additionally, a cabin crew member aboard the Jetstar plane was injured when the planes stopped abruptly, and some equipment was damaged.

The incident occurred less than two weeks after another near-miss relating to air traffic control on the tarmac at Sydney. On 27 July, a Qantas flight was cleared to cross a runway in front of one of the airline’s other planes that had just landed.

King on Monday said the delays and disruptions were unacceptable, but she was “confident” that Airservices Australia was “doing everything they can to get on top of this”.

“Airservices have committed to implementing improved rostering practices for Sydney’s Air Traffic Controllers that will be implemented from early September,” she said.

King said the situation would be “carefully” managed for the rest of August.

A new Sydney Tower simulator had also been installed to increase training capacity and enable more air traffic controllers to be trained, she said.

“It has been a big focus of ours to encourage more people to enter the profession, and 95 people are expected to be endorsed as air traffic controllers by the end of the year,” King said.

“Six controllers are currently training in Sydney Tower, with another 15 expected to commence before the end of 2027.”

King said she wanted to “give a shout out” to the air traffic controllers, who 
 are dealing with a really stressful and difficult job” and “did a very good job over the weekend to try to manage the disruptions as best they could”.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) is investigating both the Sunday incident and the 27 July near-miss involving Qantas aircraft.

The head of the ATSB, Angus Mitchell, on Monday said the two incidents were unacceptable.

“Planes should not be getting that close and we should never have to rely on, as has happened in both these instances, pilots at the last minute, making an emergency decision to prevent them coming together,” he told ABC radio.

Investigators would interview flight crew, tug operators and air traffic controllers, plus other witnesses, and review any CCTV footage, the ATSB said.

A source told Guardian Australia on Sunday that initial inquiries suggested the tug vehicle pulling the Qatar aircraft may not have followed instructions.

The tug driver was believed to work for Menzies Aviation, a UK-headquartered third party contractor that provides ground staff for Qatar Airways at Sydney Airport.

A Menzies Aviation spokesperson said in a statement that it had launched a thorough investigation into the incident and was fully cooperating with the ATSB.

“We are sorry to hear that a member of the cabin crew was injured and recognise that incidents of this nature can be concerning,” the statement said.

“The safety of our people, customers and the travelling public is our highest priority. We will carefully review the findings of both investigations to ensure any lessons identified are fully addressed.”

Michael Kaine, the national secretary of the Transport Workers’ Union, which represents air traffic controllers and airport ground crews, said the aviation industry was in “crisis” due to staff shortages and poor conditions.

“Across the industry, this revolving-door workforce is understaffed and exhausted,” he said.

“We’ve seen another worker hurt from this incident after a horrific string of injuries and a worker killed at Qantas Freight last year.”

articles.title: Albanese gives ground on gambling inducements as Labor and Coalition inch towards deal
articles.excerpt:
Prime minister and opposition leader meet in Canberra to advance agreement on gambling advertising

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or dai...
articles.body_text:
Prime minister and opposition leader meet in Canberra to advance agreement on gambling advertising

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Anthony Albanese has bowed to pressure and will limit gambling inducements as part of a deal between Labor and Angus Taylor, even as some Liberals warn it might not do enough to help vulnerable people.

The prime minister and the opposition leader met in Canberra on Monday to negotiate the deal, a week after sensational revelations about illegal drugs, sex workers and alcohol being provided to high-spending gamblers.

A deal to strengthen Labor’s bill, which has been criticised for falling short of the ambition of a parliamentary inquiry led by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy, is necessary to get the legislation through parliament this week.

Speaking to a meeting of Labor’s caucus in Canberra on Monday afternoon, Albanese promised some limits on inducements – which are designed to keep punters losing money – as well as touting new, but as-yet-unknown, rules on gambling advertising.

Communications minister Anika Wells’ office was contacted for specifics of potential amendments. Coalition sources said Taylor’s meeting with Albanese was “very positive” but stopped short of confirming any deal had been struck.

“This will be the strongest anti-gambling legislation that Australia has ever seen,” Albanese told the Labor caucus on Monday afternoon.

“I’m confident that later in the week we will have the legislation in the House of Representatives with some really practical amendments, dealing with the targeting of advertising, dealing with reducing children’s exposure, and dealing with as well, the full suite of measures in a really practical way.”

He said action on inducements would “get the balance right between people who want to go along and have a punt on a Saturday at the races, but also, that problem gambling is actually dealt with”.

Albanese also told his party room the government was seeking agreement with the Coalition on Labor’s plans to cut spending in the National Disability Insurance Scheme, as well as on the news bargaining incentive.

A deal on gambling looks set to be finalised as soon as Tuesday’s Coalition joint party room meeting. Any such deal will infuriate the Greens and crossbench, who had demanded much stronger action; Senator Sarah Hanson-Young had earlier urged Taylor not to fold, sending a message to the opposition leader at a press conference: “don’t roll over and let the prime minister tickle you on the belly”.

Earlier, Taylor said action on “predatory inducements” needed to be added to the government’s bill.

“We will approach these discussions with goodwill. We want to get a good outcome,” he said.

“We want to get the right outcome for younger, vulnerable Australians. We want to get the right outcomes for those who have gambling addictions and are trying to deal with them.

“We do need to make sure we get the balance right. We understand that personal responsibility is also an important part of this so it’s key to get this right and we will work with the government to do that in so far as that’s possible.”

But some Liberal MPs want the opposition to go further, even potentially shifting from an opt-out model for gambling ads on streaming platforms to an opt-in system. That proposal would be fiercely opposed by the industry.

The gambling industry was increasingly resigned to the paring back of inducements ahead of parliament resuming on Tuesday, but wagering sources warned MPs that restricting inducements could send gamblers to offshore operators.

Labor sources said the government was willing to deal with either the Coalition or Greens on the bill. But the Greens want even further-reaching changes, meaning the more likely pathway to passing the bill is with Taylor.

Debate on the bill was supercharged by sensational evidence from former NRL player Luke Bateman and veteran anti-gambling campaigner Tim Costello last week.

They alleged problem gamblers had been supplied with cocaine, alcohol and sex workers, part of efforts from gambling company VIP managers to keep big-spending punters betting as long as possible.

Betting giants who appeared before the inquiry said there was no evidence to support the allegations.

In June 2023, Murphy’s committee recommended the government “prohibit all online gambling inducements and inducement advertising, and that it do so without delay”.

articles.title: Victorian Liberals promise weekly red bin garbage collections for all, calling fortnightly system ‘disgusting’
articles.excerpt:
If opposition wins November’s state election, leader Jess Wilson vows households will not pay more under the change

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email...
articles.body_text:
If opposition wins November’s state election, leader Jess Wilson vows households will not pay more under the change

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Victorian Liberals have vowed to restore weekly rubbish collections if they win November’s state election, with leader Jess Wilson describing the current fortnightly system in her local area as “disgusting”.

Thirty-three Victorian councils have switched general rubbish collections from weekly to fortnightly, with a similar shift occurring in other states.

In metropolitan Melbourne they include Banyule, Bayside, Boroondara, Glen Eira, Knox, Manningham, Monash, Nillumbik and Yarra Ranges.

Merri-bek is also expected to follow from mid-2027, in a move it has said would save ratepayers $16m over 10 years, help keep food waste out of landfill and reduce pollution.

Under Merri-bek’s proposal, the standard red-lid rubbish bin would increase from 80 litres to 120 litres, while certain households, such as those with multiple children in nappies, could get bigger bins for free.

But Wilson said if elected in November, a Liberal-National government would require councils to collect general rubbish every week.

She said her government would also apply the council rate cap – which now limits annual rate increases to inflation – to waste charges, so households would not pay more as a result of the change.

The opposition leader, whose electorate of Kew falls within the Boroondara local government area, said reverting to weekly general rubbish collections was “common sense”.

“To be perfectly honest – it’s disgusting. The bins are overflowing. I have a toddler, we have nappies and we have many little kids on our street with large families,” Wilson told 3AW radio on Monday.

“You know what it’s like on bin night, when you have two or three extra bags and you’re trying to find somewhere to put them. They end up in council parks in the bins there overflowing.”

In a statement, she added that weekly rubbish collection was an “essential service that shouldn’t depend on your postcode”.

Wes Gault, the mayor of Boroondara, said he agreed that residents were “paying too much for waste disposal”, but it was due to the state government’s landfill levy, which has increased significantly in recent years.

“[This change] will cost our residents at least $3m more a year in trucks, fuel, servicing and staffing alone – not including the extra landfill levies,” Gault said in a statement.

He also said that 70% of material collected across all Boroondara’s kerbside bins was diverted from landfill.

“Bringing back a weekly landfill collection risks undermining that progress, [via] increasing emissions through more truck collections and potent landfill methane.”

The council said residents can also upsize to 120 or 240-litre bins at an additional cost if they had increased volumes of nappies.

Most councils that have switched to fortnightly collection have cited the introduction of weekly food organics and garden organics (Fogo) collection as the main reason for the change.

They have said the shift encourages residents to place food scraps in a green bin, which can then be turned into compost rather than sent to landfill, where they break down and produce methane.

Whitehorse council has considered making the change but decided to keep weekly collection. In material sent to residents as part of its consultation, the council said food waste was accounting for 40% of the weight of rubbish bins.

It said Boroondara, Knox, Manningham and Monash had “reduced the amount of waste sent to landfill by an average of 19%” in the first year after switching to weekly Fogo collections and fortnightly general rubbish collections.

It is not the first time rubbish has made headlines this year, with several Victorian councils in April pushing back against a mandated deadline to introduce a fourth, purple-lidded bin for glass by 1 July 2027 as part of a shift to a statewide four-bin system.

The government first announced the overhaul of the state’s rubbish collection in 2020, following the collapse of the state’s largest recycling company SKM a year earlier, which resulted in thousands of tonnes of recycling being sent to landfill.

The Liberals have committed to reviewing the landfill levy, if elected, as well as make the purple bin option.

In Western Australia, the One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen is using a state byelection to campaign for Rockingham council to restore weekly rubbish collection.

articles.title: Old-school campfire favorites Americans grew up eating are making a comeback
articles.excerpt:
California couple Paul and Caroline Lacitinola, authors of the Vintage Camper Trailer Cookbook, show off the original pie iron inherited from Paul's grandmother.

For Paul and Caroline Lacitinola, vin...
articles.body_text:
California couple Paul and Caroline Lacitinola, authors of the Vintage Camper Trailer Cookbook, show off the original pie iron inherited from Paul's grandmother.

For Paul and Caroline Lacitinola, vintage camper trailers aren't just restored pieces of Americana — they're rolling memory machines.

The California couple, publishers of the Vintage Camper Trailers Magazine for the past 15 years, have spent two decades immersed in the vintage trailer community.

Their latest project, a cookbook filled with more than 120 family recipes, camper favorites and restaurant classics, celebrates the meals that have long brought people together around campsites across America.

FROM YELLOWSTONE TO YOSEMITE, NEW COOKBOOK REVEALS RECIPES INSPIRED BY AMERICA'S MOST ICONIC PARKS

"We've talked about doing it forever because we're kind of foodies," Paul Lacitinola said. "A cookbook just seemed like the natural combination of our vintage trailers and cars and classic stuff along with our other hobby — eating."

But the Lacitinolas said the Vintage Camper Trailer Cookbook is about preserving something much bigger than recipes.

Paul and Caroline Lacitinola are the authors of the Vintage Camper Trailer Cookbook. They spoke to Fox News Digital outside their vintage camper trailer. (Fox News Digital)

"I really feel like the trailers have so much relationship in them that it's all about the people, and camping has a lot of emotional connection," Caroline Lacitinola said.

"A lot of times it was something people were raised doing. And, so, they walk into these vintage trailers and they remember their childhood. They remember their parents. They have connection in those ways."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

She believes younger generations are embracing vintage camping for a different reason.

"I think the American dream has shifted a little bit from doing the 9-to-5 every single day to really experiencing life," she said.

The cookbook reflects that spirit by blending recipes contributed by family members, campers, the couple's children and favorites from Paul's former restaurants.

Paul Lacitinola prepares a "Grandma Mandy" sandwich in his vintage camper trailer. (Caroline Lacitinola)

Some dishes carry especially strong childhood memories. Paul's favorite is what his family calls "Grandma Mandy" sandwiches — white bread stuffed with cheese and jelly before being toasted in a pie iron over the campfire.

"It sounds crazy," he admitted. "But believe me, they're delicious."

"When I married him, I thought, 'There's no way,'" she laughed. "But they are actually really, really tasty."

At the couple's vintage trailer rallies, however, one tradition stands above the rest.

"The thing that we're kind of famous for ... is our pancake breakfast," Paul said.

The "Grandma Mandy" sandwich is one of Paul Lacitinola's childhood favorites. (Caroline Lacitinola)

Whether it's classic pancakes or creative versions topped with peanut butter and bacon or tres leches sauce, the breakfast has become a community favorite.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"I think the essence of vintage camping is really community and connecting," she said. "Anything that you could do where you connect as a group is the essence of vintage camping to me. Because people are really the core of our hobby."

Paul Lacitinola supervises the condiment station during a vintage camper trailer rally. (Caroline Lacitinola)

The couple encourages anyone curious about the lifestyle to visit one of their trailer rallies, tour the restored campers and experience the community firsthand.

"Go out and get one, even if it's a cheap one, if it'll work for you for a while," Paul said. "It doesn't have to be your forever trailer. But go out and get one and get involved in the community."

Peter Burke is a lifestyle editor with Fox News Digital. He covers various lifestyle topics, with an emphasis on food and drink.

articles.title: Top Democrats simulate election threats as Trump continues assault on voting
articles.excerpt:
Chuck Schumer and other senators took part in exercises in which legal experts laid out election disruption scenarios

In a Washington DC conference room last month, some of the most senior Democrats ...
articles.body_text:
Chuck Schumer and other senators took part in exercises in which legal experts laid out election disruption scenarios

In a Washington DC conference room last month, some of the most senior Democrats in the US Senate gathered to plan for a prospect that only recently would have felt more akin to science fiction: they started to wargame democracy.

Chuck Schumer, the US Senate minority leader, and senators including Alex Padilla, Adam Schiff, Mark Warner, Elissa Slotkin and Raphael Warnock were among those in the room as a team of legal experts offered scenarios.

The first: realistic deepfake videos, created with artificial intelligence, showing “evidence” of widespread election fraud, spreading through social media a few weeks before voting begins.

Forensic experts discredit the videos quickly as synthetic in the given scenario, but rightwing media – and the US president – amplify the claims, nonetheless. Election workers begin receiving death threats. Armed men start appearing at polls.

If you’re a Democratic senator, what would you do?

“These tabletop exercises are a standard planning tool for experts and stakeholders to prepare for potential scenarios. We’re not predicting exactly what would happen,” said Justin Vail, who leads the DC office of the non-partisan advocacy group Protect Democracy. “But we do want to create a realistic context that can help us identify gaps, test our assumptions, and strengthen coordination, and then ultimately develop some recommendations to increase our preparedness.”

Senate Democrats have held two election disruption exercises this year. Voting rights and legal groups like Protect Democracy have also participated, along with election attorney Marc Elias, former attorney general Eric Holder, election law expert Norman Eisen and members of the left-leaning non-profit Democracy Forward.

Skye Perryman, CEO of Democracy Forward, expressed confidence in the resilience of the foundations of US democracy, pointing to the legal system and the distributed nature of American elections, which she said builds a defense against crass political interference, even from the US president.

“The president can try to imagine whatever he may wish to imagine,” Perryman said. “He can’t imagine a new constitution, and the constitution, frankly, is quite clear in no uncertain terms; there’s not a role for the president in election administration in this country.”

Nonetheless, Donald Trump’s continuous false claims about a stolen election in 2020, and his increasingly strident demand for the US Congress to pass a package of federalized oversights of elections, have raised concerns among progressive voters that the administration may mar November’s midterms with misinformation, or worse.

The administration billed Trump’s primetime TV address last month as a presentation of new evidence that the 2020 election was illegitimate, and that his administration had uncovered new findings about vulnerabilities in the US election system. Instead, Trump claimed China had illicitly acquired voter information on 220 million Americans, and that China had undermined his 2020 campaign in other unspecified ways, arguing that intelligence officials had suppressed this information.

Trump’s claims fell apart under scrutiny. His own intelligence officials had already concluded that China refrained from interfering in the US election out of concern for potential political blowback if caught.

Trump threatened the broadcast licenses of networks that refused to carry the address live. In his speech, he again implored Congress to pass the Save America Act, which would ban mail-in ballots nationwide and impose new identification requirements on voters when they register and report to polls. Republican senators refuse to dispense with the 60-vote filibuster threshold to pass the law.

Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, representing a swing state that is a favored rhetorical target of the president, described Trump’s address as “signaling his unmistakable intent to attack these elections and our voting rights, just as he tried to throw out our votes and seize the presidency in 2020”.

Voting rights advocates pointed toward Trump’s July primetime address as indicative of the president’s intentions – rhetorical attacks on the integrity of voting machines and elections offices, potentially escalating into more direct interference.

Trump’s public commentary, and the actions of agencies under his supervision, shaped the scenario building as Democratic leaders plan their possible responses.

Senators were asked at their recent session to contemplate how to react to a threat to withhold Office of Management and Budget (OMB) funding for states that don’t submit their voter rolls for federal oversight. They also considered a threat of Federal Communications Commission (FCC) action against news outlets covering deepfakes.

“The development of AI will only add to the complexity and could create confusion among voters in our fragmented media landscape,” said Vail. “Unfortunately, that confusion can be to the benefit of the administration’s strategy.”

FCC enforcement actions seem relatively mild compared to more extreme scenarios, like planning a response to armed vigilantes in tactical gear at ballot drop boxes – which was not a hypothetical problem in Arizona during the 2022 midterms. Senators were asked to plan responses for online license-plate doxxing, a midnight firebombing of an early voting site and a last-minute unilateral deployment of Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents and the national guard to polling stations.

The main lesson of the exercise “is that this is an all-hands-on-deck moment, and it is an all-hands-on-deck response”, said Perryman. “And so what that means is that, we’re not looking at any one silver bullet to be able to fully protect elections. It’s going to take all of us.”

articles.title: I’m a college athlete. The system that gave me my dream is starting to break
articles.excerpt:
Missouri Senator Eric Schmitt joins Don't @ Me w/ Dan Dakich to discuss the benefits of the Protect College Sports Act.

Every detail of my life, no matter how small, has been influenced by sports. My...
articles.body_text:
Missouri Senator Eric Schmitt joins Don't @ Me w/ Dan Dakich to discuss the benefits of the Protect College Sports Act.

Every detail of my life, no matter how small, has been influenced by sports. My parents met at a Florida Relays track meet at the University of Florida. During my childhood, my mom was a Division II track coach at the Colorado School of Mines. I would spend my afternoons at practice with her, carefully observing every throw and every cue she gave her athletes.

Although my parents signed me up for every sport under the sun, all I ever wanted was to throw. Being exposed to college track at such a young age opened my eyes to the opportunities available through athletics. I worked relentlessly to "go DI." In the process, I won multiple high school state and national championships while forming a tight-knit web of friends across the country. I can say with the utmost confidence that I would not be the person I am today without track and field.

No experience has been more transformative than my time as a student-athlete at Clemson University. Clemson athletics has opened doors I never thought were possible. Every day, I wake up with the opportunity to better myself. How much stronger can I get? How much further can I throw? How much more can I learn?

TRUMP URGES CONGRESS TO PASS PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT BEFORE RECESS: 'WE HAVE TO GET THAT DONE'

As a Clemson student-athlete, I have access to world-class facilities and a family of coaches, staff, teammates, and peers that pour into me every day. In my two years as a college athlete so far, I have learned to find my ceiling and break through it.

I pray that every American athlete has the opportunity to live out their dreams just as I have. Sports teach us how to work hard, overcome adversity, be coachable, manage our time, and build lifelong relationships in the process.

My coaches encouraged me to pursue both a B.S. and an M.P.A. rather than taking a compareatively easier academic path. They also pushed me to pursue leadership roles through the Student-Athlete Advisory Committee (SAAC) Executive Board, Atlantic Coast Conference Student-Athlete Advisory Committee (ACC SAAC), internships, pre-professional organizations, and a slew of volunteer opportunities. I would simply not be where I am without the support of Clemson Athletics.

I pray that every American athlete has the opportunity to live out their dreams just as I have. Sports teach us how to work hard, overcome adversity, be coachable, manage our time, and build lifelong relationships in the process. Every child in the United States should have the opportunity to play sports at the highest level.

TED CRUZ URGES SENATE TO STAY IN WASHINGTON UNTIL PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT PASSES THIS WEEK

Congress has the duty to protect American athletes. The NCAA v. Alston and House v. NCAA decisions have created chaos within the NCAA. The patchwork of state laws and court decisions has created an unstable landscape for college sports.

Well-funded institutions like Clemson work hard to provide both revenue and non-revenue athletes with the tools they need to succeed. However, the disparities between Power 4 and mid-major programs continue to widen, and opportunities for American high school athletes are diminishing. The combination of post-House roster caps, transfer portal reliance on high school talent, and lingering eligibility waivers has slashed roster spots for walk-ons and compressed recruiting pipelines.

The consequences extend beyond recruiting. I have witnessed some of my closest friends get cut from their teams to accommodate roster caps. Budgets continue to tighten as schools stretch to provide more scholarships and services to athletes. Some universities have eliminated Olympic sports like men’s swimming or track and field altogether, while conferences have dropped championship sponsorship for others.

I have also seen the unbridled growth of revenue sharing and Name, Image, Likeness (NIL). These changes have been both a blessing and a curse for student-athletes. On one hand, football, basketball, and other revenue-earning sports deserve to share in the value they bring in for their schools, and, as an Olympic sport athlete, words cannot describe how grateful I am for them. Not only are they fun to watch, but their success helps fund opportunities for athletes like me. At the same time, there are no guardrails to protect athletes from unregistered agents or excessive fees, leaving many students vulnerable to exploitation.

The transfer portal has also fundamentally changed college athletics, uprooting any resemblance of school loyalty that once existed. I personally know athletes who have transferred two or more times, and it’s no secret that forming a deep-rooted team culture is already difficult, let alone when the composition of your team changes every year. The tradition and loyalty that have long defined college sports are effectively dying, and without reasonable regulation, the problem will only continue to grow.

SEC commissioner Greg Sankey and Big Ten commissioner Tony Petitti meet with reporters during a joint press conference in Nashville, Tennessee. (Trey Wallace/FOX NEWS)

We are approaching a point of no return. Congress must intervene before college sports as we now know them are destroyed. Not just for current NCAA athletes like me, but also for athletes like my little brother, who is about to start his first year as a Division I lacrosse player at a mid-major program, my little sister, who dreams of playing lacrosse at a Power 4 school, and every young athlete working toward and dreaming about the chance to compete in the NCAA.

College athletics changes lives. If we don’t protect it, we will close countless doors across the country that catapult kids into better opportunities. S. 4668, the Protect College Sports Act, is our best shot to establish a level playing field for all college athletes, revenue and non-revenue. While no bill is perfect, this legislation is necessary to establish a framework of laws to govern revenue sharing and NIL, the transfer portal, and eligibility — protecting Olympic sports and millions of student-athletes.

If Congress fails to act now, the opportunities that have transformed my life may not exist for the next generation because college sports will be too far gone.

Ella Brooks is a rising junior and a member of the women’s track and field team at Clemson University, where she studies political science. She serves as vice president of external affairs for Clemson’s Student-Athlete Advisory Committee. Brooks, along with other members of the Atlantic Coast Conference Student-Athlete Advisory Committee, co-authored a letter supporting the Protect College Sports Act, federal legislation aimed at establishing a national framework for college athletics. She hopes to pursue a career in politics after concluding her athletic career.

articles.title: Which other countries could join the Turkiye-Saudi-Pakistan defence pact?
articles.excerpt:
Turkiye wants to expand its newly formed defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to include more countries, says Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, citing President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

“Under our pr...
articles.body_text:
Turkiye wants to expand its newly formed defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to include more countries, says Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, citing President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

“Under our president’s vision, we should not remain limited to three countries. We should grow and, if necessary, bring all countries under this umbrella,” Fidan told state news agency Anadolu, according to a report published on Saturday.

Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on Friday signed the Mecca Joint Deterrence Agreement, in what analysts say could be a step towards a new security architecture in the region.

So who could join the pact next, and what would an expanded alliance mean for regional security?

The Mecca defence pact builds on a previous agreement reached between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan a year ago.

Regional officials have suggested that the pact could eventually expand to include other countries, strengthening its role as a mechanism for collective security and deterrence.

The pact’s central feature is a NATO-like stipulation that an attack on any one of the three states would be treated as an attack on all of them although the details have yet to be fleshed out.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the allies will decide through consultations what degree, form and format of support they would ask for in the event of an attack but no country would be considered a threat as long as a member state is not attacked.

Turkish and Saudi officials have stressed that the pact is not meant to supplant any other strategic alliances or relationships while Turkiye, which is a member of NATO, has said the agreement does not target any country, including Iran.

Egypt is the only country whose potential membership has been publicly raised by an official from one of the pact’s signatory countries.

Fidan described Egypt as a “natural partner” and said he expects Cairo to formally join once “technical issues” are ironed out.

“I believe that at the next stage, Egypt will also be among us in the alliance,” Fidan said. “We already act towards one another as if we were alliance members.”

Ali Bakir, professor of international relations, security and defence at Qatar University, said Egypt’s inclusion would “significantly increase the pact’s political weight, regional influence and operational effectiveness” if it materialises.

Egypt already has a solid working relationship with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye, with which it is part of a group called the R4, which consults on regional issues. Egypt has also recently developed stronger military ties with Turkiye despite previous tensions over the Egyptian military’s 2013 overthrow of President Mohamed Morsi, the conflict in Libya and the discovery of gasfields in the Eastern Mediterranean.

But analysts said Cairo may be wary of the potential military obligations that could come with a binding defence treaty with states whose interests do not always align with its own as well as the implications for its existing peace treaties.

“Egypt may join only if the language protects its aid relationship with Washington, doesn’t undermine existing alliances and peace treaties, and maintains its own freedom to decide when and where it fights,” Karim Elgendy, associate fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, told Al Jazeera.

“If the pact stays a political framework with room to calibrate each response, Cairo can live with it and may eventually sign. If it hardens into an obligation that could pull Egyptian forces into someone else’s war, the answer is likely to be negative,” Elgendy said.

Technical issues holding Egypt back could be both “legal and operational”, Elgendy added. “On the legal side, Egypt needs to know exactly what it is committing to defend, and it will want assurances so that a signature never reads as a commitment against Israel or as taking Ankara’s side in Libya and the Eastern Mediterranean,” he said.

For Bakir, Cairo’s decision will come down to how it weighs the benefits of membership against the diplomatic complications.  Egypt’s decision on whether to join the pact will hinge on the level of “strategic value” it believes it brings as well as its ability to “manage relations with countries whose interests” contrast with or even “actively oppose” the alliance, he said.

Ahmed Aboudouh, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, told Al Jazeera that while Egypt broadly shares the trilateral pact’s security concerns, it “does not share its underpinning threat perception” and may be resistant to “security commitments”.

“Cairo’s preference is to be part of overlapping regional security arrangements that are narrow in scope and are issue-related … rather than being entangled in defence commitments with elevated risks/cost,” Aboudouh said.

He added that Egypt may still opt to join the pact in the future but it would be a “complex decision”.

Several officials have suggested other Gulf countries could eventually join the alliance.

In a post on X, former Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim Al Thani expressed hope that all members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) would “take the initiative to join” the pact. In addition to Saudi Arabia, the GCC includes Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman and the United Arab Emirates.

Fidan also spoke about the alliance bringing in more regional countries, saying some nations, which he did not name, had already expressed interest. “Under our president’s vision, we should not remain limited to three countries. We should grow and, if necessary, bring all countries under this umbrella,” Fidan said.

Among the Gulf states, Elgendy said, “the names to watch first are Qatar and Kuwait.”

Both countries are “close to all three signatories” and “have the strongest motive to buy extra insurance” after feeling “exposed” during the United States-Israel war on Iran and by Israel’s strike on Doha in September, he said.

Bakir similarly identified Qatar as the “most natural” Gulf state to opt in with Kuwait another possible candidate. He also said Azerbaijan, Syria and Jordan could also join “relatively quickly”.

Elgendy expressed scepticism about the pact transforming into a broader bloc. “This looks like a coalition of the willing that will grow on a case-by-case basis, shaped by each capital’s own risk calculus,” he said.

articles.title: Body of woman found in suitcase by side of road in regional NSW
articles.excerpt:
What was originally reported as a body found in Oallen on Sunday was ‘very realistic in the terms of looking like human remains’, NSW police say

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates...
articles.body_text:
What was originally reported as a body found in Oallen on Sunday was ‘very realistic in the terms of looking like human remains’, NSW police say

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

What appeared to be a woman’s body found in a suitcase by the side of a road near Goulburn in regional New South Wales was in fact a lifelike doll with markings resembling bruises and grazes, police say.

NSW police said they were called to Wolgon Road in Oallen about 12.50pm on Sunday “following reports a body had been located”.

Officers travelled to the remote location and located what was believed to be the body in the suitcase.

A police statement declaring a “a body in a suitcase” had been found was issued to media on Sunday night, leading to widespread coverage.

But on Monday morning Supt Linda Bradbury told a press conference that police now did not “have a suspicious death of a human on our hands”.

“Following forensic examinations this morning,” police later wrote in a statement, “police confirmed the item located in the bag was a life like doll, wearing clothing, with hair and a nose piercing. The item also had markings that resembled bruises and grazes.

Bradbury said it was good practice not to disturb crime scenes, which is why it took some time to determine the remains were not human. Bad weather was also a factor, she said.

“We don’t like to disturb them too much in situ, particularly when we have faced inclement weather, as we did yesterday and again today,” she said.

Bradbury said they were “very realistic in terms of looking like human remains”.

“But we’ve confirmed by other means that they are not.

“We don’t have a suspicious death of a human on our hands.”

Earlier on Monday, Bradbury had told Channel Nine the “female remains have been subject to a state of decomposition”.

“We’re conducting a number of inquiries to assist us in locating the identification of the female and also how she ended up in that location.

“We are relying a lot on forensic evidence.”

The discovery was made by two men who had pulled on to the side of the road by chance, Bradbury said.

“They were able to tell us how they had come across it,” she added.

“They were on a weekend drive, as a lot of people do over the weekend, and stopped for a break. [It was] quite a shocking discovery for them, absolutely.”

A crime scene was established and the suitcase was “seized to undergo forensic examination while detectives commence an investigation into the incident”.

Oallen is in the southern tablelands region of NSW, about 75km north-east of Canberra and 185km south-west of Sydney.

articles.title: Florida attorney general offers his response to brutal foul on Sophie Cunningham
articles.excerpt:
Megan Rapinoe's latest ridiculous rant on Sophie Cunningham and RIley Gaines makes it clear she doesn't get the real issues in women's sports

One of the wildest moments of the WNBA season — which is ...
articles.body_text:
Megan Rapinoe's latest ridiculous rant on Sophie Cunningham and RIley Gaines makes it clear she doesn't get the real issues in women's sports

One of the wildest moments of the WNBA season — which is saying a lot these days — came on Saturday between the Indiana Fever and the Chicago Sky.

DiJonai Carrington of the Sky was handed a Flagrant 2 foul for appearing to clothesline the Fever's Sophie Cunningham.

The incident has gotten people talking, with even the Florida attorney general chiming in.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT AGAINST DIJONAI CARRINGTON AFTER FLAGRANT FOUL AND 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST

Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington commits a flagrant 2 foul against Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

His take: a play like that would never happen in the Sunshine State.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier hopped on X after the incident and explained why there's not currently a WNBA club in the state.

Well, if that's the case, I can see why the league has been hesitant to head down to Florida in recent years.

Florida previously had two clubs, but the state has not been home to a WNBA franchise for over 20 years. The Orlando Miracle played in the league from 1999 to 2002, but relocated to Connecticut, where they currently play as the Connecticut Sun.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Farther south, the Miami Sol (yeah, technically that would be another team with the name "Sun") played from 2000 to 2002.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier had some thoughts after the the Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham was the target of a brutal flagrant foul. (Amy Beth Bennett / South Florida Sun Sentinel)

We've reached out to the Florida Attorney General's office for comment but have yet to hear back.

WNBA FACES DISCIPLINE DILEMMA AFTER CARRINGTON'S 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST TARGETING INDIANA FEVER

Joking or not, there's no question that what we saw on Saturday was one doozy of a foul, no matter who was on the receiving end of it.

But, in light of recent events, the fact that Cunningham was the target, and that Carrington has gotten into it before with Cunningham's Fever teammate Caitlin Clark, it's no surprise that the incident has gotten a lot of attention from all over the place.

It remains to be seen if Carrington will receive supplemental discipline for the foul, or for the controversial social media post accusing the Fever of benefiting from "white privilege" during the game.

articles.title: Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza
articles.excerpt: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insists he has rejected President Donald ⁠⁠Trump’s plan for Gaza and will not ⁠⁠withdraw forces until the Palestinian group Hamas ⁠⁠fully disarms, risking mor...
articles.body_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insists he has rejected President Donald ⁠⁠Trump’s plan for Gaza and will not ⁠⁠withdraw forces until the Palestinian group Hamas ⁠⁠fully disarms, risking more obstacles in the increasingly complex efforts to reduce escalation on multiple fronts in the region.

“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday, referring to the plan endorsed last month by Hamas.

The Israeli army “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed … and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens”, Netanyahu said, adding that Israel is “talking to the Americans about this issue”.

“They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some are not acceptable to us, and we know how to stand firm on these things,” Netanyahu said.

There was no immediate response from the White House.

In a statement published on Telegram later on Sunday, Hamas said it remained committed to fully implementing the plan.

The Palestinian armed group called on mediators and guarantor countries to “assume their responsibilities” and prevent any “violations or breaches” that could derail the process.

Israel has continued ⁠⁠to carry out near-daily deadly attacks across the Gaza Strip regardless of a so-called “ceasefire” with Hamas last ⁠⁠October.

Trump announced a “historic” agreement on on July 30 that entailed “the complete disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza”, which he called “a monumental step toward lasting peace and security”. The deal was credited to the US-led Board of Peace, inaugurated in February 2026 and including roughly 40 countries – including Israel and several Arab states, though no Palestinian representatives –  with Trump installed as its chair for life.

Speaking to his cabinet Sunday, Netanyahu vowed that “as long as I am prime minister, no Palestinian state will arise” and emphasised that Israel would not abide by the US-backed plan.

Israel’s desire for “real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament” would mean the removal of all weaponry, including lighter weapons, he said.

The 15-point plan calls for initially focusing on Hamas’s heavy weaponry, military production sites, weapons depots and the group’s extensive tunnel network.

Reporting from Washington DC, Al Jazeera’s Patty Culhane said that Netanyahu is playing a “very dangerous game” with Trump.

Israel is becoming increasingly unpopular in the US, with the Democratic Party “very much sliding towards the Palestinian cause”, said Culhane.

Furthermore, Trump could decide to “say it is time to split with Israel”, which would likely see many in the Republican Party, “the last staunchest ally of Israel in the US”, follow suit, Culhane said.

Reporting from Gaza City, Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud said Netanyahu’s statement raises “serious questions” for Palestinians about the path out of hostilities.

“The full rejection here puts the sequencing and the steps into question,” Mahmoud said.

Reporting from Bethlehem in the occupied West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said Netanyahu’s stated conditions could prove “extremely problematic for the Board of Peace and the mediators who have been working for months now to try to carry out the disarmament of Hamas”.

The roadmap would eventually involve transferring Gaza’s day-to-day administration to a technocratic Palestinian committee operating under the oversight of the Board of Peace.

But the board has “very limited power” to move forward without Israeli support, Odeh said.

“Netanyahu has hit the reset button,” she said.

Since Hamas and Israel agreed to a nominal ceasefire last October, experts have expressed scepticism that Israel would honour the agreement as its forces have continued to pummel Gaza, killing hundreds of people.

At least one child was injured in Israeli army gunfire in the Al-Najjar neighbourhood of Khan Younis on Sunday, the Palestinian Wafa news agency reported.

Since the “ceasefire” started in mid-October last year, at least 1,258 people have been killed and 4,139 wounded with more than 800 bodies recovered from rubble, according to Gaza’s health ministry.

The overall death toll in Gaza since October 2023 is at least 73,386 and 174,250 wounded.

Israeli forces and settlers continue to launch near daily attacks across the occupied West Bank, as Netanyahu’s party courts the settler vote less than three months before Israel’s general elections.

The Israeli military ransacked multiple homes after storming several villages in the Nablus governorate and multiple towns east of Bethlehem, reported Wafa.

Israeli settlers and soldiers carried out attacks in the areas of Tubas, al-Mughayyir, Masafer Yatta and Wadi al-Rakhim while also levelling farmland, according to Al Jazeera journalists on the ground.

In conjunction with Israeli police, Israeli worshippers stormed the Al-Aqsa mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem.

The compound, which is Islam’s third holiest site, is where Prophet Muhammad is believed to have ascended into heaven.

It is also the holiest site in Judaism, known as the Temple Mount, where the ancient Temple of Jerusalem previously stood.

A group of Israeli settlers protected by military forces also stormed the town of Beit Ur al-Tahta, west of Ramallah, while another group of settlers simultaneously stormed the al-Batin area on the outskirts of the village of Jaljulia, north of Ramallah, Wafa reported.

Israeli settlers conducted raids in multiple locations across the Ramallah and el-Bireh governorates.

Israeli settlers also attacked Palestinian properties near Bethlehem and cut down olive trees and damaged water tanks in Deir Sharaf, west of Nablus.

Israeli settlers under military protection attacked Palestinian farmers in Al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah.

Israeli ministers and parliament members attended an event to establish Emek Dotan, a new illegal Israeli settlement in Arrabeh, southwestern Jenin.

articles.title: Monday briefing: How the new phase of confrontation at al-Aqsa signals a challenge to the status quo
articles.excerpt:
In today’s newsletter: ​Jerusalem’s most volatile site has again become a flashpoint, with Arab states and former Israeli officials sounding the alarm over Benjamin Netanyahu’s complicity

Good mornin...
articles.body_text:
In today’s newsletter: ​Jerusalem’s most volatile site has again become a flashpoint, with Arab states and former Israeli officials sounding the alarm over Benjamin Netanyahu’s complicity

Good morning. In late July, Itamar Ben-Gvir, West Bank settler and far-right extremist minister of security in Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, joined a group of more than 2,000 Jewish extremists to storm al-Aqsa mosque compound, Jerusalem’s most sensitive holy site. The far-right group has been doing this for years. Ben-Gvir has made series of visits to the site over the last three years, eroding norms and inflaming tensions. Jordanian officials have recently warned that it could be at risk of an “imminent” Israeli takeover.

With national elections scheduled in October, and many eyes still firmly on Gaza (this weekend, Netanyahu rejected a US-backed 15 point plan for peace), the Israeli government appears to be racing to expand Israeli settlements and accelerate ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem before its mandate expires.

For this morning’s First Edition, I spoke to our senior international correspondent, Julian Borger, about the latest incursions, and how Israeli extremists are trying to create a new reality in Jerusalem. That’s after the weekend roundup.

UK politics | Sadiq Khan has called on the government to commit to revamped climate action and to reduce the UK’s reliance on oil and gas, as the UK endures a summer of drought, wildfires and heatwaves.

US politics | The US Senate voted to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general in a win for Donald Trump, who will now have his one-time personal attorney sitting atop the nation’s law enforcement apparatus.

US-Israel war on Iran | Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach on Saturday.

Russia-Ukraine | Up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers will be deployed in Russia, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. On Saturday, Turkey called for a “moratorium” on attacks by Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea after a series of strikes on civilian ships there

World news | The alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group was extradited from Dubai on Sunday and met by a huge security operation in Dublin, marking the end of a global game of cat and mouse with European, US and Gulf authorities.

The al-Haram al-Sharif site in Jerusalem’s old city, known to Jews as the Temple Mount, is one of the most contentious places on earth. It’s governed by a fragile agreement that gives Muslims exclusive rights to pray and worship there, while Jews pray at the Western Wall below. But Israel’s messianic right, which has gained a powerful foothold in Netanyahu’s coalition government, is fixated on the site as a symbol of its political project. Their vision of building a new Jewish temple on one of Islam’s holiest sites – once a fringe idea – has become increasingly widespread.

Since 2023, Jewish religious extremists have made numerous visits to the 35-acre compound which is home to both al-Aqsa mosque and Dome of the Rock, the holiest sites for Muslims in Jerusalem and one of holiest sites for Muslims in the world. “At first, you had groups of perhaps 20 Jews, mostly settlers, who were escorted by the police to the far wall of the compound to pray discreetly,” Julian tells me. “If you were just a casual visitor, you wouldn’t necessarily see them”. Over the last two years, however, the groups have grown bigger and more audacious. On 23 July, they sang the national anthem, and prayed and performed rituals in the centre of the compound, while Israeli police – who report to Ben-Gvir, who was in attendance – set up tents to provide shade to the worshippers.

“To erect structures, even if they’re temporary, is a red rag to a bull,” Julian says. “The longstanding fear is that Israelis would knock down the Dome of the Rock or the mosque, or rebuild a [Jewish] temple on the site. And these tents were part of a gradual attempt to push the boundaries.” Eight Arab nations swiftly issued a joint statement condemning “mass incursions by settlers led by extremist Israeli ministers”. Last Wednesday, the Jordanian authorities, who administer the site, held an emergency meeting of Arab and Islamic nations to discuss these risks, and afterwards, the Jordanian authorities condemned Israeli violations and warned that they constituted a “blatant provocation” to Muslims worldwide.

“All they can do is issue strong statements, saying, ‘don’t do this’,” says Julian. The Waqf, the Jordanian-appointed foundation that manages the site, is “defenceless”, he explains. In the run-up to Ramadan this year, Waqf sources told the Guardian that five of its staff had been detained by the Shin Bet, Israel’s counterintelligence service. Meanwhile, Israeli police have begun actively recruiting extremist activists to serve in the Temple Mount Unit, the force responsible for policing the compound. According to Haaretz, the deputy commander of the police’s Temple Mount Unit published a callout to officers on social media and in WhatsApp groups associated with West Bank settlers. “Anyone who wants to take part in implementing sovereignty is welcome to contact me,” he wrote.

The site’s history is constantly enlisted in attempts to justify the present. Muslims know the raised compound in the south-east of Jerusalem as al-Haram al-Sharif (the Noble Sanctuary), or simply al-Aqsa, after the mosque located at its southern edge. Next to the mosque, at the centre of the compound, is the Dome of the Rock, one of the oldest surviving Islamic places of worship. It’s on this site the prophet Muhammad is said to have ascended to heaven.

At the base of the compound is the Western Wall, a section of retaining wall that survived the destruction of the second Jewish temple in 70CE. The Temple Mount is also the holiest site in Judaism, the site of two temples which were built and then destroyed by invaders in ancient times.

Access to the site has been delicately managed for centuries. After the six-day war in 1967, when Israel captured East Jerusalem from Jordan, the Israeli government agreed that Jordan would continue to be the site’s custodian. Since then, the “status quo”, as it is known, has sought to prevent violent conflict by circumscribing the rights of Muslims and Jews to access the compound. While Jews are permitted to visit the site at specific times, they cannot pray there. Many Jews opt not to visit the site, out of fear of treading on holy ground while ritually impure.

“The status quo represented a historic compromise. Jews got the Western Wall. Muslims got Haram al-Sharif,” Julian says. “But the site has always been a detonator, sitting right there in the centre of the old city, with strong religious beliefs crammed together in a small area.”

It’s not uncommon in the region for holy sites to be carefully managed with intricate arrangements. Elsewhere in the Old City, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre is divided up between six Christian denominations, with its keys held by two Muslim families. At the Cave of the Patriarchs in the occupied city of Hebron, a mosque and synagogue share one building.

Past Israeli moves to challenge the status quo at al-Haram al-Sharif have been incendiary, sparking deadly violence. In 2000, then Israeli opposition leader and future prime minister Ariel Sharon made a visit to the site in an attempt to demonstrate Israeli sovereignty, sparking a chain of events that helped ignite  the second intifada. More recently, Hamas gave the name “al-Aqsa flood” to its attack on Israel in October 2023 that killed 1,200 Israelis and triggered the war on Gaza, claiming it was provoked by Israeli violations at the Jerusalem mosque.

Some Jewish extremists have begun marching under the temple flag – a star of David overlaid with a picture of the (as yet nonexistent) third temple they hope to build. “You see these flags on the bulldozers that are flattening neighbourhoods in Gaza, and soldiers wearing patches with a picture of the third temple on them,” Julian says.

The rise of the third temple movement comes at a time of surging attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, with the scale of violence prompting urgent calls for intervention from the heart of the Israeli establishment.

Earlier this year, dozens of Israelis, including two former prime ministers, former heads of its security services and former judges, signed a “final warning” threatening legal action against their government over its support for “Jewish terrorism” in the occupied West Bank. They argued the actions of the government had isolated Israel internationally and put its security at risk.

“There’s a feeling that the far-right side of Netanyahu’s government is now creating unnecessary, long-term security problems for Israel,” Julian says. That extends to attempts to change the status quo at al-Aqsa.

Netanyahu has publicly backed Jewish prayer at the site, claiming that changes pushed by Ben-Gvir were coordinated with him. “This isn’t the stuff of radicals any more,” Julian says. “It has government approval.”

Wednesday | A partial solar eclipse will be visible across the whole of the UK, with the south-west of England getting the best of British views. Parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain will experience a total eclipse.

Thursday | Clacton-on-sea residents will vote in the byelection Nigel Farage triggered last month, with the Reform leader taking on 33 mostly novelty candidates. Results are expected early Friday.

Thursday | The Office for National Statistics will publish UK GDP figures for the second quarter of 2026.

So many horror stories have emerged from ICE raids and arrests in the US. Alex Hannaford reports expertly on the ongoing nightmare for one young man snatched in upstate New York. Michael

Young people – particularly those who came of age during the pandemic – have had a pretty raw deal. I enjoyed this piece on what “Neets” need, by William Davies (£). Hettie

I was already looking forward to reading Symeon Brown’s new book, and this interview has confirmed it’ll be on my holiday reading list. Michael

Cycling | Demi Vollering won the final stage to seal her second Tour de France Femmes title but runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma reiterated her unhappiness with her rival team’s tactics on the penultimate stage.

Football | London City Lionesses’ headline signing, Alexia Putellas, talks expectations, the lure of playing in England and the prospect of being kicked by her former teammates.

Football | Fifa last night issued a thinly veiled attack on Uefa and other leading figures in European football in a statement which alleged there is a “concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president”.

“Labour wants ‘deeper’ ties to EU under Burnham, says minister”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Times writes “PM’s adviser ‘concerned’ over Labour wealth taxes”, Metro has “Andy wants a cancel culture” and the Mail says “Labour jail plan to spark 89,000 more crimes”.

The Telegraph has “Chinese spy cameras found on Navy drones”, while the Express leads on “You must keep our Fenella’s killer in jail”. On the heatwave, the Mirror says “Days of danger”, and the i Paper’s headline is “Car washes and swimming pools could face water bans in UK’s next heatwave”.

Are Gen Z the most financially savvy generation of them all? Economics correspondent, Richard Partington, charts the rise of investors like social media influencer James Beckett and those even younger, and explores why Gen Z are different from those who came before them when it comes to personal finance.

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

From paddleboarding the River Esk where you can experience tranquil wildlife and views of Whitby, to wild camping along the River Dart, a place which offers pristine moorland, oak-lined valleys and solitary swims in deep pools. There are many places to mess about on the river and find some peace and joy.

For more solo adventures you can relax with some fly‑fishing along the River Dove, a place which blends tricky casts, and pastoral beauty, where wild brown trout rise in crystalline, fast‑flowing pools. Something more strenuous might be a hike to find the sources of the Severn and Wye, a journey which blends scorching moorland with the wildlife‑rich upper Wye valley.

Or take it all in by canoe along the River Tay in Perthshire, and enjoy kingfisher spotting and the view of beaver lodges.

Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday

And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

articles.title: Eight teenagers charged with murder over alleged attack after Queensland party
articles.excerpt:
Man, 21, dies six days after being taken to hospital in critical condition after alleged attack in Bahrs Scrub, Logan

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news ema...
articles.body_text:
Man, 21, dies six days after being taken to hospital in critical condition after alleged attack in Bahrs Scrub, Logan

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A “preconceived plan” to do harm at a party has resulted in a young man’s death and murder charges for eight teenagers, police say.

The group of teens allegedly attended an Airbnb gathering south of Brisbane armed with various weapons before it erupted into violence and left the 21-year-old man with catastrophic head injuries.

He was gravely injured after the party at the rented home in Bahrs Scrub, a suburb of Logan, on 26 July, Det Insp Ian Galpin told reporters on Monday.

‘‘A 21-year-old Redbank Plains man was located in an unconscious state, suffering head injuries,’’ he said.

He was transported to hospital in a critical condition and died six days later.

A group of young men have been accused of arming themselves before they arrived at the party which left several vehicles destroyed, a home extensively damaged and a street shut down, police said.

‘‘The police will allege that this group had a preconceived plan, which included arming themselves with various weapons before attending Bahrs Scrub with the common purpose of inflicting harm on persons at that address,’’ Galpin said.

The fatal attack triggered a major homicide investigation.

‘‘More than 80 police were involved in the execution of 14 search warrants across three police districts,’’ Galpin said.

Four teens were initially charged with murder on 6 August – two 18-year-olds and two 19-year-olds.

Another four were located and charged on Sunday – a 17-year-old and three 18-year-olds.

“Our investigations have continued, and [on Sunday] … we located an additional four persons at short-term accommodation in Morayfield, and those persons were also arrested and charged with murder,” Galpin said.

Police have warned more arrests are possible.

‘‘It is an ongoing investigation, so that is a possibility. If we identify more persons involved in this offence, then they will be charged.’’

Police liaison officers and community leaders have been working to prevent any retaliation.

‘‘Everyone that we have spoken to, they want nothing but peace within their community, and that’s why I’m confident there won’t be any further retaliation,’’ Galpin said.

‘‘We’ll continue to support the community, and we’ll also continue to deliver our message that any form of violence will not be tolerated.’’

Galpin praised the response from local residents, saying community cooperation had been “nothing short of amazing”.

‘‘If not for this cooperation, I don’t think we’d be in the position that we’re here in today and I think it highlights the importance of police working with the community and vice versa to solve these serious crimes.’’

articles.title: British national shot dead in Kashmir by Pakistani security forces
articles.excerpt:
Mohammad Akhtar, 50, from Peterborough killed during clashes between authorities and protesters

A British national was shot dead in Pakistan-administered Kashmir during clashes between security force...
articles.body_text:
Mohammad Akhtar, 50, from Peterborough killed during clashes between authorities and protesters

A British national was shot dead in Pakistan-administered Kashmir during clashes between security forces and protesters, the Guardian can reveal.

Another Briton has been held in a regional prison for more than two months despite his family’s efforts to secure his release through the Foreign Office.

The details, which have not been previously reported, shed light on how Britons with familial ties to the region have been affected by the clashes, which have killed dozens in the Himalayan territory and posed the biggest challenge for Pakistani authorities in recent years.

Mohammad Akhtar, 50, a resident of Peterborough, was killed on 9 June after his family said Pakistani security forces opened fire on a gathering where protesters were demanding economic and electoral reforms in the disputed region that is also claimed by India.

Akhtar was staying in the city of Kotli, close to the area where the clashes occurred, and his family said he was hit by a stray bullet.

“He wasn’t taking part in protests but the demonstrations were happening close to his house,” said Mohammad Saad, Akhtar’s cousin.

“There was firing by the forces that day and he was hit by a stray bullet. There was a bullet wound on the side of his chest,” said Saad, adding that Akhtar’s children decided not to pursue the matter with British authorities.

They could not get a police complaint registered in Kashmir and feared that the family could be targeted if the case was highlighted, said Saad.

The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) said: “The UK is deeply concerned by the situation in parts of Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

“FCDO ministers and the UK high commissioner in Islamabad are in touch with their counterparts, and UK travel advice was updated on 7 August and continues to advise against all but essential travel to affected areas.”

It is understood that MP Hamish Falconer, during his previous role as a Foreign Office minister, raised the situation in Kashmir in talks with his counterparts during a 16-17 June visit to Islamabad. Stephen Doughty, who currently holds the role in the Foreign Office, has also been in touch with his counterparts.

Pakistan’s foreign ministry and its high commission in London did not respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment.

Islamabad has been accused of launching a violent crackdown on supporters of the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a civil society group that launched protests in Kashmir months ahead of a three-phase vote in the region that began on 27 July and which have been repeatedly disrupted by the unrest.

Pakistan declared the JAAC a terrorist organisation and has imposed a communications blackout in the region since 5 June. Its security forces have been accused of fatally shooting at least 30 people during demonstrations last month – charges the government has rejected.

The JAAC said Pakistani authorities were trying to suppress dissent and have detained scores of its supporters, who it said were ordinary Kashmiris. It has described the current elections as a “sham”, being held “at gunpoint”.

Waqas Arif, 38, a British national from Nottingham, was among those detained in the Kashmiri city of Mirpur after protests on 5 June, but his family said he did not take part in the demonstrations.

His sister Sumera said: “Waqas was not involved in any kind of protests. But since my other two brothers were involved and they went for the protests with everybody else, the Pakistani forces along with the Rangers came into my house and they took my brothers away.

“There is no charge. He hasn’t done anything. This is my brother, but I think there are thousands of other brothers like him from everywhere who they have put in [prison] so they can minimise the protest power … they have not even been taken to court,” she said.

Arif’s wife, Varisha Kampulvi, said British authorities had not been able to make direct contact with him since he was taken to the prison in Mirpur.

Kampulvi has highlighted Arif’s case to British authorities. A Foreign Office email sent to her on 26 June said: “Consular staff have been able to make contact with officials at the prison where Waqas is currently being held, although we have not had direct contact with Waqas.

“The authorities have confirmed that Waqas is in good health, which we were extremely pleased to hear.”

articles.title: UK manufacturers face rising hacking risk as survey shows 30% were hit last year
articles.excerpt:
Big companies describe being under constant threat but only half have a plan in place to respond to an attack

Nearly a third of British manufacturers have been hit by a cyber-attack on them or a comp...
articles.body_text:
Big companies describe being under constant threat but only half have a plan in place to respond to an attack

Nearly a third of British manufacturers have been hit by a cyber-attack on them or a company in their supply chain, according to a survey that highlighted the growing hacking risk to companies.

The findings come almost a year after Britain’s largest automotive employer, JLR, was hit by an attack that forced it to halt production for weeks.

The report by MakeUK, a lobby group for British manufacturers, found that 30% of manufacturers had experienced a cyber-incident in the past 12 months, leading in many cases to lost production time and increased costs. However, only half had a plan in place to respond to an attack.

The risk of attacks has risen in recent years as hackers, often backed by hostile states, have become more numerous and more adept at penetrating company defences. Large businesses describe being under near-constant attack from people trying to access their systems, and the UK government has said cybercrime costs the economy £14.7bn a year. The rise of generative AI systems, some of which have been able to hack into other businesses autonomously, has added extra urgency to efforts to upgrade defences.

Manufacturers have sought to improve productivity by connecting their factories, allowing them much quicker insight into their operations. However, the larger number of links has also meant that once attackers are inside the system, the scope for harm is much larger. JLR was forced to shut down systems across all its factories, offices and retail operations after it discovered digital intruders on the last day of August last year.

The independent Cyber Monitoring Centre said the JLR hack cost the UK economy at least £1.9bn, probably making it the most expensive cyber incident ever in Britain, mainly because of lost output at JLR and its suppliers. The New York Times reported in June that British law enforcement had concluded that Russian hackers were behind it.

Other big attacks reported publicly in recent years include two FTSE 100 manufacturers who reported attacks within days of each other early in 2025: the valve maker IMI and the components maker Smiths Group. In the retail sector, Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods all suffered costly breaches last year.

Jonathon Ellison, director of national resilience at the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which was involved in the response to the JLR attack, said: “In today’s landscape, no manufacturer can afford to treat cybersecurity as anything other than a business-critical priority. The NCSC is working to help organisations of all sizes strengthen their cyber defences.”

Among companies affected by a cyber-attack on their supply chain, about 30% of 123 manufacturers surveyed said they had suffered delays of deliveries to customers or output cuts, and almost a quarter reported supplier delivery delays or shortages of components and materials.
