articles.title: Pakistani grooming gang suspect ‘refuses to give date for return to UK’
articles.excerpt:
Rukhsar Ahmed was recently elected an MP in Pakistan while on bail over alleged child rape in 1990s Manchester

A grooming gang suspect released on bail in the UK and then re-elected as an MP in Pakis...
articles.body_text:
Rukhsar Ahmed was recently elected an MP in Pakistan while on bail over alleged child rape in 1990s Manchester

A grooming gang suspect released on bail in the UK and then re-elected as an MP in Pakistan has reportedly declined to say when he would return to face rape charges.

The Guardian disclosed that Rukhsar Ahmed, a former Pakistan state minister, was arrested at Manchester airport in July 2024 on suspicion of raping and trafficking at least two underage girls from care homes in the city’s Rusholme area during the 1990s.

He was released on bail and flew to Pakistan nearly two months ago, missing an appointment at a police station after telling officers he was too unwell to fly back to the UK.

He was elected an MP for prime minister Shehbaz Sharif’s centre-right Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz party days later.

He did not respond to requests for a comment when approached by the Guardian last week.

It emerged on Sunday that Ahmed, 61, had been located in his office in Khari Sharif, a village in Mirpur district.

According to the Mail on Sunday, he told a reporter he would fly back to Britain to meet his bail conditions, but declined to give a date. “Everything is with my legal team in Manchester and London, they told me I can’t discuss this,” he told the newspaper.

“What they done, this media in the United Kingdom and Europe, is out of order. I have not been convicted of anything nor charged for anything, so what is going on? I don’t want to discuss it, because if I discuss it, things may go wrong.”

Asked directly whether he had raped two underage girls, he refused to answer, telling the reporter: “You are doing wrong now, I told you not to talk to me like this … please don’t talk to me like this, I told you I have nothing to do with it, OK.”

Ahmed published a statement on his Facebook account on Friday. It read: “I categorically deny all the allegations against me and will address these matters through the appropriate forums. On legal advice, I will not comment further while these matters remain ongoing.”

Ahmed was a minister in various state governments from 2006 until he lost his seat in 2021.

The Guardian understands that Greater Manchester police (GMP) had wanted to restrict Ahmed’s ability to travel abroad as part of his bail conditions, but a judge rejected tougher measures in July 2024.

Ahmed was arrested at Manchester airport on 18 July 2024 in relation to past child sexual abuse allegations linked to the Rusholme area, where he lived for many years.

According to the report, he received a string of visitors in his office. He is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile.

The ongoing investigation relates to allegations from several women about sexual abuse of children at care homes in the early 1990s, when Ahmed was in his late 20s.

He is understood to be expected to answer police bail in the next six weeks. If he does not attend, GMP may issue a warrant for his arrest or take steps to extradite him.

The Guardian has approached Ahmed for comment again.

Richard Scorer, the head of abuse law at Slater and Gordon who has acted in many Manchester grooming gang cases said: “Rusholme has regularly featured in grooming gang investigations over the past 30 years, with many cases involving allegations of children being abused in and around the area.

“Not all of those allegations have been adequately investigated. I hope that a comprehensive investigation is taking place here”.

articles.title: Pentagon urges faster US weapons production amid stockpile concerns
articles.excerpt: The Pentagon has called on the United States defence industry to accelerate production of weapons to help replenish its diminished stockpile of munitions, including those depleted in the ongoing war w...
articles.body_text:
The Pentagon has called on the United States defence industry to accelerate production of weapons to help replenish its diminished stockpile of munitions, including those depleted in the ongoing war with Iran.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement on Saturday that the department was actively focused on boosting munitions acquisitions to provide “the weapons our warfighters need at the pace the threat demands”. He confirmed the department’s efforts over the last week to significantly speed up the process, but insisted it was part of a broader modernisation effort that predated the five-month-old conflict.

Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg wrote to industry leaders on Wednesday, giving them no more than 21 days to submit plans to “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities,” according to a memo obtained by The Washington Post.

“Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” Feinberg wrote. “We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.”

The memo comes as recent fighting with Iran used up more of the US military’s already diminished stockpiles of advanced missile interceptors. Experts say shortages in both offensive and defensive weapons could leave US forces less secure.

Shrunken inventories of Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors may force the US and its Middle Eastern allies to take greater risks to conserve those air defences, according to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank. For example, it said, American forces may launch fewer missiles against incoming Iranian drones and missiles, raising the chance of one getting through.

US President Donald Trump has bristled over public reports of a munitions shortage. On Thursday, he again denied that the US faced any strategic disadvantage when it came to weapons stores after five months of war.

“The US has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social account. He added that “large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the US as needed” and that defence contractors are “building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history”.

On Saturday, Parnell affirmed that Feinberg’s memo seeking a rapid escalation of weapons production is “real,” adding that it “will inform the fiscal year 2028 budget submitted to Congress for funding, and it is entirely consistent with our ongoing push to rebuild the defense industrial base.”

A defence spending bill is currently stalled in the US Congress, with lawmakers fuming over Trump’s military action against Iran and resisting the White House request to substantially increase Pentagon spending to $1.5 trillion, up from about $900bn last year. Experts have warned that even with an influx of funding, it will likely take at least three years to restore Patriot and THAAD interceptors to pre-war levels.

The number of Patriot interceptors fell from 2,330 before the war to 1,030 when the April ceasefire took effect, CSIS estimated last month. Following recent fighting, the stockpile is now estimated to be between 759 and 827, a decrease of at least 65 percent since before the conflict began.

The number of THAAD interceptors fell from 452 before the war to between 232 and 262 at the start of the April ceasefire, CSIS said. The US was able to replenish some of the inventory to between 234 and 278 interceptors. But the stockpile is still at least 38 percent smaller than it was before the conflict.

Earlier this month, the US Department of Defense penned a new deal with defence giants Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman in an effort to ramp up production capacity for parts used in missile defence systems.

“We don’t have that many [interceptors] left, and there are no good substitutes,” retired US Marine Corps colonel Mark Cancian, one of the authors of the CSIS analysis, told Al Jazeera on Wednesday. “If we run out of Patriots, then the missiles get through.”

articles.title: Burnham vows crackdown on ‘rip-off’ business practices to ease cost of living
articles.excerpt:
First of PM’s ‘everyday fixes’ to be banning fake discounts and making it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptions

Andy Burnham: I’ll end the rip-offs that people hate

Andy Burnham has promised a ser...
articles.body_text:
First of PM’s ‘everyday fixes’ to be banning fake discounts and making it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptions

Andy Burnham: I’ll end the rip-offs that people hate

Andy Burnham has promised a series of measures to tackle the cost of living, including a ban on fake discounts and making it easier for people to escape unwanted subscriptions.

The crackdown on “rip-off” business practices is expected to benefit consumers to the tune of £400m a year and will be the first in a range of “everyday fixes” to be implemented in the coming months.

Writing for the Guardian, the prime minister said his government would step in wherever it could as he sought to put the cost of living at the heart of his premiership.

“We won’t be able to solve every frustration overnight,” he wrote. “But where the government can save people money, remove an unnecessary obstacle or simply make something work better, we should and we will.”

The government will ban misleading pricing practices that retailers use to make discounts appear better than they really are, including fake “was” prices, invented reductions and misleading recommended retail prices.

Ministers will consult in the autumn on the precise practices covered and how the ban will work, before introducing the changes through secondary legislation.

Downing Street hopes the measures can be implemented as soon as possible and does not expect a lengthy parliamentary process.

The changes are intended to stop retailers inflating the price of an item before cutting it to give shoppers the false impression they are receiving a bigger discount.

Burnham wrote: “If something is advertised as half price, it should actually be half price. We’ll make sure that when families snatch a deal, they can be confident they’re actually saving. That’s the least they deserve when budgets are so tight.”

The government is also speeding up new protections against subscription traps, bringing forward their introduction from next spring to January. The rules will force businesses to provide clearer information when people sign up, regularly remind customers about their subscriptions and make it easier for them to cancel. Customers will also be given a 14-day cooling-off period after a trial ends or a long-term contract renews.

The average person has about three subscriptions and spends about £500 a year on them, according to government figures. There are about 155m active subscriptions across the UK, and about £1.6bn a year is spent on unwanted ones.

Ministers estimate consumers will save an average of £14 a month for each unwanted subscription they are able to leave early.

“Too many companies want you to sign up in seconds but then make it feel impossible to leave. It’s exhausting,” Burnham wrote.

The challenge for the prime minister will be whether smaller consumer-oriented interventions can provide savings households notice when many are still under pressure.

The two measures will be followed by more over the coming months as he attempts to show voters his government can make a noticeable difference to household finances.

Burnham also promised “bigger plans to make life easier and fairer for people over the longer term”, but Downing Street has yet to set out what those will include.

Burnham wrote: “As far as I’m concerned, whatever the size, big or small, if it’s a problem for you, it’s a problem for us. That’s why I’ve made it clear from day one that creating room to breathe is my number one priority, and the whole of government is united on that.

“Every single unexpected payment, rip-off or hidden catch chips away at hope. That might sound dramatic – but it’s true. Every single one is another message that thiscountry is built to catch people out rather than help them get on.”

Citizens Advice welcomed the changes but said they “can’t be the end of the story”.

The announcement comes as Burnham prepares to spend the rest of his summer travelling around Britain in an attempt to reconnect the government with voters, particularly in areas where Labour has lost support.

“I’ll be asking people what action they want to see on the cost of living,” Burnham wrote. “Because if we want to find the problems that make everyday life harder, we need to listen to the people dealing with them.”

Downing Street has not said whether what Burnham hears on the tour will shape the next round of “everyday fixes”.

NSW deputy premier asks for moratorium on take-home assessments for students amid AI review

Prue Car, the NSW deputy premier, has asked the NSW Education Standards Authority (Nesa) to impose a ban on unsupervised, take-home assessments during a broad review of AI’s impact on student learning.

Car said she has asked Nesa to “urgently” examine artificial intelligence and move to protect student learning amid growing evidence the technology is affecting student’s cognitive development. Half of students’ HSC result is based on school-based assessments, some of which is finished outside the classroom.

double quotation markArtificial intelligence has enormous potential to support teaching and learning, but it should never replace the thinking, creativity, and hard work that education is designed to develop.

The purpose of schooling extends beyond producing an assessment task. It is to build knowledge, judgement, resilience, and critical thinking over time. If students rely on AI to bypass that learning process, we risk undermining both their education and the integrity of the HSC.

Subject to Nesa’s advice, any interim changes would be applied from the beginning of term 4

Good morning, and happy Monday. Here’s what’s on deck:

Catherine King, the federal minister for transport, said she has asked Air Services Australia to come and talk to her today about a “pathway forward” after two aircraft were involved in a near-miss at Sydney airport on Sunday.

And the former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull and former foreign minister Bob Carr will speak before a public inquiry into the Aukus submarine deal today. Stick with us.

articles.title: WNBA media defends DiJonai Carrington after dangerous Sophie Cunningham hit reveals glaring bias
articles.excerpt:
Megan Rapinoe's latest ridiculous rant on Sophie Cunningham and RIley Gaines makes it clear she doesn't get the real issues in women's sports

WNBA media wasted no time jumping to DiJonai Carrington's...
articles.body_text:
Megan Rapinoe's latest ridiculous rant on Sophie Cunningham and RIley Gaines makes it clear she doesn't get the real issues in women's sports

WNBA media wasted no time jumping to DiJonai Carrington's defense after her dangerous hit on Sophie Cunningham earned her a Flagrant 2 and an early shower Saturday.

Carrington got the boot after catching Cunningham above the neck as the Fever guard went airborne for a transition layup.

But instead of taking her lumps, Carrington retreated to the locker room and immediately pulled out her phone, posting "WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever" on Threads.

Just like that, Carrington turned punishment for her own reckless play into an accusation about race. If anything, that response warranted even greater scrutiny. Instead, WNBA media circled the wagons around Carrington, downplaying the hit.

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham (8) questions a referees call during a game against the Golden State Valkyries on July 15, 2026, at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Brian Spurlock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) (Brian Spurlock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

DiJonai Carrington of the Chicago Sky was ejected after a brutal foul on Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever. (Kamil Krzaczynski/Imagn Images)

ESPN quickly joined the defense when analyst Andraya Carter rationalized the hit as little more than a product of Carrington's aggressive style of play.

ESPN BURIES DIJONAI CARRINGTON DIRTY FOUL ON SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM, 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST

"These are plays we've seen from DiJonai, right? So getting in the right position, jumping over the top, getting these transition blocks," Carter explained.

"She's always gonna make that effort. So even for some of these, she's behind the offensive player coming over the top. So again, she was behind Sophie Cunningham. She wasn't able to get over the top. Had she got over the top and made that play, we wouldn't have been talking about it. She was too far behind the play. The contact above the head was too much. But that's what DiJonai Carrington does. Like, this wasn't, to me, because it was Sophie Cunningham making the layup."

Carter's own analysis undermined the defense she was making.

She acknowledged that Carrington was behind the play and that the contact above the head was "too much," only to excuse it with a familiar refrain: "that's what DiJonai Carrington does."

JD VANCE PRAISES SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FOR 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' ACTIVISM

It's clear that Sophie Cunningham is in the WNBA's crosshairs for speaking out against male athletes competing in women's sports and refusing to toe the league's preferred line.

Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever talks with head coach Stephanie White during the first half against the Chicago Sky at the United Center on July 27, 2025, in Chicago, Ill. (Michael Reaves/Getty Images)

That stance has created an environment where she carries a target on her back, leaving players like Carrington to expect their aggression toward her to be rationalized after the fact.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT AGAINST DIJONAI CARRINGTON AFTER FLAGRANT FOUL AND 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST

The response to Saturday's incident exposes a persistent imbalance within WNBA coverage.

When physical aggression is directed at White players such as Cunningham or Caitlin Clark, commentators have repeatedly shown a willingness to search for explanations that soften the actions of the offending player.

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham fights with Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington after being Carrington fouled Cunningham with a hit to the Fever guard's head. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

DiJonai Carrington No. 7 of the Chicago Sky reacts against the Indiana Fever during the first half at United Center in Chicago on Aug. 8, 2026. (Getty Images)

The disparity becomes even harder to ignore when the circumstances are reversed.

Imagine a white player drilling a Black opponent above the neck, getting tossed and then immediately posting a racial accusation aimed at the opposing team.

Saturday was not Carrington's first go at controversy. During the 2024 postseason, Carrington struck Clark directly in the eye, leaving the league's signature star with a visible black eye, then mocked the ensuing public outrage online.

REPUBLICAN LAWMAKERS PRESS WNBA COMMISSIONER CATHY ENGELBERT TO PROTECT CAITLIN CLARK

Less than two years later, another dangerous play involving Carrington has produced another controversy, followed by another effort to shift the conversation away from her own responsibility.

The facts from Saturday are straightforward. Carrington delivered a dangerous hit that officials deemed serious enough to warrant a Flagrant 2 and an ejection, then responded by invoking race.

Rather than scrutinize both actions, prominent voices within WNBA media devoted their energy to explaining her conduct.

Player safety cannot depend on who delivers the hit, just as media scrutiny should not depend on the racial identities of the players involved.

articles.title: Teen burglary ring linked to nearly 80 Bay Area break-ins dismantled after months-long investigation: PD
articles.excerpt: Concord police surveillance video shows suspects breaking into vehicles, entering residential garages with stolen garage door openers and carrying out a Bay Area burglary spree. Credit: Concord Police...
articles.body_text:
Concord police surveillance video shows suspects breaking into vehicles, entering residential garages with stolen garage door openers and carrying out a Bay Area burglary spree. Credit: Concord Police Department

A gang of teenage burglars accused of targeting nearly 80 Bay Area homes and vehicles is behind bars after investigators unraveled a months-long crime spree that included stolen firearms, high-speed chases and an alleged fencing operation that netted roughly $250,000 in suspected stolen property.

Concord police also released surveillance video of the burglary spree, dubbing the compilation "Teamwork Leads to Arrests in Regional Armed Burglary Series."

The video shows the suspects breaking into parked vehicles in the early morning hours before using stolen garage door openers to gain access to attached garages, where investigators said they stole power tools, firearms and other valuables.

NEW WARRANTS EXPOSE CHILLING, DISTURBING DETAILS IN GREG BIFFLE HOME BURGLARY

Surveillance video released by Concord police shows an armed burglary suspect pointing a firearm toward a home's interior door during the investigation. (Concord Police Department)

In one of the most brazen moments captured on camera, investigators said the suspects pointed a firearm at the interior door connecting a garage to a home, apparently waiting for a homeowner to emerge. During another burglary, the crew allegedly stole 14 firearms from a single residential garage.

By the time the investigation wrapped up, detectives had linked the suspects to 37 vehicle and residential burglaries in Concord and approximately 40 more across Contra Costa and Solano counties. Police said the group also stole multiple vehicles, which they allegedly used to commit additional crimes.

The suspects repeatedly slipped away from officers as the burglary spree unfolded.

In May, an officer spotted a possible suspect vehicle and attempted a traffic stop, but the driver allegedly sped away. Police launched a pursuit before calling it off over public safety concerns.

OREGON BURGLARY SUSPECT NABBED AFTER CRASHING SUV DURING POLICE CHASE: VIDEO

Two burglary suspects break into a parked pickup truck before allegedly using a stolen garage door opener to access nearby homes in California. (Concord Police Department)

During another string of burglaries in June, officers located a different suspect vehicle, but the suspects again escaped.

Later that month, the juveniles allegedly fled another burglary, crashed a vehicle and ran from the scene on foot. They evaded capture once again, though officers recovered a firearm.

The break in the case came in late June, when Concord detectives working with the Richmond Police Department identified four juveniles believed to be behind the burglary spree.

One suspect was already being held in juvenile hall in connection with an unrelated case. Investigators then obtained arrest and search warrants for the remaining three.

Police said the suspects targeted parked vehicles before using stolen garage door openers to enter residential garages. (Concord Police Department)

In July, the Concord Police Department SWAT Team executed simultaneous warrants with assistance from the Antioch Police Department, Pittsburg Police Department, Central County SWAT and the U.S. Marshals Service.

All three outstanding suspects were arrested.

Searches of their residences led to the recovery of two firearms stolen during the burglaries, police said. A third stolen firearm had previously been recovered by the Richmond Police Department during a separate investigation.

As detectives dug deeper, they uncovered what prosecutors describe as an organized fencing operation.

CHICAGO POL SAYS WALGREENS SHOULD BE CHARGED WITH 'FIRST-DEGREE CORPORATE ABANDONMENT' OVER CLOSURE OVER THEFT

Surveillance video released by Concord police shows a masked burglary suspect during a string of home and vehicle break-ins across the Bay Area. (Concord Police Department)

Investigators identified 37-year-old Wuillian Cordova-Cubias of Oakland as the alleged buyer of stolen property, accusing him of purchasing power tools from the juvenile suspects, often shortly after the burglaries occurred.

On Aug. 5, detectives with the Concord Police Department, Oakland Police Department and the U.S. Marshals Service executed a search warrant at Cordova-Cubias' Oakland home.

Police said the search uncovered what investigators believe was the hub of a regional fencing operation. Inside, detectives found at least 500 suspected stolen power tools, along with a stolen ATV, a stolen forklift, an unregistered firearm and numerous other high-value items. Authorities estimated the recovered property was worth approximately $250,000.

The Contra Costa County District Attorney's Office charged Cordova-Cubias with receiving stolen property, two counts of receiving stolen motor vehicles, unlawful firearm activity and conspiracy with juvenile co-conspirators. Prosecutors also filed sentencing enhancements that could increase any potential penalties if he is convicted.

Exterior of the Contra Costa County District Attorney's Office in Martinez, California, where charges were filed in the burglary investigation. (Contra Costa County District Attorney's Office)

"As organized theft offenses have increased, my office has responded by building an effective Organized Theft Unit that works closely with law enforcement to file strong cases we believe we can prove beyond a reasonable doubt in court," Contra Costa County District Attorney Diana Becton said in a statement. "Concord Police Department's thorough investigation into these burglaries and the fencing operation reflects the kind of collaboration that holds individuals accountable."

Cordova-Cubias remains in custody at the Martinez Detention Facility and is scheduled to be arraigned Monday afternoon in Contra Costa County Superior Court.

The Contra Costa County District Attorney's Office also filed complaints against the three juvenile suspects. Their identities have not been released under California law.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Cyclospora fears are sending shoppers to farmers markets for local produce
articles.excerpt: NYU Langone gastroenterologist Dr. David Bernstein analyzes the Cyclospora and Salmonella outbreaks linked to contaminated produce. He details key symptoms, infection sources and essential food safety...
articles.body_text:
NYU Langone gastroenterologist Dr. David Bernstein analyzes the Cyclospora and Salmonella outbreaks linked to contaminated produce. He details key symptoms, infection sources and essential food safety tips. The health alert follows reports of multiple deaths and hundreds of infections nationwide.

Concerns surrounding the ongoing Cyclospora outbreak are changing how some consumers shop for produce, with farmers markets reporting a surge in shoppers seeking homegrown greens.

Demand for locally grown lettuce has increased across Ohio, with some farmers market vendors selling out within 30 to 60 minutes of opening, Ohio news publication Axios Columbus reported.

The increased interest comes as shoppers pay closer attention to where their food comes from amid concerns about produce distributed through larger commercial suppliers.

CRUISE SHIP HIT WITH THIRD STOMACH ILLNESS OUTBREAK IN TWO MONTHS, REVIEW UNDERWAY

Cyclospora outbreak concerns are driving more shoppers to farmers markets for locally grown greens. (iStock)

Grocery store lettuce sales and visits to restaurants with produce-heavy menus have declined this summer, while farmers markets are seeing increased demand for locally grown alternatives, according to Axios.

Locally grown produce, however, is not immune from Cyclospora. Local greens typically have a shorter journey from farm to consumer than produce handled through larger commercial supply chains, which may mean fewer opportunities for contamination, the publication said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

The shift in shopping habits comes as federal health officials continue investigating the outbreak and encouraging consumers to take precautions when preparing produce.

The CDC advises consumers to wash their hands and rinse fresh fruits and vegetables thoroughly under running water before preparing or eating them. Washing produce, however, does not guarantee that Cyclospora will be eliminated, according to the agency's food safety alert.

The growing interest comes as shoppers become more mindful of where their produce is sourced. (iStock)

Concerns about the outbreak have also spread online, where some consumers say the uncertainty has left them anxious about what they eat.

"I've been coping by pretty much only eating things that are cooked," one Reddit user wrote.

Another commenter pointed to the time between exposure and potential symptoms as a source of worry.

"The incubation period is what's making me anxious," the user wrote.

Cyclospora outbreak concerns are also growing online, with some consumers expressing anxiety about food safety. (iStock)

"Any time I feel a little off I absolutely panic that I have this parasite," another user commented.

The concerns come as the outbreak has grown to thousands of confirmed cases across the country.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Fox News Digital previously reported that over 6,300 cases had been confirmed across 15 states, resulting in 278 hospitalizations and two deaths.

Taylor Farms de Mexico recalled all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico on July 17 after health officials linked the product to the outbreak. The recalled lettuce reached consumers, restaurants and retailers in at least 27 states.

People who develop Cyclosporiasis can experience diarrhea, loss of appetite, weight loss, cramping, bloating, nausea and fatigue. Symptoms most often develop about a week after infection, although they can begin as early as two days after exposure or take two weeks or longer to appear, according to the CDC.

Fox News Digital's James Cirrone contributed to this report.

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Germany warns of ‘daily hybrid warfare’ after explosive-laden drone found
articles.excerpt:
Germany is facing daily “hybrid warfare” attacks from abroad, an official has said, days after an explosive-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt t...
articles.body_text:
Germany is facing daily “hybrid warfare” attacks from abroad, an official has said, days after an explosive-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the local newspaper Bild am Sonntag on Sunday that foreign powers wanted to subdue Germany politically and socially by stirring up fear.

“We’re not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare,” Dobrindt said.

“Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilising Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality.”

He did not identify any countries behind the alleged attacks.

The minister’s comments come after a drone loaded ‌with explosives was discovered at the Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany on Tuesday.

Some German lawmakers pointed the finger at Russia, which has been at war with Ukraine since its full-scale invasion of the country in 2022.

The Russian embassy in Berlin on Friday dismissed the Leipzig event as a “fabricated provocation”, saying it was another example of unsubstantiated accusations against Moscow.

Germany is planning to strengthen its ability to counter drones amid concerns over the threat, Bild reported, citing government sources.

The newspaper said Dobrindt’s ministry wanted to double the federal government’s team of anti-drone experts from 150 to 300 and increase its network of related bases from four to eight.

Germany’s armed forces said on Saturday that two drones were spotted late on Thursday over a German military base site in Mechernich, in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Separately, a drone exploded on Saturday in Bulgaria near the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline.

Bulgaria’s defence ministry said there was no reason to suspect the incident was intentional. Ukraine said it was working with Bulgarian authorities to clarify the circumstances.

The drone incidents across Europe have renewed concerns that Russia’s war in Ukraine could increasingly affect neighbouring NATO states.

NATO and European Union officials have blamed Russia for previous drone sightings. Russia has rejected all the allegations.

articles.title: Drones spotted over German base days after Leipzig bomb incident
articles.excerpt:
Two drones were spotted over a military base in western Germany just days after an explosive-laden device was found at Leipzig airport.

Germany's armed forces (Bundeswehr) confirmed they were seen on...
articles.body_text:
Two drones were spotted over a military base in western Germany just days after an explosive-laden device was found at Leipzig airport.

Germany's armed forces (Bundeswehr) confirmed they were seen on Thursday evening at a base in Mechernich, near Bonn, reportedly housing components for US-made Patriot air-defence systems.

A spokeswoman for the Bundeswehr Joint Force Command said military police were deployed to the site before the matter was handed over to local police.

It is the latest instance of drones being spotted near military bases or airports in European nations supporting Ukraine in its war with Russia, on which suspicion has fallen. Moscow has consistently denied any involvement.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told newspaper Bild on Sunday that Germany had become a regular target of "destabilising" attacks.

"We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," he said.

Germany is currently investigating how a drone laden with explosives was able to reach a runway at Leipzig/Halle airport, which is used by Nato, the Germany military and serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines.

The Bundeswehr declined to comment on the ongoing investigation when asked by the BBC on Sunday about the suspected origins of the drones spotted above Mechernich.

The local police force has been contacted for comment.

German media reports that the base has a storage facility for equipment ​and spare parts used to maintain the Patriot missile batteries.

The air-defence systems have become crucial to Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles since Moscow's full-scale invasion began in 2022.

However, President Volodymyr Zelensky this week pleaded to allies for further supplies, warning that Ukraine was running out of interceptor missiles.

After initially offering Ukraine license to make Patriots in early July, US President Donald Trump last week denied any such agreement.

A spate of drone sightings in European airspace last year left the continent on high alert, prompting the EU to discuss a continent-wide "drone wall" of air defences.

Some European officials have blamed Russia for these drone sightings, claims Moscow has previously described as "absurd".

articles.title: Incumbents secure Hawaii primary wins, defying progressive challengers
articles.excerpt:
US Representative Ed Case of Hawaii has defeated a progressive Democratic challenger in the Hawaii primary, election results showed late Saturday.

Securing 57 percent of the vote against state Senato...
articles.body_text:
US Representative Ed Case of Hawaii has defeated a progressive Democratic challenger in the Hawaii primary, election results showed late Saturday.

Securing 57 percent of the vote against state Senator Jarrett Keohokalole, compared with his 34 percent, Case is set to face Republican nominee Adriel Lam come November.

The seventy-three-year-old, who is broadly viewed as a centrist, has held the seat since 2019 and has also ‌‌served in the House between 2002 and 2007. His latest victory over Keohokalole, 43, marks the latest front of the battle miring US Democratic politics, in ⁠⁠which veteran politicians are being pitted against younger, more progressive opponents. Progressive Democrats had criticised Case after he voted to support Republican US President Donald Trump’s Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which they say erodes US voting rights.

Keohokalole had cited Case’s corporate campaign contributions to argue the incumbent is increasingly detached from constituents.

Three other candidates also vied for the safely Democratic Honolulu seat.  As a senior member of a crucial spending committee, Case had argued that Hawaii would lose federal funding if he were not re-elected.

Case’s win stands out from a recent surge for left-wing candidates in states including Colorado, Kentucky and New York.

In Hawaii’s other congressional district, US Representative Jill Tokuda easily won her Democratic primary with 84 percent of the vote.

Hawaii Governor Josh Green, who has led the state since 2022, also defeated several challengers for the Democratic nomination.

articles.title: Omar Marmoush scores two goals as Man City defeat Atletico Madrid in Seoul
articles.excerpt:
Egyptian forward Omar Marmoush grabbed a brace as Manchester City came from behind to beat Atletico Madrid 3-1 in their final preseason friendly in Seoul, South Korea.

Atletico took the lead late in ...
articles.body_text:
Egyptian forward Omar Marmoush grabbed a brace as Manchester City came from behind to beat Atletico Madrid 3-1 in their final preseason friendly in Seoul, South Korea.

Atletico took the lead late in the first half on Sunday when Jorge Dominguez poked in the opener after City had failed to clear a corner.

City, led by new boss Enzo Maresca, had been on top before conceding, with Tijjani Reijnders, Josko Gvardiol and Savinho all missing decent chances to score.

City’s pressure eventually told, and they found the equaliser in the 57th minute through Marmoush, set up by the skilful Antoine Semenyo, who beat his marker to cross for the Egyptian to convert from close range.

The two combined again two minutes later as Marmoush latched onto another Semenyo cross to give City the lead.

Atletico, who gave a debut to new signing Lee Kang-In, started to create more chances as they rung the changes in the second half.

But it was City who struck again in the 90th minute as Rayan Ait-Nouri was sent clear to finish past substitute goalkeeper Carlos Esquivel.

City will next play Arsenal in the Community Shield at Wembley next Sunday, while Atletico will begin their La Liga campaign at home to Malaga on August 19.

articles.title: Young conservatives reveal what’s top of mind as GOP, Democrats battle for 'hopeless' Gen Z voters
articles.excerpt: College students attending Young America’s Foundation’s America at 250 conference in Washington, D.C., sounded off on affordability, border security, political polarization and fears that AI and socia...
articles.body_text:
College students attending Young America’s Foundation’s America at 250 conference in Washington, D.C., sounded off on affordability, border security, political polarization and fears that AI and social media algorithms are shaping their generation.

Both parties see Gen Z voters as a crucial bloc that could help tip the balance in November as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of Congress, with the GOP seeking to keep President Donald Trump’s agenda moving and Democrats pushing to retake Capitol Hill and steer the legislative agenda.

And as the Democratic Party grapples with the growing appeal of democratic socialism among young voters, Republicans are seizing on the trend to rally their own young base.

But conservative college students gathered at Young America’s Foundation’s Freedom at 250 conference in Washington, D.C., told Fox News Digital that economic pressures — from inflation to the housing crunch — are not only helping drive some of their peers toward democratic socialism, but that they themselves share those same concerns.

College students across the country gathered in Washington, D.C., for Young America's American at 250 conference held between July 6 to July 8. (Young America's Foundation)

DEMOCRATS LURE ‘POLITICALLY HOMELESS’ GEN Z TOWARD SOCIALISM — A COUNTERATTACK IS TAKING SHAPE

"I think a lot young people are feeling a little bit hopeless right now, Courtney Graves, a rising senior at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told Fox News Digital. "They want to be able to have a home when they grow up. They want to be able to have a nice life and a good-paying job. And what we’ve been seeing is that when those things don’t come to fruition, people tend to go to the extremes."

Graves' comments come as financial milestones such as buying a home, have been perceived as increasingly difficult for younger Americans. A Pew Research Center survey published in July found that 87% of Americans say buying a home is harder for young adults today than it was for their parents’ generation.

A recent report from Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies found that nearly half of renters spent more than 30% of their income on housing in 2024, and nearly half of Americans ages 18 to 29 received financial help to cover an expense over the past year, according to a Federal Reserve report released in May.

But Graves, who is the granddaughter of immigrants who escaped Communist-controlled Latvia, argued that embracing free-market policies is the best way for people to achieve the American Dream and that the Republican Party needs to work on its messaging to make that case more clear to young Americans.

Housing affordability remains a central issue as the Trump administration touts its economic agenda ahead of the midterms. (Paul Bersebach/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register/Getty Images)

THE AMERICAN DREAM NOW COMES WITH A ZIP CODE: HERE'S WHERE STARTER HOMES ARE STILL WITHIN REACH

"I think free markets are the way to have a successful and prosperous life," Graves said. "It's what leads to job growth, it's what leads to being able to buy a home at the end of the day, have a family and just overall live a great quality of life and have a strong country."

While affordability remains top of mind for Americans this midterm cycle, Brody Baker, a University of Iowa student, praised President Donald Trump for bringing more accountability to the White House compared to former President Joe Biden's presidency.

"I think we get more clarity of what's happening with the United States as of today," Baker said.

"With the administration being able to say, 'hey, we have some criticisms', Baker said. "There's some issues with gas being so high, with how the economy, for some it's hurting a lot, and for some, it's hurting a little."

BESSENT CREDITS TRUMP IMMIGRATION POLICIES WITH HELPING RETURN JOBS TO AMERICANS AS WAGE GAINS RESUME

For University of Minnesota senior Jackson Barrick, pocketbook concerns are just one slice of the pie.

He pointed to the country's immigration and border security policies and foreign policy as issues weighing most heavily on him. Barrick said Trump has done a "fantastic" job with his immigration enforcement agenda.

"I think it's a really good step in terms of making sure that we have a good future going forward in the United States and protecting the homeland," Barrick said.

But college students are also worried about a newer issue: artificial intelligence.

Nick Kammerzell, a recent University of Georgia graduate, said AI is the issue that most concerns him about America’s future.

Humans are using laptops and computers to interact with AI, helping them create, code, train AI, or analyze big data with fast, cutting-edge technology. (Getty Images/Wanan Yossingkum)

AI CHATBOTS TAKE HEAT OVER LEFT-WING BIAS: ‘NO LONGER BE CONSIDERED NEUTRAL’

"I think that it's very scary," Kammerzall said. "I think one of the biggest things that I'm concerned about with the AI issue is censorship and bias within AI. I think a lot of young people are becoming very dependent on it as their source of truth."

"I think there's a lot of opportunities for abuse and manipulation with that," Kammerzall added, arguing the technology could potentially be used to warp people's opinions.

Young Americans are also more skeptical of AI than older generations. A Pew Research Center survey published in June found that 48% of adults ages 18 to 29 expect AI to have a negative impact on society over the next two decades, compared with 37% of those 50 and older. Younger adults were also more likely to worry that AI could negatively affect their own lives.

Baker also expressed concerns over the algorithms created by social media companies.

"You are given by Instagram — all these big platforms — your algorithm, your viewings, and you’re leaned towards, and you push towards a certain agenda or you’re pushed towards a certain idea," Baker said, arguing this is creating staunch political divides with Americans.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

articles.title: Is your Social Security number on the dark web?

If you suspect your Social Security number is on the dark web, the right move is not to panic. It is to act quickly, methodically and in the right order.

A leaked Social Security number can be used in ways that go far beyond one fraudulent credit card charge. Criminals may try to open new credit accounts, file fake tax returns, hijack benefits or combine your SSN with other stolen details to impersonate you. The good news is that you can take concrete steps to check for signs of exposure and reduce the damage if your information has already been compromised.

This guide walks through how to check whether your SSN may be exposed, what to do next and how ongoing monitoring can help you catch problems earlier.

Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats

New! Join us on Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.

Check account alerts, credit reports and financial activity for signs that someone may be using your personal information. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Not directly in most cases. Rather than trying to search the dark web yourself, it is safer to rely on breach notices, account alerts, credit reports and reputable dark web monitoring tools. In real life, SSN exposure usually shows up first through warning signs like a breach notice, a strange credit inquiry or suspicious account activity.

Some warning signs are obvious, and others are easy to dismiss until they pile up.

None of these signs proves your SSN is being sold on the dark web. However, they may indicate identity exposure that needs immediate attention.

IS ID.ME SAFE TO USE? WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

A leaked Social Security number can be difficult to recover, so freezing your credit and monitoring for fraud are critical. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

If a company says your personal information was exposed, do not ignore it. Read the notice closely to see what data may have been involved, note the dates and save a copy for your records.

A dark web monitoring or exposure scan service can help you check whether your information appears in known breach data without trying to search hidden sites yourself. Some credit monitoring services offer a free scan and include dark web monitoring.

Look across all three credit bureaus for unfamiliar hard inquiries, new accounts, wrong addresses or collections that are not yours. Fraud often appears here before you see bigger damage.

Check bank accounts, credit cards, payment apps, buy-now-pay-later services and retirement accounts for anything unusual. Turn on alerts for big purchases, password changes and profile updates if you have not already.

Review financial documents carefully and keep records of unfamiliar accounts, inquiries and transactions you may need to dispute. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

If you think your SSN is already exposed, move through these steps as quickly as possible.

A credit freeze is one of the strongest steps you can take. It makes it much harder for someone to open new credit in your name because lenders generally cannot access your credit file while it is frozen. If you are not actively applying for credit, freezing your file at all three bureaus is usually the safest default.

A fraud alert tells lenders to take extra steps to verify identity before opening new accounts. It is not as strong as a freeze, but it can still be a useful layer of protection.

Start with your primary email account, then update passwords for banking, retirement, shopping, payment and healthcare logins. Use a reputable password manager to create and securely store strong, unique passwords for every account. Turn on multifactor authentication wherever possible. This matters because many identity theft cases begin with account takeover, not only new account fraud.

If your SSN is compromised, watch for signs of tax fraud or benefits misuse. Unexpected mail, rejected tax filings or notices about claims or services you did not request should be investigated immediately.

Keep records of breach notices, account alerts, calls with banks, dispute reference numbers and dates. If fraud appears later, that paper trail can save time and reduce stress.

If someone has already used your information, report it to the relevant financial institution right away and file an identity theft report through the proper government channels. That documentation can help when disputing fraudulent accounts and charges.

Usually, no. Once sensitive data is leaked, copied, sold and reposted, it is rarely possible to claw it back completely. That is why the smartest response is not to focus on "getting it removed" from criminal spaces. It is to reduce how useful that information is to criminals. In practice, that means freezing credit, tightening account security, removing extra personal information from public-facing sources when possible and keeping ongoing watch for fraud signals.

How identity monitoring can help without replacing the basics

An identity monitoring service can add another layer of protection after you complete the immediate cleanup steps. Depending on the service, it may monitor dark web sources, credit reports, financial accounts and changes to your personal information.

Some services also provide restoration specialists who can guide you through disputes and recovery if identity theft occurs. These tools may help you spot warning signs sooner, but they do not replace credit freezes, strong unique passwords, multifactor authentication and regular account reviews.

See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

If your Social Security number may be on the dark web, speed matters more than certainty. You do not need perfect proof before acting. Start with the signs you can verify: breach notices, account alerts, credit reports and unusual activity across your financial life. Lock down what you can, freeze your credit, strengthen account security and keep monitoring. And if you want ongoing help after the first round of cleanup, an identity theft protection service can add another layer through dark web monitoring, data broker removal, financial alerts and restoration support when identity issues get messy.

articles.title: UAE extradites alleged international crime boss Daniel Kinahan to Ireland
articles.excerpt: Alleged Irish cartel boss Daniel Kinahan has been charged in Dublin with directing a criminal organisation after the 49-year-old accused of running one of the world’s biggest drug and weapon smuggling...
articles.body_text:
Alleged Irish cartel boss Daniel Kinahan has been charged in Dublin with directing a criminal organisation after the 49-year-old accused of running one of the world’s biggest drug and weapon smuggling and money laundering organisations was extradited from the United Arab Emirates.

Kinahan appeared before the Special Criminal Court in Dublin late on Sunday after leaving Dubai aboard an Irish government jet earlier in the day.

Irish media reported that a major security operation was under way ahead of Kinahan’s arrival, involving armed police, the military and prison authorities.

After landing at a military base on the outskirts of Dublin, Kinahan was taken directly to court for a highly unusual Sunday night sitting.

The non-jury court, which hears cases involving terrorism and organised crime offences, was guarded by armed police during the brief hearing. Crowds gathered outside, some filming on their phones, as unmarked police vehicles sped away from the courthouse afterwards.

Kinahan, dressed in a black hoodie, black trousers and flip-flops, appeared before a panel of three judges without a lawyer present. He told the court he understood the charges and said he had been isolated in Dubai since Friday and had not had time to arrange legal representation.

One of the judges told Kinahan that any application for bail would have to be made through the High Court.

“I think we know I won’t be getting bail, but thank you so much for explaining,” Kinahan replied.

He was remanded in custody and later transferred to the high-security Portlaoise Prison, according to Irish broadcaster RTE.

Kinahan is due to appear before the court again, either in person or via video link, on October 5.

Kinahan’s extradition followed a final ruling by the Dubai Court of Cassation and was carried out under an extradition treaty between the UAE and Ireland, according to a joint statement by the justice ministers of both countries.

Kinahan was arrested in Dubai in April on an Irish warrant over alleged serious organised crime offences. He had lived openly in the emirate for about a decade.

An Irish government jet flew from Casement Aerodrome outside Dublin to Dubai on Saturday and departed the UAE on Sunday morning with Kinahan on board.

“Kinahan is considered one of the most wanted individuals in cases related to transnational organised crime,” Sunday’s joint Emirati-Irish statement said.

“He has been accused of leading an organised criminal group, murder and illicit trafficking of narcotics, pursuant to an official request submitted by the Irish authorities,” it added.

Ireland’s Justice Minister Jim O’Callaghan and his UAE counterpart, Abdullah bin Sultan bin Awad Al Nuaimi, said the extradition sent “a clear message” that those suspected of serious and organised crime would find “no safe haven from justice”.

In 2022, the United States named Kinahan as one of three leaders of the Kinahan Organised Crime Group (KOCG), which US and European authorities have linked to drug trafficking, money laundering, firearms trafficking and murder.

The group is alleged to have risen from the streets of Dublin to become one of the world’s largest international criminal organisations, with links to South American cartels, Chinese mafia groups and Hezbollah, among others.

US authorities imposed sanctions on Kinahan and other family members and offered a $5m reward for information leading to their arrests.

He is the second senior figure linked to the cartel to be extradited from Dubai.

Sean McGovern, described by an Irish judge as a senior lieutenant in the organisation, was extradited from the UAE following his arrest in 2024. He was sentenced in June to 24 years in prison after pleading guilty to directing organised crime and attempted murder.

The Kinahan group has been involved in a long-running and violent feud with the rival Dublin-based Hutch gang. Irish police estimate the organisation’s wealth at more than one billion euros ($1.15bn).

Kinahan has previously denied allegations that he is a crime boss. A lawyer representing him told the BBC in 2021 that he had no criminal record or convictions and that the allegations against him were false.

articles.title: 'Dallas' star Linda Gray reveals the bizarre way Larry Hagman avoided kissing scenes
articles.excerpt:
The actor, who was a sex symbol in the '80s, recalled playing the love interest of Brooke Shields and Linda Gray. Atkins now wants to work behind-the-scenes as a filmmaker.

The actress, who played Su...
articles.body_text:
The actor, who was a sex symbol in the '80s, recalled playing the love interest of Brooke Shields and Linda Gray. Atkins now wants to work behind-the-scenes as a filmmaker.

The actress, who played Sue Ellen Ewing, the glamorous, famously troubled wife of villain J.R. Ewing on "Dallas," is teaming up with Julien's Auctions for "Ladies of the '80s," which goes live Aug. 12.

The sale gives bidders the chance to own costumes, props, personal archives and other rare memorabilia from some of the decade's most beloved television stars. It features two of Gray's original "Dallas" scripts from the episodes surrounding the infamous "Who Shot J.R.?" saga.

ANN-MARGRET, 85, REVEALS THE HABIT THAT KEEPS HER FEELING FOREVER YOUNG

"Dallas" aired from April 2, 1978, to May 3, 1991. At its peak in the 1980s, it was one of the biggest shows on television, (CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images)

Ahead of the auction, Gray looked back on her "Dallas" years, including the less-than-romantic kissing scenes she shared with her on-screen husband, Larry Hagman, who died in 2012 at 81.

"The first time we kissed, he had a mouthful of peanut butter," the actress told Fox News Digital. "I thought, 'Oh no.' And I had to keep going with this kiss. The camera didn't know what was going on. But here I was, kissing him with peanut butter. I almost killed him. I was like, 'You are so bad and very inappropriate, Larry.' And he didn't care. He just kept laughing. He thought that was funny."

Linda Gray told Fox News Digital that Larry Hagman wasn't a fan of filming kissing scenes. He'd often pull silly pranks to ease the awkwardness and keep everyone laughing. (CBS/Getty Images)

"And then it was onions," said the 85-year-old. "It was kissing him with peanut butter, onions, whatever he could find in a jar. That wasn't some romantic thing. On camera, it looked pretty good, but that was not my reality."

WATCH: CHRISTOPHER ATKINS LOOKS BACK AT ‘THE BLUE LAGOON’ AND ‘DALLAS’

Gray later discovered that Hagman wasn't a fan of on-screen kisses. Rather than endure the awkward moments, he turned them into practical jokes.

Larry Hagman died on Nov. 23, 2012, at the age of 81 in Dallas. (Gregg DeGuire/WireImage)

"He had told me quite honestly that he didn't like kissing scenes," said Gray. "And I thought, 'Well, we're going to be kissing a lot!' So when there was a kissing scene, Larry cringed, just cringed. He did not like it. But I think the pranks, psychologically, were his way of getting over the anxiety of having to kiss me on camera."

The "Dallas" set was notorious for its practical jokes, and everyone got caught in the crossfire.

Linda Gray (right, seen here with Larry Hagman) is offering treasures from her personal collection in Julien's Auctions' "Ladies of the '80s," featuring screen-used scripts, director's clapperboards, cast photos, awards, and more from her iconic career. Bidding is open now, with the live online auction taking place on Aug. 12, 2026. (Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images)

"It was a daily prank, if you can imagine," said Gray. "And you never knew who it was going to come from. But it was mainly Larry. Larry was the prankster. I remember there was one episode where Sue Ellen was in the hospital. I was attached to all kinds of tubes and things on my wrists, arms and nose — all this hospital stuff. Larry came in, and he was supposed to talk to Sue Ellen. And Sue Ellen was out of it. She wasn't speaking, which was great for me."

Linda Gray's personalized director's chair, used while directing episodes of "Dallas," is estimated to sell for $800–$1,200. (Julien's Auctions)

"So Larry sits beside my bed and starts telling Sue Ellen how much he loves her," she shared. "Very soap opera dialogue. He's going, 'Oh, Sue Ellen!' and I'm lying there with my eyes closed, my eyes rolling underneath my eyelids. Then the door opens again. I thought, 'Who is in this scene that I didn't know about?' It's Patrick Duffy. He stands next to Larry and says, 'I did not know this was in the scene. Would it help if we sang that old song we used to sing?' Larry says, 'Yes.' And then the two of them started singing this very inappropriate song. I can't even repeat the words to you."

An original drawing created by Tony Bennett for Linda Gray is estimated to sell for $300–$500. (Julien's Auctions)

"I just burst out laughing," she continued. "The tube came flying out of my nose. I was totally blindsided. I thought I had ruined the scene, but everyone just started laughing hysterically. That was just how it was every day."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

From left: Patrick Duffy, Linda Gray and Larry Hagman pose during the 18th annual Screen Actors Guild Awards broadcast at The Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles on Jan. 29, 2012. (Kevin Mazur/WireImage)

Hagman's practical jokes were one thing. Facing Texas women in real life was another altogether.

"I was at a Dallas hotel for an event," she recalled. "I went to the ladies' room to put on lipstick. Next to me was this lovely lady with a little Judith Leiber bag. She opened it to put on her lipstick. I glanced down, and there was a gun in her purse. That was all she had in it: a gun and lipstick. I thought, 'Oh boy, I'm in Texas. Who carries a gun around?' So I said, 'Excuse me, is that a gun?' Really stupid, I know. She said, 'Of course, darling. This is Texas!'"

From left: Charlene Tilton, Linda Gray, Larry Hagman, Patrick Duffy and Sheree J. Wilson won the TV Land Pop Culture Award for "Dallas." An award presented to Gray is estimated to sell for $500–$700. (L. Cohen/WireImage)

"I had never been to Dallas in my life," she reflected. "I remember landing in Texas. Everything was beige and flat. I thought, 'I've got to know the women here.' And where do the wealthy women of Texas go? Neiman Marcus, of course, to get their hair done. And that's what I did. I remember seeing big, big hair. It was unlike anything I saw in California. These women dressed a certain way. Their shoes were always very stylish. And apparently, they carried guns in their tiny evening bags."

In "Dallas," Linda Gray starred as Sue Ellen Ewing, the glamorous, resilient and unforgettable wife of J.R. Ewing (Larry Hagman) on the hit CBS series Dallas. (CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images)

Gray got a crash course in Texas high society over one unforgettable lunch.

"One woman invited me to lunch, and she wore a special outfit just for it," said Gray. "I didn't have any friends in California who would do that. We're having lunch, and then she looks at her watch. She says, 'Oh, I'm so sorry. I have to go home. I have to fluff and fold.' I'm thinking, 'She has to do laundry? Fluff her towels and fold them?' No. She had to fluff her hair, put on her makeup and turn into the woman her husband expected."

Two of Linda Gray's original *Dallas* scripts from the iconic "Who Shot J.R.?" storyline are estimated to sell for $300–$500. (Julien's Auctions)

If learning Texas customs was intimidating, keeping the show's biggest twist under wraps was downright terrifying.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Linda Gray arrives at the Larry Hagman and Linda Gray VIP Preview Party at Julien's Auction on June 1, 2011, in Beverly Hills. (Tibrina Hobson/WireImage)

The "Dallas" Season 3 finale ended with one of television's most famous cliffhangers: J.R. was shot by an unseen gunman, leaving viewers to wait eight months to learn not only who pulled the trigger but whether he survived.

Gray recalled that the writers were searching for a jaw-dropping way to end the season with a bang when one of them blurted out, "Let's just shoot the bastard." After a brief silence, everyone agreed: "What a great idea. We'll shoot him."

Linda Gray is seen here as Sue Ellen Ewing in a scene from "Dallas." The Ewing family returned to primetime in 2012 when "Dallas" was revived on TNT. After three seasons, the reboot concluded in 2014. (United Archives via Getty Images)

As "Who Shot J.R.?" became a worldwide obsession, Gray found herself fielding the question everywhere she went, including during an interview with David Hartman.

In the "Dallas" Season 3 finale, "A House Divided," J.R. Ewing (Larry Hagman) is gunned down by a mysterious assailant, setting off the legendary "Who Shot J.R.?" cliffhanger. The mystery captivated millions of viewers and became one of the biggest pop culture moments in television history. (© Lorimar Film Entertainment/Courtesy Everett Collection)

"I was not very smart, but I said, 'Yes, I do,'" Gray recalled when asked whether she knew the shooter's identity. "'I know, and one of my children knows.' After that, I thought, 'Oh my God, I just opened Pandora's box. I thought everyone was going to call my house and one of my kids would answer the phone and reveal who it was. And then it would be all over.'"

The moment the interview ended, Gray said she rushed to call home.

Linda Gray's 1986 megaphone, signed by the cast and crew of Dallas, is estimated to sell for $600–$800. (Julien's Auctions)

"I remember telling my kids, 'Somebody's going to call you, and they're going to ask you who shot J.R. You cannot answer.' My heart was racing because it all could have been ruined. But nobody called, thank God."

Linda Gray still loves reminiscing about her years as Sue Ellen Ewing. Now, she's passing along some of those memories through Julien's Auctions' "Ladies of the '80s," where fans can discover memorabilia from "Dallas" and celebrate one of television's most decadent decades. (Paul Archuleta/Getty Images)

Decades after "Dallas" first captivated audiences, Gray said the memories were meant to be shared.

"I don't look at it as letting these items go," she said about the auction. "I look at it as sharing. There are a lot of people who still feel very connected with the show. And it feels good to share."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Florida AG James Uthmeier says Fauci probe could uncover grounds for criminal liability despite pardon
articles.excerpt: COVID-19 pandemic policies undergo intense scrutiny as Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier investigates Dr. Anthony Fauci's official role. Uthmeier outlines state-level legal challenges following ...
articles.body_text:
COVID-19 pandemic policies undergo intense scrutiny as Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier investigates Dr. Anthony Fauci's official role. Uthmeier outlines state-level legal challenges following Fauci's refusal to answer Senate questions, noting he pleaded the Fifth 111 times. Multiple states now coordinate actions to demand accountability regarding federal healthcare decisions and mandates.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said on "Sunday Morning Futures" that his office is examining potential claims ranging from fraud and deceptive trade practices to public nuisance as part of its investigation into Dr. Anthony Fauci, adding that the probe could uncover grounds for criminal liability.

Uthmeier said Florida investigators plan to use "every tool under Florida law" as they examine whether Fauci engaged in any self-dealing or profited from COVID-era policies.

Former NIH Director Anthony Fauci listens during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on July 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Fauci declined to answer questions, asserting his Fifth Amendment right. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

FAUCI HELD IN CONTEMPT AS COVID CELLPHONE LANDS IN HANDS OF SENATE INVESTIGATORS

Asked whether he believes Fauci committed a crime, the attorney general said, "I can't say that right now."

"We follow rules of procedure and evidence. I mean, I could say generally, I think what he did to the American people was horrific. People died because of him. People got hurt because of him. People couldn't be there for the birth of their first child or the loss of a loved one because of him," he added.

"If he is making money on the side while perpetrating this fraud, there could very well be criminal liability," he said. "But we're going to start with civil, criminal, everything from public nuisance to deceptive trade, to fraud. We're going to look at every aspect of Florida law and do everything in our power to seek truth and accountability."

James Uthmeier spoke at the National Conservative Convention on Sept. 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Dominic Gwinn/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

Uthmeier's investigation is ongoing. Criminal wrongdoing has not been established at this time.

Former President Joe Biden issued Fauci, who served as the principal architect for the government's COVID-19 guidelines, a full and unconditional pardon for all actions taken between Jan. 1, 2014, and Jan. 19, 2025. This pardon does not protect Fauci from prosecution under state law, however.

Uthmeier's comments follow Fauci's congressional hearing, during which he declined to answer questions, instead invoking the Fifth Amendment, more than 100 times.

CAN FAUCI HIDE BEHIND THE FIFTH? GAME-CHANGING BIDEN PARDON MAY NOT PROVIDE COMPLETE COVER, EXPERTS SAY

Dr. Anthony Fauci, the top U.S. infectious disease expert, wears a face mask as he arrives for the the White House COVID-19 Response Team's regular call with the National Governors Association in the South Court Auditorium in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building on the White House Campus, Monday, Dec. 27, 2021, in Washington. (AP Photo/Carolyn Kaster)

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted on sharp party lines to charge the former chief medical advisor to the president with contempt after he refused to answer questions from both sides of the aisle over fear of self-incrimination.

"I don't know why you need a pardon if you didn't do anything wrong," Uthmeier said.

"Dr. Fauci clearly doesn't want to answer questions, but the American people still have a lot of questions, especially Floridians."

Fox News Digital reached out to Dr. Fauci but did not immediately receive a response.

Fox News Digital's Elaine Mallon, Alex Miller and Elizabeth Elkind contributed to this report.

Max Bacall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital covering media, culture and comedy.

articles.title: Is cyberbullying hiding in your child's group chat?
articles.excerpt: Child and adolescent family therapist Darby Fox explains how teens view social media. New research indicates that while some find platforms like Snapchat beneficial for friendships, most encounter onl...
articles.body_text:
Child and adolescent family therapist Darby Fox explains how teens view social media. New research indicates that while some find platforms like Snapchat beneficial for friendships, most encounter online harassment or bullying on TikTok, Instagram, and other platforms. Fox advises parents to implement strict monitoring and maintain open dialogue to protect their children's mental well-being.

"It was only a joke." Those five words can stop an important conversation before it begins. Maybe your child or grandchild posted a rude comment in a group chat. Another kid added an embarrassing picture. Soon, classmates were sharing it and piling on with laughing reactions.

To the children taking part, it may feel like ordinary online drama. To the child being targeted, every notification can feel like another person joining the attack. The warning signs of cyberbullying are not always obvious. Some children hide what they are experiencing. Others take part without realizing their behavior has crossed a line.

That is why cybersecurity education needs to go beyond strong passwords, antivirus software and password managers. Those protections remain essential. However, children also need guidance about empathy, privacy and the consequences of what they post. Parents play a central role. Grandparents can also become trusted listeners, especially when a child feels nervous about telling Mom or Dad. Share this article with the adults in your family. Then use it to start a conversation before a child needs help.
