articles.body_text:
Central Gaza – Sahar al-Bardini prepares breakfast for her three children in a tent at the al-Zawaida camp in central Gaza. She watches them eat but is already worried about finding their next meal.

The 35-year-old is the sole breadwinner for six-year-old Omar, four-year-old Sama and Mahmoud aged three since her husband was killed in Israeli shelling of northern Gaza three years ago.

Like many families in Gaza, they are struggling with soaring food prices, largely due to Israel’s long-running siege, with concerns that the population could be plunged into famine again.

During last year’s famine, the whole family – Omar and Sama in particular – suffered from a lack of food and vital nutrients. Eggs and vegetables were difficult to find in markets and when available, almost impossible to afford.

Even though the family can eat more regularly today, they still only have one meal a day. Omar and Sama’s bodies are still counting the cost of the months of famine between August and December 2025.

“Omar and Sama became very weak during the famine and lost a lot of weight. Even after food became more available, it took them around six months to gradually regain their health and weight,” she told Al Jazeera.

“My biggest fear is that my children will become weak again. I want to see them healthy, but the food they need isn’t easy for me to provide every day.”

Their plight comes as the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned last week that Gaza faces a severe food emergency that could develop into another famine.

Justin Brady, head of OCHA in Palestine, warned that 67 percent of Gaza’s population was suffering from food insecurity. More than 200,000 people – around 10 percent of Gaza’s population – were living in conditions that usually precede a formal famine declaration by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification.

In the area where Sahar lives, community kitchens have become the main source of food for many families. The meals they serve – mostly rice and other basic ingredients, but very rarely meat – are enough to stave off starvation, but children still lack essential nutrients and protein that are essential for growth.

“The meal fills their stomachs, but it doesn’t contain everything a child’s body needs to be properly nourished and regain strength,” Sahar said. “The children need a more varied diet – they need eggs, vegetables, fruit, meat and other things. I try to provide whatever I can but my means are limited.”

With little money, Sahar makes the most of any food vouchers or assistance she receives, but it is never enough. That means prioritising the family’s most urgent needs which begin with food, followed by clothes, medicine and then other basic necessities for the youngsters.

“When I receive food vouchers, I try to make the most of them. Everything is expensive, and I’m carrying the responsibility of three children on my own,” she said.

Shimaa, 25, was unable to find enough milk for her two-year-old daughter, Selina, during the last famine, so was forced to find any alternative to fill her stomach.

“I tried to feed her whatever I had. Sometimes I gave her lentils instead of milk because I didn’t have milk to give her,” she told Al Jazeera. “I work day and night so I can provide her with food and everything she needs – everything I do is so I can see her in better health.”

Still, the family struggle to afford enough money for food and so Selina remains weak and severely malnourished.

“Even after the famine eased, its effects didn’t go away for my daughter,” Shimaa said. “I’m worried about her and I’m trying to do everything I can to help her get better.”

Nutrition specialist, Dr Ghada Jibril, said the current food crisis has forced parents to rely on rice and lentils to feed their infants. While they contain some nutrients, it means a gap in kid’s diets, particularly for those who starved during the famine.

“A child who has experienced severe malnutrition needs a period of regular nutrition and follow-up care to regain their weight and resume healthy growth,” Jibril said.

“The end of acute hunger does not mean that the effects of malnutrition disappear immediately. Children need a varied diet, not simply enough food to fill their stomachs – protein, iron, vitamins and minerals are essential for growth, brain development and a strong immune system. Recovering from malnutrition takes time, appropriate food and follow-up care.”

articles.title: Fever coach Stephanie White defends DiJonai Carrington after flagrant foul ejection on her own player
articles.excerpt: Michele Tafoya joins the program and calls Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham a HERO for standing up for women's sports despite intense backlash from Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve, Seattle Storm...
articles.body_text:
Michele Tafoya joins the program and calls Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham a HERO for standing up for women's sports despite intense backlash from Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve, Seattle Storm leadership, and activist critics.

Sophie Cunningham took a forearm to the head Saturday night. And for some inexplicable reason, her own coach is defending the player who delivered it.

Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White raised eyebrows after Saturday's 90-86 win over the Chicago Sky when she pushed back on Cunningham's assertion that DiJonai Carrington intentionally leveled her during a first-quarter drive to the basket.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Carrington chased Cunningham down from behind as the Fever guard went up for a layup and caught her across the head and neck area, sending Cunningham crashing to the floor. Officials reviewed the play, upgraded it to a Flagrant 2 and ejected Carrington.

Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington commits a flagrant 2 foul against Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham. (Kamil Krzaczynski/Imagn Images)

Cunningham had no trouble saying exactly what she thought happened.

"Clearly, I think it was like unnecessary. I've never really spoken to her and have no beef with her, but I guess she has some pent up stuff. So get your s— off. That's fine. I can take it ... Yeah, it's intentional," Cunningham said after the game.

"Yeah, I mean, look, it was a hard foul. I don't think that DiJonai intentionally came out to get her across the neck like she did. But it did happen and I thought it was the right call," White said.

Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever talks with head coach Stephanie White during the first half against the Chicago Sky at the United Center on July 27, 2025, in Chicago, Ill. (Michael Reaves/Getty Images)

"But you know, one of the things about Nay is that she's gonna play her butt off, man. She's gonna compete. Nobody's gonna go walking in for a layup. And so, I don't oppose the hard foul. But I also don't think that she intentionally went for the neck."

That's an awfully generous interpretation of the play that got Carrington thrown out of the game.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT AGAINST DIJONAI CARRINGTON AFTER FLAGRANT FOUL AND 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST

Maybe White was simply trying to keep an already-heated situation from escalating. Coaches don't necessarily need to accuse opposing players of intentionally trying to hurt their athletes every time there's a nasty foul.

Still, there's a difference between de-escalating and going out of your way to explain away the actions of the player who just blasted one of your own.

Indiana Fever head coach Stephanie White talks to a referee on the sideline during the second half against the Portland Fire. (Ali Gradischer/Getty Images)

White coached Carrington for two seasons with the Connecticut Sun in 2023 and 2024 before returning to Indiana. So White knows Carrington well, perhaps well enough to feel confident speaking to her intentions.

But Cunningham is the player in White's locker room now.

And Cunningham clearly didn't believe what happened was merely a routine example of an aggressive defender refusing to surrender an easy basket.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"I don't even know her. She wasn't even on the team last year when all that was going on," Cunningham said. "But I do think when people play the Fever, we're nationally televised, there's a lot of eyes on us and people just want attention. And that's her just trying to get attention."

Carrington certainly didn't do much afterward to cool things down herself.

Following her ejection, she posted "White Privilege" on Threads and tagged the Indiana Fever. She did not explain whether the message was directed at Cunningham, the officials or the Fever organization.

Cunningham dismissed the suggestion that Carrington's ejection had anything to do with race.

"I think the league is taking care of that. This has nothing to do with race. Last year, I did the same thing and I got kicked out. And I deserved to be kicked out," Cunningham said. "There's no reason even to play that card."

Sophie Cunningham confronts DiJonai Carrington after the latter committed a hard foul that led to her being ejected in the first quarter of Saturday's game between the Indiana Fever and the Chicago Sky. (Kamil Krzaczynski/Imagn Images)

White declined to comment on Carrington's social media post.

Of course, White didn't have to declare her former player an evil villain.

But considering everything that happened, Cunningham probably could have used a little more unequivocal support from the coach standing on her own sideline.

articles.title: Sports Illustrated edits Sophie Cunningham 'karma' headline after creating social media firestorm
articles.excerpt:
Dan Dakich breaks down Megan Rapinoe's latest unhinged rant targeting Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham and OutKick legend Riley Gaines over their stand to protect women's sports.

The hard foul th...
articles.body_text:
Dan Dakich breaks down Megan Rapinoe's latest unhinged rant targeting Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham and OutKick legend Riley Gaines over their stand to protect women's sports.

The hard foul that left Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham with a bloody mouth against the Chicago Sky was a result of karma. At least, that was Sports Illustrated's initial reaction to Chicago's DiJonai Carrington clotheslining Cunningham during a layup attempt.

With two minutes remaining in the first quarter of the Fever's eventual 90-86 win on Saturday night, Carrington delivered a very hard foul on Cunningham underneath the basket. The foul was upgraded to a Flagrant 2, resulting in Carrington's ejection from the contest.

After seeing Carrington swipe her forearm across Cunningham's face at full speed in what certainly did not appear to be an attempt at the basketball, Sports Illustrated opted to publish a story about the moment titled "Sophie Cunningham Got a Bitter Taste of Karma After Drawing Flagrant Foul in Fever-Sky."

Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington commits a flagrant 2 foul against Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham. (Kamil Krzaczynski/Imagn Images)

The title of the story sparked immediate and intense reaction across social media as Cunningham has dominated headlines for weeks after sharing her opinion that transgender athletes should not be allowed to play in women's sports.

Citing "karma" as the reason behind Cunningham taking a hard foul while she's received constant backlash for stating that men do not belong in women's sports came across, to many, as a pointed effort from Sports Illustrated.

The story, written by breaking news writer Kristen Wong, was later updated with the following title: "Sophie Cunningham's Enforcer Role Gets Reversed Onto Her With Hard Foul in Fever-Sky."

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham fights with Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington after being Carrington fouled Cunningham with a hit to the Fever guard's head. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

OutKick has reached out to Sports Illustrated requesting comment about the title change of the story.

The Sports Illustrated story claimed that the "karma" Cunningham received on the play stemmed from a hard foul she committed during the 2025 WNBA season, in which she wrapped her arms around Jacy Sheldon while she was attempting a layup. Sheldon played for the Connecticut Sun last season, but is now a member of the Sky.

Cunningham was assessed a Flagrant 2 for her foul on Sheldon and was ejected from the game. When asked about being on the receiving end of Carrington's hard foul and the ejection on Saturday, Cunningham admitted she deserved to be ejected for her foul on Sheldon last season.

"Last year I did the same thing, and I got kicked out, as I deserved to be kicked out. There’s no reason to even play that card," Cunningham told the media.

That "card" Cunningham referred to is in reaction to Carrington posting the words "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagging the Fever on her Instagram Threads account shortly after being ejected from Saturday's contest.

Sophie Cunningham #8 of the Indiana Fever looks on against the Minnesota Lynx in the fourth quarter at Target Center on Aug. 2, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The Lynx defeated the Fever 108-100. (David Berding/Getty Images)

"We saw it," Cunningham said, when asked about Carrington's post. "I think the league is taking care of that. I mean, this has nothing to do with race."

WNBA FACES DISCIPLINE DILEMMA AFTER CARRINGTON'S 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST TARGETING INDIANA FEVER

Indiana head coach Stephanie White actually went on to defend Carrington during the post-game press conference, but did agree the flagrant foul and ejection were the correct calls.

"Yeah, I mean, look, it was a hard foul. I don't think that DiJonai intentionally came out to get her across the neck like she did. But it did happen and I thought it was the right call. But you know, one of the things about Nay is that she's gonna play her butt off, man. She's gonna compete. Nobody's gonna go walking in for a layup. And so, I don't oppose the hard foul. But I also don't think that she intentionally went for the neck," White said.

White declined to comment on Carrington's "white privilege" post.

articles.title: Taylor Swift songs removed from Trump and White House’s social media posts
articles.excerpt:
Rage-baiting efforts of Trump accounts silenced after posts such as a video linking her Red album to Republicans

Some of Taylor Swift’s songs have been removed from videos posted on social media by D...
articles.body_text:
Rage-baiting efforts of Trump accounts silenced after posts such as a video linking her Red album to Republicans

Some of Taylor Swift’s songs have been removed from videos posted on social media by Donald Trump’s campaign and the White House, silencing efforts to mock the pop star.

A video posted 3 August featuring the US president and the first lady, Melania Trump, watching fireworks was posted this month on TikTok with Swift’s song August.

“I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august,” the accompanying text states.

Trump’s campaign later published another post, needling Swift over the title of her 2012 album, Red. “Did you know Taylor Swift wrote a whole album about the color of the Republican party?” it said, suggesting parody track titles.

Trump-related social media accounts have used Swift’s music in other campaign videos, too, but several of those also no longer have sound.

As the text with the August video suggests, Trump’s social media accounts have used pop stars’ songs as rage bait. They have featured music from artists including Ariana Grande, Katy Perry, Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo and Kenny Loggins, all of whom publicly objected to the use of their music.

“Please do not use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense,” Grande posted after the White House posted her music over a montage of ICE agents handcuffing and detaining people.

When Trump’s White House used one of Carpenter’s songs to soundtrack a video of immigration raids in 2025, the singer wrote: “this video is evil and disgusting. Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.”

In this latest case, Swift has not commented.

Trump had previously attacked Swift, who endorsed then Democratic vice-president Kamala Harris during the 2024 election. “I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!” Trump declared at the time.

Last year he ​wrote: “Has anyone noticed that, since I said ‘I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT,’ she’s no longer ‘HOT?’”

Swift’s Eras tour was the the highest-grossing tour of all time, according to Pollstar, generating about $2.2bn worldwide. Her album The Life of a Showgirl became the most pre-saved album ever on Spotify ahead of its October 2025 release.

articles.title: Chinese EV sales surge to new high in Europe putting tariffs under scrutiny
articles.excerpt:
Imports this year now account for 14% of the market amid claims vehicles are being dumped in the EU and UK

Chinese electric car sales have risen across Europe to a record high driven by strong demand...
articles.body_text:
Imports this year now account for 14% of the market amid claims vehicles are being dumped in the EU and UK

Chinese electric car sales have risen across Europe to a record high driven by strong demand and low tariffs in the UK and a surge in buyers in Italy.

Against a backdrop of claims that Chinese carmakers are “dumping” state-subsidised vehicles in the EU and UK to gain market share, the figures will give impetus to calls for quotas and higher tariffs to protect European manufacturers.

The share of electric cars sold by Chinese brands rose to 14.2% across western European markets – or one in every seven battery electric vehicles (BEVs) – in the first five months of this year, according to Schmidt Automotive Research. The 171,800 sales represented an increase in market share of nearly five percentage points versus the same period in 2025.

Brands including BYD, Chery, SAIC and Xpeng have targeted Europe for exports, as the Chinese industry seeks to dominate the global electric vehicle market. This has put traditional European manufacturers under intense pressure when tougher emissions rules are forcing them to increase their own BEV sales.

The increase in European sales comes despite EU tariffs of up to 35.3% for electric cars made by some Chinese manufacturers, on top of the standard 10% import duty.

The UK is the largest European market for Chinese cars because the government has declined to follow the EU’s lead in imposing extra levies. The UK accounted for a quarter of Chinese BEV sales across the 18 biggest Western European markets.

Although Italy accounted for a fifth of the total, Schmidt said this was an “anomaly”. One manufacturer, Leapmotor, sent thousands of its cheap T03 electric cars into the country to take advantage of purchase subsidies from the government. The subsidies meant that the T03 was as cheap as €5,000 at one point – far below even the most keenly priced models sold by rivals.

Chinese manufacturers have sold more than 120 different models in Europe this year – compared with about 100 from European brands.

However, Matthias Schmidt, the founder of Schmidt research, said China’s share of the BEV market may have peaked, in part because they have shifted some of their focus to plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. PHEVs, which combine a polluting petrol engine with a smaller battery, are not yet subject to EU tariffs.

“I think they are hitting a wall when it comes to pure electric models,” said Schmidt. “They will prioritise PHEVs over the next 12 months given hybrids are omitted from extra tariffs placed on BEVs only. With that loophole set to close in the next 12 months, they will aim to maximise that gap in the door for as long as possible.

“Given shipping capacity remains limited, more PHEVs means fewer BEVs, which have likely peaked for now. BEVs will take priority again once local EU production comes online.”

Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, last month called for that to change. Blume said European PHEVs were uncompetitive against Chinese equivalents. The German newspaper Handelsblatt has reported that the EU is considering extending the levies to PHEVs.

The figures also showed a rebound in sales for Tesla across Europe. The US carmaker suffered a steep decline in sales last year amid a backlash against chief executive Elon Musk’s alliance with Donald Trump and European far-right political parties.

Tesla sales rose by 60% year-on-year, helped by an increase in demand for cheaper versions of its Model 3 and Model Y. The Model Y was the bestselling individual model across Europe during the period.

articles.title: Sweet, soft and strong: TikTok turns Japanese milk bread into latest UK food craze
articles.excerpt:
Natto toast, fresh fruit sandwiches and soufflé pancakes all part of growing interest in east Asian cuisine

Golden brown and glistening with melted butter, a tray of freshly baked bread fills the scr...
articles.body_text:
Natto toast, fresh fruit sandwiches and soufflé pancakes all part of growing interest in east Asian cuisine

Golden brown and glistening with melted butter, a tray of freshly baked bread fills the screen in a TikTok video. The camera lingers on the glossy tops before one bun is gently pulled apart, revealing a cloud-soft interior.

The clip is one of countless videos of Japanese milk buns that have racked up millions of views and thousands of comments and shares, helping to propel the pillowy rolls into UK supermarkets.

Japanese milk bread (shokupan) and buns are having a viral moment. The lightly sweet, fine-crumbed yeast breads trace their roots to a bakery tradition introduced to Japan through western contact, but modern Japanese milk bread evolved during the 20th century as bakers adapted European techniques to local tastes.

They are far from the only Japanese food to find global fame on social media. Japan’s deep-fried sandwiches have inspired queues around the block, while fluffy soufflé pancakes, delicate crepes and Japan’s distinctive fruit sando – fresh fruit and cream layered between slices of soft milk bread – have all found devoted followings online and beyond.

The growing appetite for Japanese cuisine is being reflected in supermarkets. Waitrose says sales of Miso Tasty ramen paste are up 41% compared with last year, while sales of Miso Tasty soup paste have increased by 22%.

But it is the rise of milk bread that Emilie Wolfman, the world foods product developer at Waitrose, said was “one of the most exciting food trends we’ve seen cross over from social media into mainstream kitchens”. Searches for “Japanese milk buns” on Waitrose’s website have risen by 617% over the past month, while sales are up 27% over the same period.

As well as their viral success online, Wolfman attributes the growing popularity of milk buns to “London’s cult burger restaurants and east Asian bakeries”.

Black Bear Burger, a London-based chain, has built a loyal following by serving its smash burgers and crispy fried chicken in soft milk buns. In London’s Chinatown, Bun House showcases Cantonese-style baked milk buns with both savoury and sweet fillings.

Outside the capital, Tomás Gormley, the chef-patron of Scottish fine dining restaurant Cardinal, said it opened with milk buns on the menu. “My first pastry chef, Mia, developed an incredible recipe that we still use today. We switch to sourdough every now and then to keep things interesting but always seem to end up back at the milk buns,” he said.

Gormley believes part of the appeal to chefs is how quickly and easily they can be made. “I have all the time in the world for slow-fermented sourdoughs and overnight focaccias, but logistically a bread you can bash out in a couple of hours is a winner in the kitchen,” he said. “It’s also usually less butter-heavy than the French equivalent, brioche, which helps with costs, but also with balancing a menu and how much a guest can really eat over the course of a tasting menu, in my case.”

Michael Booth, the author of Sushi and Beyond and The Meaning of Rice, said Japanese cuisine’s “huge focus on presentation, aesthetics” and social media were a perfect match, with the country having been ahead of the curve for at least a decade. “I can remember visiting a restaurant in Kyoto that was specifically tailored to presenting its food for social media,” he added.

Booth said he became “totally obsessed” with milk buns and Japanese baked goods when he first visited Japan in the 1990s. “They had long ago mastered that super-light crumb.”

The MasterChef winner and restaurateur Tim Anderson notes the huge variety of milk breads available in Japan, which range from mildly milky and sweet to those rich with eggs, butter, cream and honey that are more akin to brioche. “I think if British bakeries and supermarkets are trying to nail what makes milk bread special they should focus on the yudane and gluten development, which are what give milk bread its unique combination of strength and softness,” he added.

Anderson said he would recommend using it to make natto toast, which features fermented soya beans under a layer of crisp melted cheese. Failing that, it works well for an egg sandwich, or “pizza toast is fantastic”.

He added that in the US at the moment it was “peach and tomato season”, both of which would pair well with it. “A toasted nut butter and peach jam sandwich would be exquisite,” he said.

Use it with tomatoes in a bacon, lettuce and tomato sandwich with Kewpie mayo, thick-cut streaky bacon, iceberg lettuce and the best-quality tomatoes you can get,which should be “sliced thick, patted dry and pre-seasoned with sea salt and MSG [monosodium glutamate]”.

articles.title: ‘Watch The Odyssey for free online’: scam targets film fans with fake streaming sites
articles.excerpt:
Those tempted to access fake websites run risk of phishing scams and having computer infected with malware

The Odyssey is the hottest release this summer and you have been looking forward to seeing t...
articles.body_text:
Those tempted to access fake websites run risk of phishing scams and having computer infected with malware

The Odyssey is the hottest release this summer and you have been looking forward to seeing the much-acclaimed adaptation of Homer’s epic ancient Greek poem. But you have been unable to go to the cinema, so when you spot an ad to watch online, you jump at the chance.

There are positive reviews posted on the site so you decide to sign up. Although it asks for your bank details – which is unusual for a “free” trial – you are so eager to watch the blockbuster you input your details.

The site is a fraud, however, and there is no version of the film to watch. Reviews are fake and your bank details are in the hands of criminals.

You have fallen for a common type of scam that piggybacks on the release of a popular new film, TV show, or even a video game. By offering early, or easy access, fraudsters hope that victims will input their financial details.

However, anyone who is tempted has been warned they run the risk of having their computer infected with malware and becoming the target of future phishing scams.

BeStreamWise, a UK campaign body set up to alert the public to the dangers of illegal streaming, says people who submit their personal details are at risk of being targeted by fraudsters again, as well as having money taken from their accounts.

“Criminals are quick to exploit excitement around major releases, such as The Odyssey, using fake streaming links and websites to trick people into handing over personal information and exposing themselves to fraud,” it says.

A number of websites have been set up in different languages in an attempt to make the scam appear more convincing.

In some cases consumers are targeted via pop-up adverts; in others, the sites appear in search results, or are accessed via other websites. Reviews and ratings – all fake – are left by “users” who have supposedly watched the film on the site.

The cybersecurity company Kaspersky says some of the fake sites claim to offer dubbed versions of the film in the victim’s native language. The language is selected depending on the geolocation of the victim.

Typically, when the victim tries to play the film, they are asked to register to unlock the content, which they are told is free.

They are asked to submit their email address and full name. Later, they are asked to input their bank details, which the site claims are needed in order to activate the trial. The sites typically claim that those who sign up will be offered unlimited access to content over multiple devices.

Olga Altukhova, an analyst at Kaspersky, says consumers should be particularly wary if a film that has only just been released, and is still showing in cinemas, pops up on an unfamiliar platform.

“We strongly encourage people to access content only through official services to protect their personal data and avoid potential financial losses,” she says.

Among the risks from illegal streaming is the potential for malware to be downloaded on to a computer. This could result in a hacker gaining control of the device and accessing information remotely.

Kaspersky also advises that people closely check the URL to ensure it is a legitimate page.

If someone discovers that they have been defrauded, they are advised to immediately inform their bank and then change passwords on sites, and apps, such as their bank, investment and pension providers. Then turn on multi-factor authentication to bolster security.

In the UK, you should contact Action Fraud, the national fraud reporting centre.

articles.title: Costa Rican diplomat emerges as strong contender to be first female head of UN
articles.excerpt:
Rebeca Grynspan seen as continuity candidate with tacit support from current secretary general, António Guterres

A Costa Rican diplomat and former vice-president whose parents were refugees from the ...
articles.body_text:
Rebeca Grynspan seen as continuity candidate with tacit support from current secretary general, António Guterres

A Costa Rican diplomat and former vice-president whose parents were refugees from the Holocaust has become the surprise frontrunner to lead the United Nations as its first female secretary general.

Rebeca Grynspan, whose parents emigrated to Central America from Poland – and whose maternal grandparents were killed by the Nazis – is the current head of the UN conference on trade and development (UNCTAD), a body that has exhaustively tallied the economic damage inflicted by Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territories.

The current secretary general, António Guterres, will complete his second term on 31 December 2026 and under an informal system of regional rotation his successor is expected to come from Latin America.

In a secret first straw poll of the UN security council, the five permanent and 10 temporary members were asked to say whether they supported, objected to or were neutral about each of seven candidates.

Grynspan secured 10 “encourage” votes, four “no opinion” votes and one “discourage” vote. The identity of the discourage vote is not known, but the fact that she had only one objection places her in a strong opening position. The process is likely to conclude in October.

Grynspan’s closest rival is Carolyn Rodrigues-Burkett, Guyana’s former UN envoy, with nine encourages, two discourages and four no opinions. At the close of a Bloomberg-sponsored debate at the general assembly last month she secured 49% of the vote among those attending, with Grynspan second on 14%.

“Grynspan is seen by some as the continuity candidate, having the tacit support from Guterres,” said one western diplomat. “But the key is the source of the candidate’s discouragement votes: if [the votes] are coming from Russia, China or the US, there is a risk of deadlock.”

The election comes at a critical moment for the legitimacy of multilateralism, as the UN suffers 20% job cuts and the secretary general’s role as mediator is supplanted by other actors, leaving the world body as a largely ignored moral conscience, or as a venue in which all sides vent their well-rehearsed differences.

If elected, Grynspan would be the UN’s first Jewish secretary general. The UN has been criticised for overly focusing on Israel in its debates, but Grynspan has invoked her Jewish heritage to argue for the importance of ending conflict.

She told the UN general assembly: “Peace is what made it possible for my parents, two refugees from the second world war, to find respect and dignity in a small country, Costa Rica. I am the daughter of this peace, a demonstration of what peace makes possible.”

Her sister moved to Israel as a 17-year-old to study chemistry at the Hebrew University. As a result, her niece and nephew have completed compulsory service in the Israel Defense Forces.

Under her leadership, however, UNCTAD has factually and starkly documented the economic damage wrought by Israel’s long-term occupation of the Palestinian territories.

Its landmark February 2026 report found that “cumulatively, the Palestinian economy lost an estimated $212.2bn (in constant 2015 dollars) from 2000 to 2024. This partial, estimated lost potential, equivalent to nearly 20 times the entire Palestinian GDP of 2024, stems directly from Israeli occupation policies, restrictions, closures, and recurrent military operations.”

In November 2025 Grynspan pointed out that Gaza’s GDP per capita had plummeted to $161 per person per year, one of the most severe economic contractions in modern history.

Three other candidates, including Michelle Bachelet, have probably met with too much influential opposition to secure the job. Bachelet, the former president of Chile and a former UN human rights commissioner, faces opposition from the US government, which claims she was soft on China’s human rights record. But the Trump administration’s recent suggestion that the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, should get the job symbolises America’s drift away from the UN mainstream.

The secretary general is elected to serve an initial four-year term after the 193-strong general assembly is requested to endorse a single recommendation by the security council. A candidate needs nine positive votes and no veto by a security council member.

The new candidate must be elected by the end of the year, and there will be further meetings of the security council to test opinion.

articles.title: Russian family denied asylum in Finland fear reprisals for pro-Ukraine activism
articles.excerpt:
Nikita and Olga Belov say they will be persecuted on return to Moscow but are yet to convince Finnish authorities

A Russian family faces deportation from Finland after repeatedly being denied asylum ...
articles.body_text:
Nikita and Olga Belov say they will be persecuted on return to Moscow but are yet to convince Finnish authorities

A Russian family faces deportation from Finland after repeatedly being denied asylum – despite the threat of arrest, imprisonment and potential torture for their pro-Ukrainian activism.

Nikita and Olga Belov fled their homeland in 2022 after attracting the attention of Russian authorities – including military summons, threatening messages and attempts to locate them – after expressing opposition to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Nikita, 25, left his engineering job at a research institute in Moscow specialising in metallurgical technologies after finding out the work he was doing was connected to the Russian war effort.

Since arriving in Finland on visas, Nikita and his mother, Olga, 55, a nurse anaesthetist, have been vocal supporters of Ukraine and public in their active support and coordination of aid sent to the country and its armed forces. But the Finnish immigration service told the mother and son that despite this they face “no real risk” if they return to Russia.

In April, they were detained by Finnish authorities pending deportation. They were later released after a court intervention but are now awaiting a decision that could result in them being deported within weeks.

The Belov case is understood to be one of many of Russians being denied asylum in neighbouring Finland where legal experts deem their future risk and human rights have not been sufficiently assessed.

Between February 2022 and June 2026, the Finnish immigration service deported 1,039 Russians according to official statistics: the most of any nationality. During the same period, 1,109 of 1,342 Russians were refused entry to Finland in connection with a negative asylum application.

Since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Finland’s relationship with its neighbour has shifted drastically. Previously, Finland was a popular tourism destination for Russians and there were several well-used border crossings. It has since indefinitely closed its entire border, accusing Moscow of directing asylum seekers to Finland in a “hybrid operation”.

Russia has also expanded its military bases on the border, while Nato – which Finland joined in 2023 – has conducted training exercises in the country.

Nikita said his problems in Russia started when he realised that his boss had lied when he had told him that the project he was working on was not linked to the war effort. When he tried to come off the project, he said his boss threatened him with arrest or being sent to the frontline.

“After that I realised I cannot leave this job without consequences and that we had to think about the situation,” Nikita said. His mother, he said, was then called by the military to ask about him and their house was visited by police. They soon came to the conclusion that they had no option but to leave Russia. “Now we realise if we come back we will be arrested immediately and go to jail and be tortured,” Nikita said.

In Finland they have volunteered at their local Ukraine centre and contributed to humanitarian support, including help for first aid, food, clothes, Starlink equipment and a 3D printer, for which they received a video thank you message from Ukrainian soldiers.

“We try to adapt, try to support Ukraine, try to state our opinion, because it is very important to help Ukraine. Help them strike back,” he said.

The mother and son first applied for asylum in Finland in 2022 but it was refused, after which they unsuccessfully appealed. This year they applied again and were refused and were sent a deportation order. They were then placed in a detention centre awaiting deportation but after a court intervention were allowed to go home before a final decision. “There were all bad things in our minds. It was like the start of torture because it was a totally traumatic experience,” Nikita said. “At the time we really tried to prepare for our death.”

Since then they have suffered with their mental health and undergone panic attacks as they wait for the decision of the court.

Their lawyer, who requested not to be named for security reasons, said the Belovs are very likely to be at risk if they are deported to Russia. Nikita’s work history will also put them at risk, the lawyer said. In a previous role he said he had access to confidential government information.

While it has long been difficult to get asylum in Finland, the lawyer said that recent changes on the border and to asylum procedure, including reduced access to legal aid, has made it even harder. “It’s even more difficult to get refugee status, even with clear political opinion showing. We really have to fight these cases to get the status that was earlier easier to get.”

The political activist and Putin critic Bill Browder, who is the head of the Global Magnitsky Justice Campaign, said the case is “a defining test of Europe’s commitment to protecting those who have risked everything to oppose Putin’s war”.

Browder, whose friend and lawyer Sergei Magnitsky died at the hands of Putin’s regime, added: “If people who refused to support aggression, openly opposed the regime, and now face persecution are denied protection, it could create a dangerous precedent that discourages others from taking a stand against authoritarianism.”

A Finnish immigration service spokesperson said it could not comment on individual cases.

Antti Lehtinen, the director of the department for international protection, which is part of the Finnish immigration service, added: “The situation of each applicant is assessed individually, taking into account their personal circumstances.

“For example, opposition to the war in Ukraine and related activities may constitute grounds for persecution based on political opinion. If we assess that a person’s political opinion or activities place them at risk of persecution or serious harm in Russia, they will be granted international protection.”

articles.title: Israel announces tender for 627 settler units in occupied West Bank
articles.excerpt: Israeli authorities have issued a tender for 627 new housing units in the Kochav Yaakov settlement in the occupied West Bank, according to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (...
articles.body_text:
Israeli authorities have issued a tender for 627 new housing units in the Kochav Yaakov settlement in the occupied West Bank, according to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (CRRC).

The Israel Land Authority on Thursday published the tender for the project, which will be built on land in the Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate, the commission said on Saturday.

Israel set November 30 as the deadline for construction companies to submit bids, moving the project from planning to construction just 15 months after it was first approved, it said.

CRRC slammed the expansion, saying it is designed to “deepen the separation between Jerusalem and its Palestinian surroundings”.

The illegal Israeli settlement of Kochav Yaakov sits between northern Jerusalem and the twin cities of Ramallah and el-Bireh, within a cluster of settlements Israel administers under the name “Binyamin”.

According to CRRC, the new project covers 253.7 dunams (25.37 hectares or about 63 acres) and was approved by Israeli authorities on April 27, 2025.

It says the tender marks the transition from planning to the “marketing and implementation” stage of settlement construction, with the new units expected to expand the illegal settlement’s built-up area and strengthen its links to nearby settlements and access roads. It added that the decision reflects growing investment in settlements’ economic infrastructure, not just housing.

The Israeli decision is one of several the commission has tracked this year aimed at tightening Israel’s illegal control and pressure on the Palestinian region.

According to CRRC, Israeli authorities have made 12 illegal settlement tenders in the first half of 2026, including 1,138 housing units concentrated in five main settlements, alongside a separate wave of tenders for industrial zones, offices, nursing homes and tourism facilities.

Illegal settlement expansion and settler violence have surged dramatically across the occupied West Bank this year. Palestinian monitors have recorded more than 11,000 attacks by Israeli forces and settlers across the West Bank since January 2026.

United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has repeatedly said Israeli settlements have “no legal validity” and constitute a “flagrant violation” of international law.

A 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion deemed Israel’s continued occupation of Palestinian territory unlawful.

articles.title: 'Harry Potter' actor says OnlyFans videos earned her more than her entire acting career

"Harry Potter" star, Jessie Cave, is opening up about how joining OnlyF...
articles.body_text:
Shannon Elizabeth opens up about joining OnlyFans, exploring boundaries and finding empowerment during a major life transition.

"Harry Potter" star, Jessie Cave, is opening up about how joining OnlyFans "saved" her and her family.

During a recent interview with The Times, the 39-year-old actress shared how much money she's made from the subscription-based social media platform, noting she has "earned more, easily, than my entire acting career within one year."

"I thought I’d make five grand, be on it for a few months, and it would buy me time to work out what we’re going to do," she shared. "But it’s now been over a year and a half, and it’s genuinely saved our lives."

The actress charges subscribers $6 a month for non-explicit "hair content," which includes videos of her fully-clothed, brushing her hair while dressed in costumes, braiding it, tying it in a ponytail or anything else her followers want to see.

"Harry Potter" star Jessie Cave says she made more money in one year on OnlyFans than her entire acting career. (©Warner Bros./courtesy Everett Collection; Kate Green/Getty Images, File)

‘AMERICAN PIE’ ALUM SHANNON ELIZABETH TURNS TO ONLYFANS FOR ‘FRESH START’ AS DIVORCE UNFOLDS

Cave had her big break in Hollywood playing Lavender Brown in the final three films in the Harry Potter franchise, from 2009 to 2011. She later appeared as a guest in a number of projects, including "Black Mirror" and "Industry," and worked on the stage.

Her decision to transition to OnlyFans came after she was rejected by a callback audition, and her need to support herself and her four children, who she shares with her fiancé, Alfie Brown, admitting "it was a point of complete desperation."

"I couldn’t go and, say, work in a supermarket because I can’t afford the childcare, and also I don’t want people shouting Harry Potter spells at me as I work at Tesco," she explained. "I could retrain, but I can’t afford to do a degree. I had a breakdown and I thought, ‘That’s it with acting, I give up.’ But also we have no money."

According to The Times, she earned roughly $20,200 in just one day on the platform.

Cave shared she made around $20,000 in just one day on the platform. (Mike Marsland/WireImage, File)

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Her one rule when creating her content is that her "hair is the main character," she said. "That's how I justify it.

"And yes, [OnlyFans] is largely porn. But there are cooking videos, tarot readings, personal training — it’s just all done with a sexy edge," she added. "It is about wanting some kind of gaze… I wear baggy T-shirts on stage, I’ve never posted a bikini shot, I wear huge glasses. For so long I’ve just been this quirky figure. After having four kids and feeling invisible for so long, that was really appealing to me."

Cave said that she can foresee other artists turning to "other platforms to make money when they’re not being an artist."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Cave first opened up about joining OnlyFans in March 2025, saying she would try it for a year. (Keith Mayhew/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images, File)

She first spoke out about starting her OnlyFans account in March 2025, writing on her personal Substack account that she started the account in an effort to "get out of debt."

"I’ll try for one year," Cave wrote. "My aim? To get the house safe, cover the arsenic/lead wallpaper, build a new roof etc. My aim? To get out of debt. My aim? To empower myself? To prove to those in the past who have misjudged me that I’m not so sweet? To put time into something I never invested in before: self-love."

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Paris tells e-scooter riders to wear safety gear or face fines
articles.excerpt:
The new rules apply to privately owned electric scooters, as rental versions have been banned

Electric scooter riders in Paris face being fined if they fail to comply with new safety rules, as police...
articles.body_text:
The new rules apply to privately owned electric scooters, as rental versions have been banned

Electric scooter riders in Paris face being fined if they fail to comply with new safety rules, as police try to curb the number of accidents in the French capital.

Some 79 people were killed in e-scooter accidents last year, a sharp rise from the 45 who died the year prior, police said on Saturday, citing figures from France's road safety watchdog.

In a bid to address "the concerning rise in serious and fatal accidents" involving the motorised vehicles, it is now mandatory for riders to wear a helmet and high-vis vest on public roads.

Those who don't face fines of €135 (£129) for failing to wear an approved helmet, and smaller fines of €35 (£30) for not wearing a vest or retro-reflectors.

The regulations also cover other electric transportation devices, such as electric unicycles and hoverboards.

Official figures show that around 1,100 people were injured in e-scooter accidents in Paris last year, a rise of 33% on the year before.

This is despite Paris banning rental e-scooters in 2023 over safety concerns, while allowing privately owned ones to continue being ridden.

E-scooters remain popular with the commuters in the city, where narrow roads can become congested.

Private e-scooter ownership in France is the highest in Europe, according to the EU.

Some 2.5 million people owned e-scooters there as of 2023, with hundreds of thousands more purchased since. Many of these are thought to be in the capital, though exact figures are not kept.

Existing rules in Paris ban e-scooter riding for under-14s, prohibit carrying passengers and set a maximum speed limits of 25km/h (16mph).

Helmets and high-visibility vests are already mandatory in several French regions, including Seine-et-Marne, Alpes-Maritimes and Vaucluse.

Paris was one of the first cities to adopt e-scooters, but growing concern about dangerous driving and obstructing pavements led to for-hire e-scooters being outlawed.

Their fate was decided in a city-wide referendum, which saw 90% voters back a rental ban even though only 8% of eligible voters turned out.

Other European cities have moved to ban rental e-scooters in recent years, with Madrid outlawing them in 2024 and Brussels announcing it will follow suit in June.

articles.title: Heartbroken fathers find divine hope in secret notes left by girls killed in Camp Mystic flood
articles.excerpt: Ryan Dewitt, Wade Lytal, and Cole Naylor join host Kayleigh McEnany to share the powerful faith and legacy of their daughters who passed away in the tragic 2021 Camp Mystic flash flood. The grieving f...
articles.body_text:
Ryan Dewitt, Wade Lytal, and Cole Naylor join host Kayleigh McEnany to share the powerful faith and legacy of their daughters who passed away in the tragic 2021 Camp Mystic flash flood. The grieving fathers discuss their podcast, 'Heaven Meets Earth,' and how their families find comfort through God and scripture. They reflect on the girls' diaries and unwavering belief during this emotional interview.

One year after flash flooding at Camp Mystic took 28 lives, three fathers are sharing how their young daughters’ private faith continues to lift their families.

Speaking on "Saturday in America," Ryan DeWitt, Wade Lytal and Cole Naylor shared how their daughters' deep-rooted faith has sustained them through tragedy. DeWitt and Lytal said they found journals their daughters left behind filled with Bible verses, prayers and messages to God, bringing them comfort as they grieved.

"We knew that she was deeply rooted in her faith, but she wasn't outward about it or braggadocious about it. She just felt it. She felt very deeply," Ryan DeWitt said of his daughter Molly, who was 9 years old when she died in the floods.

"She just had the biggest heart, and we taught her as much as we could, but there was certainly something else at play, and that was her faith, and it was comforting. As difficult as those days were and still are, it's comforting to know how close she was to God," he added.

DEVASTATED MOTHER BLAMES SOFT-ON-CRIME POLICIES AFTER CAREER CRIMINAL IS CHARGED IN SON’S DEATH

Composite photo showing Kellyanne Lytal, Molly DeWitt and Wynne Naylor, three of the young victims of the Camp Mystic flood in July 2025. (Photos provided by the Lytal, DeWitt, and Naylor families)

The fathers each recalled moments when they learned more about the depth of their daughters’ faith. DeWitt shared that Molly kept notebooks under her bed filled with hand-drawn crosses and Bible verses, including one page that read, "I can do anything through Christ."

Wade Lytal recalled entering the bedroom of his 8-year-old daughter, Kellyanne, weeks after the tragedy and pulling open a drawer to find a journal entry that read, "Jesus I love you. Thank you for dying on the cross for all of our sins."

"I think that's the most important responsibility that we have as parents is making sure that, you know, our children are raised to love the Lord," Lytal said.

YOUNG TEXAS CAMP SURVIVOR DESCRIBES HARROWING MOMENT SHE PREPARED FOR WORST DURING DEADLY FLOOD

Lytal said that after the flood, he no longer believes in coincidences and views finding her journal as a gift during a dark time.

"We were going through her things and the first drawer I pulled open, that was the notebook that was in there. We saw what she wrote, and it did bring some comfort to us in a very, very dark moment in our life," he said.

Alli Naylor, whose daughter Wynne Naylor died in the July 2025 Camp Mystic flood, listens during a hearing at the Travis County Courthouse on March 4, 2026, in Austin, Texas. The hearing involved an effort to block the camp from reopening and halt construction while litigation over the deadly flood continues. (Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

Cole Naylor, father of 8-year-old Wynne, emphasized that reliance on daily prayer has carried his family through the loss. He shared that he refuses to speak about his daughter in the past tense, standing firm in the promise that they will be reunited.

"Our girls are very much alive," Naylor said. "They are more alive than any one of us are. Alive in heaven, we don't get to see them, we don't get to touch them, we don’t get to kiss them anymore, but they're with us, and we will see them again."

CAMP MYSTIC PULLS PLAN TO REOPEN THIS SUMMER AFTER BACKLASH FROM GRIEVING FAMILIES

In April, Camp Mystic announced it would not be reopening for the 2026 season despite having previously planned to welcome hundreds of girls back to the property.

Debris covers the area of Camp Mystic in Hunt, Texas, July 7, 2025, after a flash flood swept through the area. (AP Photo/Eli Hartman)

"No administrative process or summer season should move forward while families continue to grieve," the camp said in a statement.

"This decision is intended to remove any doubt that Camp Mystic has heard the concerns expressed by grieving families, members of the Texas House and Senate investigating committees and citizens across our state. Respect for those voices requires that we step back now."

Madison Colombo is a writer for Fox News Digital’s Flash, Media, and Culture team, covering daily breaking news and trending topics with an award-winning background in broadcast and digital journalism.

articles.title: WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert sends trans inclusion memo after Enes Freedom, Royce White announcements
articles.excerpt:
Former NBA first-round pick Royce White told Fox News Digital that he will be declaring for the 2027 WNBA Draft, just hours after fellow former NBA player Enes Kanter said he would.

WNBA Commissioner...
articles.body_text:
Former NBA first-round pick Royce White told Fox News Digital that he will be declaring for the 2027 WNBA Draft, just hours after fellow former NBA player Enes Kanter said he would.

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert sent a letter to teams on Friday addressing concerns over the inclusion of transgender athletes in the league as two former NBA players announced their intentions to declare for the next WNBA Draft.

"I know many of you have received questions in recent weeks regarding transgender athlete participation in women’s basketball, and I expect this topic will continue to receive significant attention," Engelbert wrote in the memo, per The Associated Press.

"I wanted to reach out to share how we are approaching these conversations at the league office and to thank those of you who have responded to questions from the media with thoughtfulness and professionalism."

THE WNBA HAS LIMITED OPTIONS AFTER TWO MEN DECLARED FOR THE DRAFT, AND THOSE OPTIONS AREN'T GREAT

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert speaks prior to the 2026 WNBA Draft at The Shed on April 13, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images)

Engelbert went on to call the debate "nuanced."

"We recognize that this is a complex and nuanced topic, and we will continue to have important conversations with all of you and the Players Association in the weeks and months ahead," Engelbert said in the memo. "We also plan to convene additional discussions and offer listening sessions for any team leaders who would like to participate. Your perspectives and feedback are invaluable, and I appreciate those who have already reached out to share their thoughts."

Engelbert's memo came on the same day that two former NBA pros, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, said they plan to declare for the 2027 WNBA Draft. The announcements became the top trending topic across social media, as sports fans across the world mocked the WNBA for its policy that doesn't clearly define who is allowed to play in the league based on genetic sex.

The WNBA players’ association also released a statement on social media Friday that emphasized diversity and inclusion while saying the group "will not be used as political pawns."

WNBPA ISSUES STATEMENT EMBRACING DIVERSITY AND INCLUSION AMID TRANS ATHLETE DEBATE IN WOMEN'S SPORTS

"We embrace justice equity, diversity, and inclusion," the statement read. "Those are the values that unite this Union and allow it to protect women’s sports while creating transformational change. Hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people, only fuel fear, division, and harm. We will continue to have hard conversations. But we will not be used as political pawns."

The entire WNBA has become the epicenter for the national debate on trans athletes in women's sports in recent weeks after Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham, a fan favorite teammate of Caitlin Clark, revealed her stance supporting the protection of women's sports in an ESPN interview in July.

Since then, four head coaches have gone on record with responses to questions about the issues, with two of them, Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve and Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase, appearing to support the inclusion of trans athletes in women's sports.

Now, Kanter and White's entrance into the conversation has amplified the discussion across the sports realm, and it appears that Engelbert now has to address the issues.

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

articles.title: Everyone wants what one minor league baseball team put out as a hilarious tribute to the Carolina Hurricanes
articles.excerpt:
Megan Rapinoe's latest ridiculous rant on Sophie Cunningham and RIley Gaines makes it clear she doesn't get the real issues in women's sports

That's because, while at the top levels they're often wor...
articles.body_text:
Megan Rapinoe's latest ridiculous rant on Sophie Cunningham and RIley Gaines makes it clear she doesn't get the real issues in women's sports

That's because, while at the top levels they're often worried about taking political stands to the point that the WNBA is like, "Meh, we're not going to slam the door on letting fellas play just yet," minor league teams have to focus on putting butts in seats. The best way to do that is with fun promotions.

So, that's what we're getting from one minor league ballclub's unintentionally — or, I think more likely, intentionally — hilarious tribute sweaters to the Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes.

A minor league baseball team's jersey giveaway to honor the Carolina Hurricanes is getting attention for a very funny reason. (Photo by Bruce Bennett/Getty Images)

The Fayetteville Woodpeckers — the Single-A affiliate of the Houston Astros — don't play too far from Raleigh, home of the Hurricanes. So, it makes sense that they would want to bathe in the warm glow of a Stanley Cup win.

And the best way to do that? This phenomenal jersey!

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Imagine wearing that jersey outside a 100-mile radius of Fayetteville. There's a good chance no one will have any clue why you own a hockey sweater that says "PECKERS" across the front.

And, frankly, I don't think it's anyone's business. You do you, pal.

I also get the feeling at least one kid will have to take a detour to the principal's office or flip their jersey inside-out in a couple of weeks when school gets underway. I promise you, some humorless school marm who only knows baseball from Ernest Lawrence Thayer's 1888 poem, "Casey at the Bat," won't get it (but will somehow still understand that "pecker" is a slang term for male genitalia).

The Fayetteville Woodpeckers — the Single-A affiliate of the Houston Astros — have a giveaway jersey honoring the Carolina Hurricanes that is going to be in high demand. (Andrew Craft / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

But the public response has been about as good as the organization could hope for.

You rarely do anything on the internet that garners universal acclaim — trust me; I know — but I think the Peckers sweater may have done it.

Unfortunately, unless the plans change, only the first 1,350 fans at the Woodpeckers' game on August 15 will be able to cop them.

articles.title: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to what the Senate did and didn’t do overnight
articles.excerpt: Fox News' chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the Senate's race to clear a packed agenda before the recess, including President Donald Trump's demand for a vote on the 'Save Amer...
articles.body_text:
Fox News' chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the Senate's race to clear a packed agenda before the recess, including President Donald Trump's demand for a vote on the 'Save America Act' amid legislative hurdles.

The Senate wrapped up its summer session at 4:57 a.m. ET.

Senators knocked two major items off their checklist. They confirmed Todd Blanche as the nation’s 88th Attorney General.

They also approved a bipartisan interim spending bill that likely goes a long way toward preventing a government shutdown in October.

But nearly as important as what senators accomplished is what didn’t get done.

The U.S. Capitol Building seen at sunset. (Emma Woodhead/Fox News Digital)

The Senate did not stay in session and attempt to pass the SAVE America Act.

In fact, there was not even procedural stunting by the pro-SAVE America Act Republicans, who advocated blowing up the August recess.

TRUMP PUMPS BRAKES ON SENATE BUDGET PLAN, DELAYING GOP SAVE AMERICA PUSH

Moreover, the Senate did not take a vote on a budget framework which could enable them to eventually tack on some election integrity measures – and pass them at a later date in a bill not subject to a filibuster.

Expect some conservatives to rail against the Senate for not working this out.

Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio., speaks at the U.S. Capitol. The Senate blocked his voter ID measure in a test vote ahead of the August recess. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The SAVE America Act continues to lack votes. However, advocates of the bill can use the decision by the Senate to leave town without passing it as an opportunity to apply pressure on its opponents.

That said, the Senate did take a test vote on a more narrow voter ID bill backed by Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. The Senate blocked that bill.

But the test vote got Democrats on the record for opposing it. And giving Husted a vote on his measure was a tactical move to boost his chances in a competitive race this fall against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio.

The Senate did not take a test vote on the bipartisan bill to regulate money for intercollegiate athletics – despite the endorsement by the Big 10 and SEC.

PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT STALLS IN OVERNIGHT SENATE SHOWDOWN, VOTE PUSHED TO SEPTEMBER AFTER CHAOTIC EVENING

In fact, President Trump even implored the Senate to stay in session in August to pass the bill authored by Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the top Democrat on the panel.

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said the Protect College Sports Act will be "one of our first orders of business" in September. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

The legislation was beset by an internecine fight among Republicans about whether the legislation kept men from competing in women’s sports.

The President published a full-throated endorsement of the legislation Friday night, declaring that the measure did go far enough. "Anyone who tells you otherwise is lying," wrote the President on Truth Social.

In an overnight statement, Cruz said that the bill was still in play.

"The good news is that when the Senate returns in September, the Protect College Sports Act will be one of our first orders of business, having locked in a vote," said Cruz.

However, no vote is officially secured on the Senate docket.

But what about a test vote on a bill to regulate cryptocurrency?

It was thought that the Senate might pursue that bill in the closing days of the summer session. But the differences were just too wide to close.

However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., teed up a procedural vote on cryptocurrency for September 15.

Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

articles.title: University of Michigan plans to shield 2027 freshman letter grades from transcripts in new mental health plan
articles.excerpt:
‘Fox News Saturday Night’ host Jimmy Failla discusses the University of Michigan's decision to drop letter grades for some 2027 freshmen on ‘America Reports.’

Freshmen at the University of Michigan n...
articles.body_text:
‘Fox News Saturday Night’ host Jimmy Failla discusses the University of Michigan's decision to drop letter grades for some 2027 freshmen on ‘America Reports.’

Freshmen at the University of Michigan next year are set to get a semester-long break from having letter grades appear on their transcripts, as school officials look for new ways to combat the "mental health crisis" affecting higher education.

Starting in fall 2027, incoming first-year students enrolled in the public research university's College of Literature, Science, and the Arts (LSA) will have their first-semester grades designated as pass or no credit on their transcripts in an attempt to "curb the mental health crisis unfolding among college-aged individuals," according to the university.

"Our goal is to help first-year students acclimate to the demands of college and allow intrinsic motivations to guide personally meaningful academic journeys — core elements of a liberal arts and sciences education," the statement continued.

EDUCATION SECRETARY LINDA MCMAHON RIPS CALIFORNIA TRANS ATHLETE ‘COMPROMISE,’ TELLS NEWSOM TO ‘PICK A SIDE’

University of Michigan students walk on the UM campus in Ann Arbor, Mich., on April 3, 2025. (Bill Pugliano/Getty Images)

The LSA, which is the largest of the university’s 19 colleges and serves approximately 19,700 undergraduate students, will provide students with their letter grades throughout the semester — but will not include the final average on their transcripts.

Transcripts will instead show a "P" for pass or "NC" for no credit.

The covered grades will not be factored into students' grade point averages, a move university officials say will give first-year students greater freedom to explore academically.

"For example, they can explore a subject that may not come easily to them or take a course in a new field without the fear that a low grade may have long-term consequences," the university added. " LSA is investing in students’ well-being and growth by fostering a culture of connection and collaboration — rather than competition."

HARVARD FACULTY VOTE TO CAP 'A' GRADES AT 20% IN SWEEPING EFFORT TO COMBAT DECADES OF GRADE INFLATION

A University of Michigan flag hangs on the Michigan Union building on the school's campus in Ann Arbor, Mich., on Monday, July 28, 2025. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Under the new policy, university officials will keep students' first-semester letter grades internally for administrative purposes, including academic advising, potential academic awards and scholarships, internship and other professional applications, athletic eligibility, compliance reporting, degree progress and financial aid determinations.

Additionally, the 2027 policy only applies to incoming freshmen enrolled in the LSA, with school officials adding there is no opt-out option.

"An opt-in structure would defeat the purpose of facilitating students’ transition to campus, supporting mental health and well-being, and bolstering intrinsic motivations for learning," the university said.

Michigan is now the latest in a small group of schools throughout the country that have chosen to enact similar policies, including Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Swarthmore College and the California Institute of Technology.

CALIFORNIA PROFESSOR ARGUES NEED FOR 'OBJECTIVE MEASURES' AFTER STATE DROPS ACT/SAT REQUIREMENT

A student walks through the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Mich., on Monday, July 28, 2025. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

While the program is aimed at supporting students’ mental health, psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert believes it runs the risk of doing more harm than good.

"We’re raising a generation of students to believe that discomfort is dangerous," Alpert, author of "Therapy Nation," told Fox News Digital. "It isn’t. A bad grade can be upsetting, embarrassing and stressful. That’s not a mental health emergency. That’s college."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Alpert went on to add that while the policy was created to relieve students of the pressure and stress from the first semester of college, it could actually risk harming their preparedness for life outside of the learning environment.

"This is therapy culture invading the classroom. We’ve spent years turning normal human emotions into symptoms. Stress becomes a mental health issue," Alpert said, adding, "College should be one of the places where young people discover that they’re tougher than they think."

"A bad grade isn't psychological harm," Alpert continued. "Sometimes it's the wake-up call a student needs."

Fox News Digital reached out to the University of Michigan for comment.

Julia Bonavita is a media and culture writer for Fox News Digital, and a Fox Flight Team drone pilot. You can follow her at @juliabonavita13 on all platforms and send story tips to julia.bonavita@fox.com.

articles.title: Navy says it is spending 25% more time monitoring Russian vessels around UK waters
articles.excerpt:
Warning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North Sea

The Royal Navy has warned of increasing Russian activity around the UK’s waters a...
articles.body_text:
Warning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North Sea

The Royal Navy has warned of increasing Russian activity around the UK’s waters after it spent 21 days in July monitoring Moscow’s ships.

Naval operations to monitor Russian vessels increased by 25% last month compared with the previous year, with warships making repeated voyages through the strait of Dover and the North Sea.

Offshore patrol vessels HMS Tyne, HMS Mersey and HMS Severn, alongside Wildcat helicopters from 815 Naval Air Squadron and Merlin submarine-hunting aircraft, were deployed throughout the month to shadow Russian frigates Neustrashimy and Admiral Grigorovich, which are tasked with escorting so-called “shadow fleet” tankers.

Last month, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in its annual report that Royal Navy vessels had been “activated” 116 times in the year to March 2026, shadowing 61 Russian warships and 28 merchant vessels around the UK’s waters.

This reflected a 30% increase in Russian naval activity over the previous two years and included operations to deter the spy ship Yantar, which was spotted near undersea cables off Scotland last November.

Vladimir Putin has been accused of using the Kremlin’s shadow fleet of ageing vessels to evade international sanctions on its oil and fund the war in Ukraine.

The increase in Russian naval activity follows the seizure of the tanker Smyrtos by Royal Marines in June, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel.

The MoD said the diversion of ships from Russia to escort shadow fleet vessels meant the country was “using up valuable operational capacity to constantly guard cargo”.

The UK has already imposed sanctions on more than 500 vessels, and Russia’s oil and gas revenues fell by 24% year on year in 2025.

HMS Tyne was also tasked with monitoring the Neustrashimy as it carried out a live-firing exercise outside British and French waters on 20 July.

Another ship, the frigate HMS Somerset, has been involved in monitoring Russian activity in the North Atlantic as part of a four-month Nato deployment searching for submarines, alongside helicopters from the Navy’s Fleet Air Arm.

Somerset’s commanding officer, Cmdr Matt Millyard, said on Saturday: “This deployment demonstrates exactly what the Royal Navy exists to do: protect the UK and our allies from wherever our interests are threatened.

“I am immensely proud of every single member of the ship’s company for what we have achieved over the past four months.”
